exp.0:0:
In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem and laid siege to it. The word "besieged" in the verse above means that he surrounded it with his army to attack it.

The account is in the book of Daniel, which tells how the exile of Judah began, around 605 B.C. according to most scholars. Jeremiah 25:1 speaks of the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and this is explained in several ways, probably because of different ways of counting the years. The following verse makes clear that it was the Lord who gave Jehoiakim into Nebuchadnezzar's hands, not only the strength of Babylon.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, God has not lost control. You can trust Him, even in difficult times you do not understand.
exp.0:1:
This verse tells that God allowed Jehoiakim, king of Judah, to fall into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar. Part of the sacred objects of the temple also fell into his power. The Babylonian king took those objects to the house of his god and kept them in the treasure house.

Daniel is not the one speaking here; the account is told by a narrator. It wants to explain that the defeat of Jerusalem was not only a triumph of Babylon: the Lord gave him over. This prepares the story of Daniel and his friends, young men taken to live in a foreign land.

For today: when things fall apart and it seems that everything is lost, remember that God is still sovereign. Even in difficult times, you can keep trusting Him and remain faithful wherever you are.
exp.0:2:
This verse tells us that King Nebuchadnezzar gave an order to Ashpenaz, the master of his eunuchs, that is, of his trusted officials in the palace. He was to bring some young men from Israel, from the royal family and from the nobles.

The narrator explains how Babylon, after conquering Jerusalem, carried off treasures from the temple and also people. The king wanted to train capable young men to serve in his court. Many understand this as a way of bringing them into Babylonian culture. The Bible does not say here how many there were or what their exact ages were.

Even when everything seems lost, God is still at work. These young men were taken against their will, but God would keep them in mind. Today, if you are in a place you did not choose, you can trust that God is with you and remain faithful there.
exp.0:5:
This verse names four young men from the tribe of Judah who were chosen from among the captives: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. They were part of the group selected to serve in the palace of the king of Babylon.

The narrator tells how King Nebuchadnezzar commanded that capable young men be chosen to be educated for three years in the language and learning of the Chaldeans. Judah had been carried into exile. The text wants us to know the Hebrew names of these young men before Babylon changes their names, since those names connected them to the God of Israel.

Even far from home and under pressure, we can keep our identity and our faithfulness to God. Today, in a workplace or study where others think differently, we can remember who we are in God and act with respect, but with firmness.
exp.0:9:
Here the chief of the palace officials answers Daniel that he cannot grant his request. He is afraid of the king, who was the one who ordered what to eat and drink. If the king sees them thinner or sadder than the other young men, he could have him put to death. The phrase about putting his head in danger means risking his life. The eunuchs were the court officials, and the old spelling of a word is simply the one we use today.

The one speaking is the chief of the officials of Babylon. Daniel, a young exile, had decided not to defile himself with the king's food. God had given him favor before this man, and yet he feels fear. His answer is not mockery; it is real concern.

For today: when we do what is right, sometimes others hold us back out of fear. We can answer them with respect, without fighting, and look for a kind solution, trusting that God works even in the doubts of others.
exp.0:11:
Daniel asks Melzar, the official in charge of the young men, to test them for ten days. He asks only for vegetables to eat and water to drink. "Vegetables" here refers to foods that come from sowing, such as grains and greens.

Daniel speaks in Babylon, where he and his friends were taken captive. The king had ordered that they be given his food and his wine. Daniel did not want to defile himself with them; the text does not spell out all his reasons, and several have been proposed, such as motives tied to the law or to idolatry. Melzar feared for his life, so Daniel proposes a brief and reasonable test.

Today, when you want to be faithful to God in a difficult setting, act with respect and wisdom. Propose simple solutions, without rebellion, and trust that God will look after you.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that the time of preparation the king had set had come to an end. Then the chief of the court officials, who was the official in charge of the young men, brought them before Nebuchadnezzar. Here the word for these officials refers to royal court officers, and the word for chief means head or person in charge.

The book tells, in the third person, how Daniel and his three friends, young Jews taken to Babylon, were trained for three years to serve the king. They had asked not to defile themselves with the king's food, and God gave them wisdom. Now the moment of the examination before the king arrives, which will show the results.

For today: faithfulness in small things and in hidden places prepares the way for great things. Stay firm in your convictions during times of waiting and formation, trusting that God knows when to bring you to where He wants you.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that King Nebuchadnezzar personally spoke with the four young Hebrews, and among all the candidates he found no one like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. That is why they stood before the king, meaning they entered his service.

It is part of the account in the book of Daniel. The young men had been taken captive to Babylon and trained for three years to serve in the court. The narrator tells us that God gave them wisdom and understanding. When that time was over, the king examined them. Earlier, they had decided not to defile themselves with the king's food, and the text presents their good outcome as the work of God.

For today: you can be faithful to God even in an environment that does not share your faith. Do your work with excellence and humility, trusting that God is the one who gives the ability and opens the doors.
exp.0:19:
This verse tells us that in every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king questioned them, the four young men proved to be far better than all the magicians and astrologers in his kingdom. The phrase "ten times better" probably points to a very great superiority rather than an exact measurement.

The narrator is the author of the book of Daniel, who recounts what happened in Babylon. Daniel and his companions, taken captive from Judah, had been trained for three years to serve King Nebuchadnezzar. When the training ended, the king examined them himself. The text credits their outstanding ability to God, who had given them knowledge and wisdom (1:17).

For today: do your work or your studies with excellence and integrity, even in settings that do not share your faith, and recognize that your abilities are a gift from God.
exp.1:1:
Then, troubled by his dreams, King Nebuchadnezzar ordered that all his advisers be called: the magicians, the astrologers, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans. He wanted them to tell him what he had dreamed. The verse says that they were to shew the king his dreams, which means to make them known to him, or to explain them. They came and stood before the king.

The narrator describes the scene in Babylon. The king had great power, but he could not sleep or calm his mind. So he turned to the wise men of his court, who were believed to be able to interpret messages from the spiritual world. The text sets up the contrast with Daniel, who will later acknowledge that only God reveals mysteries.

When something troubles us, we often look for answers in many places before turning to God. Today we can pray first, asking for wisdom and peace, and then seek good counsel.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that the Chaldean wise men once again ask the king to tell them his dream. They promise that, if he does, they will give him the verse. "Servants" here means the king's attendants, and "interpretation" means the verse or meaning of the dream.

These are the king Nebuchadnezzar's advisers, who were wise men, magicians, and astrologers of Babylon. The king had a dream that troubled him, but he had forgotten it, or so he indicates when he says he has lost what he dreamed. He demands that they tell him the dream and its meaning, under threat of death. They insist on what is customary: that he tell the dream first. The king suspects they are stalling for time.

For today: when we face situations that exceed our ability, it is wise to acknowledge our limits. These wise men could not do the impossible, and this prepares the way for God to reveal what only He knows. Let us ask Him for wisdom with humility.
exp.1:8:
Here the king Nebuchadnezzar speaks very angrily to his wise men. He tells them that if they do not make known to him the dream and its meaning, they will receive only one punishment: death. The word "decree" in the verse means an order or judgment. He thinks they are preparing false and deceitful words to gain time, while the time changes, that is, while the circumstances shift.

The king speaks to the magicians, enchanters, and Chaldeans of Babylon. He had had a dream that troubled him. He distrusted them and wanted a test: if they could tell him the dream, he could trust their interpretation. They answered that this was impossible for any human being. In this way the scene is set for God, through Daniel, to show his power.

Today we can remember that human wisdom has limits. When we face something that is beyond us, instead of pretending or looking for excuses, let us come humbly to God, who knows what is hidden.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that King Nebuchadnezzar became very angry and gave the order to kill all the wise men of Babylon. The words for anger and fury in the verse are rage and wrath. The "wise men" were the king's advisers, magicians, and astrologers.

The king had been troubled by a dream. He demanded that the wise men tell him the dream and also its meaning. They answered that no one on earth could do this, and that only the gods could. The king saw their answer as an excuse and responded with violence. Daniel and his companions were also included in the order, even though they did not yet know anything about the matter.

When someone in authority acts in anger, it can cause unjust harm. Daniel shows us another way: he spoke with wisdom and calm. When you face tension, pause, think, and respond with respect, trusting that God can guide you.
exp.1:13:
Daniel spoke to Arioch with wisdom and good judgment. Arioch was the captain of the king's guard, and he had already gone out to execute the wise men of Babylon.

King Nebuchadnezzar was furious because no wise man could tell him his dream or its meaning. He had ordered that all of them be put to death, and Daniel and his companions were also going to die. Daniel did not respond with panic or arrogance, but with respect and calm questions. In this way he got a hearing and opened a door to ask for time.

When we find ourselves in the middle of a crisis or tension, we can pause, speak calmly, and ask God for wisdom before we react. A calm and respectful word can open paths that fear would close.
exp.1:16:
Then Daniel went quickly to his house and told the matter to his three friends: Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The word "matter" here means the situation at hand, and his "friends" were his close companions. (Their names in Babylon were Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.)

King Nebuchadnezzar had ordered that all the wise men of Babylon be put to death, because none of them could tell him his dream or its meaning. Daniel and his friends were in danger. Daniel had gained some time with the king, and now he brought the news to his friends so they could pray together.

When we face a great trouble, we do not have to carry it alone. Daniel turned to his faithful friends to pray together. Today we can do the same: share our need with trusted brothers and sisters and ask God for help together.
exp.1:17:
The verse says that Daniel and his three friends were to ask the God of heaven to show compassion to them and reveal the mystery. Asking here means pleading or begging for help. The mercies are acts of compassion and help. Their perishing means dying. In addition, the companions are his friends Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, and the secret is a hidden matter.

King Nebuchadnezzar had ordered that all the wise men of Babylon be put to death, because no one could tell him his dream or its meaning. Daniel asked the king for time and went home to tell his friends about the problem. The text does not say how long they prayed, but it does say that they sought God together. Afterward, God revealed the secret to Daniel.

When you face a great problem, do not carry it alone. Ask God for help and find believing friends to pray with you. He cares about your needs.
exp.1:20:
This verse says that God is the one who changes the times and the seasons of history. He removes some kings and sets up others. He also gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who understand.

Daniel speaks here, a young Jew taken captive to Babylon. That night God had revealed to him the secret dream of King Nebuchadnezzar, and with that the lives of the wise men of the kingdom were saved. Daniel does not claim the credit; he responds with a prayer of praise, acknowledging that all power and all wisdom come from God.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, whether in the country, at work, or in the family, we can rest in the knowledge that God still governs. And if we have some talent or understanding, let us remember to thank Him, not to boast.
exp.1:23:
This verse tells how Daniel went to Arioch, the man the king had appointed to kill the wise men of Babylon. Daniel asks him not to kill them and to take him before the king, because he will give the king the interpretation of the dream.

Daniel speaks here after praying with his friends and receiving from God the secret of the dream. King Nebuchadnezzar had ordered all the wise men put to death because no one could tell him his dream. Daniel was also in danger, but he acts to save lives, including those of people who did not share his faith.

For today: when God gives us light or help, we should not keep it only for ourselves. We can use it with humility to bless and protect others, even those who think differently from us.
exp.1:25:
King Nebuchadnezzar addresses Daniel, who was also called Belteshazzar, which was his Babylonian name. He asks whether Daniel really will be able to make known to him the dream he had and what it means. The word "interpretation" in the verse means explanation of the meaning. The king's question is full of doubt.

The king had a dream that troubled him, and none of the wise men of Babylon could tell him what it was or explain it. In his rage he ordered all of them put to death. Daniel stopped that order, and now he stands before the king. The question sounds skeptical: Daniel was a young man and one of the exiles from Judah.

For today: when others doubt you or see you as small, you do not have to defend yourself with pride. Daniel, in the answer that follows, directs attention to God, who reveals mysteries. Trust God and let Him be the one who acts.
exp.1:27:
Daniel tells the king that, although none of the wise men of Babylon can explain his dream, there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets. That God has shown Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the days to come, that is, in the future or at the end of time. Then Daniel announces that he is going to tell the dream and the visions the king had while he was sleeping.

Daniel speaks as a young Jewish man taken captive to Babylon. The king had demanded that someone tell him the dream and its meaning, and the wise men could not do it. Daniel does not claim the credit for himself, but points to God as the one who reveals. The following verses confirm this: he is not wiser than others.

For today: when you have no answers, ask God for light and do not take the credit yourself. He knows what you cannot see, and humility opens the door for others to look to God.
exp.1:28:
This verse says that King Nebuchadnezzar, while lying in his bed, began to think about what would happen in the future. Then God, the one who reveals hidden things, showed him what was going to happen. The phrase about his thoughts rising up means that his mind was filled with questions about what lay ahead.

Daniel speaks here, a young Jew who had been taken captive to Babylon. The king had had a dream that troubled him, and he demanded that his wise men tell him the dream and its meaning. No one could. Daniel makes clear that it is not by his own intelligence, but that the God of heaven is the one who makes known what is hidden.

For today: it is natural for us to think about the future and to worry. Instead of looking for answers only in our own minds or in doubtful sources, we can bring those questions to God in prayer, trusting that he guides history and also our lives, even though we cannot see everything.
exp.1:31:
This verse says that King Nebuchadnezzar saw a great statue made of several materials. The head was of fine gold, the chest and arms of silver, and the belly and thighs of bronze. Each material seems to be worth less than the one before it.

It speaks of Daniel, a young Jew taken captive to Babylon. The king had a dream that troubled him, and either he forgot it or did not want to reveal it, and the wise men could not tell him what it was. Daniel makes clear that God revealed the dream to him, not his own wisdom. Later, Daniel explains that the head of gold is Nebuchadnezzar. The other kingdoms have been interpreted in various ways, and scholars do not fully agree.

For today: empires and human powers seem enormous, but they pass away. We can trust that God still guides history, and give Him the credit, as Daniel did, when He gives us some talent or knowledge.
exp.1:32:
This verse says that the legs of the great statue were iron, and that the feet were a mixture: part iron and part baked clay, that is, clay hardened by fire. Iron is strong, but clay breaks easily, so that mixture spoke of something both strong and fragile at once.

Daniel speaks to King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon and describes the dream that the king had forgotten. God showed it to Daniel to reveal that He rules over human kingdoms. Many believe that the parts of the statue represent kingdoms that follow one another, although there is debate about exactly which ones they are. All agree that in the end the stone, the kingdom of God, remains.

For today: do not place your trust in human power, however impressive it may seem. Everything we build without God has some crack in it. Rest in the kingdom of God, which does not end.
exp.1:33:
Here Daniel describes to King Nebuchadnezzar what he saw in his dream: a stone broke loose without anyone's hands cutting it or throwing it. That stone struck the feet of the great statue, which were made of iron mixed with baked clay, and broke them into pieces.

Daniel speaks before the Babylonian king, who was troubled by a dream he had forgotten. God gave Daniel both the dream and its meaning. Daniel explains that the statue represents successive human kingdoms, and that the stone points to a kingdom that God himself establishes. Christians often see this as a reference to Christ and his kingdom, though some interpret it in other ways.

For today: human powers may seem strong, but they do not last forever. You can rest in the fact that God continues to guide history, and place your trust in his kingdom, not in what is falling apart.
exp.1:34:
What it says: The whole statue from the dream was broken to pieces, and its materials (iron, clay, bronze, silver and gold) became like the chaff that is separated from the wheat when it is threshed, the light husk the wind carries off. The wind carried them away and no trace was left. The stone that struck the statue, however, became a great mountain that filled the whole earth.

Context: Daniel speaks before King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, explaining the dream God gave him, which no one else could tell. The metals represent successive human kingdoms. Interpreters disagree about exactly which kingdoms they all are, but almost all see the stone as the kingdom of God, which is not a human work.

For today: The powers of this world seem firm, but they pass away. You can rest in the knowledge that God's kingdom endures, and place your hope and your priorities in what lasts forever.
exp.1:38:
After you, another kingdom will arise, inferior to yours, and then a third kingdom, represented by the metal bronze, which will rule over all the earth. "Will rule" means it will govern with authority. The phrase "inferior to yours" could refer to less glory or power, and the text does not say exactly in what way.

Daniel explains to King Nebuchadnezzar the dream of a great statue, which God had shown him and which the king could not remember. The head of gold was Babylon. Many understand the kingdoms that follow to be Medo-Persia and Greece, although there are other interpretations. Daniel speaks to show that God governs history.

For today: powerful empires and leaders rise and fall, but God remains in control. If you are worried today about the direction of the world or of your own life, trust that God holds the future, and pray with hope rather than fear.
exp.1:40:
It says that the feet and toes of the statue were partly of clay fired in a kiln and partly of iron. This represents a divided kingdom, which keeps some of the strength of the iron, but mixed with clay.

Daniel speaks to King Nebuchadnezzar, who had a dream that no one could explain to him. God gave Daniel the dream and its meaning. The statue shows a succession of human kingdoms. Interpreters debate exactly which is the fourth kingdom; many think of Rome, though not all agree. The central point is that God governs history.

For today: do not put your trust in human powers, which, however strong they seem, have cracks and divisions. Rest in God, whose kingdom never breaks or ends.
exp.1:41:
This verse says that the feet of the statue were part iron and part baked clay. That means the kingdom they represent would have two sides: it would be strong in some ways and fragile in others. The clay in question is earth hardened by fire, like the material of a pot.

Daniel explains to King Nebuchadnezzar the dream of a great statue that the king had seen and did not understand. Daniel makes clear that God is the one who reveals the future. Interpreters disagree about exactly which kingdom the feet represent (many think of Rome or its later divisions), but all see that the central message is that human powers are unstable, and that God will raise up a kingdom that never ends.

For today: do not place your ultimate security in human powers, however strong they may seem. Rather, trust in the kingdom of God, which remains forever.
exp.1:44:
This verse says that Daniel reminds the king of the stone that broke loose from a mountain without anyone cutting it with human hands. That stone struck and destroyed the statue made of iron, baked clay, silver, and gold. Daniel states that the great God has shown the king what will happen in the future. He adds that the dream is true and its explanation can be trusted.

Daniel is speaking before Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, after telling him the dream the king had forgotten and explaining it to him. The statue represents successive human kingdoms, and the stone represents the kingdom that God establishes. Christians often see in this the kingdom of Christ, although there are different ways of interpreting the details of each kingdom.

For today: human empires and powers pass away, but the kingdom of God endures. Today you can rest in that promise and not place your security in what is temporary.
exp.1:45:
This verse says that King Nebuchadnezzar, deeply impressed, fell to the ground before Daniel. He also commanded that offerings be made to him and sweet odours. Fell upon his face means that he prostrated himself as a sign of respect.

Daniel had just told the king his dream and its meaning, something none of the wise men of Babylon could do. Daniel gave the credit to God, not to himself. Scholars debate whether the king intended to worship Daniel or only to honour him as God's messenger. What follows shows that the king recognized Daniel's God as the God of gods.

When God works through us, we do not seek applause. Like Daniel, we can humbly point toward God, so that others come to know Him and do not fixate only on us.
exp.1:47:
What it says: After Daniel explained his dream to him, King Nebuchadnezzar honored him. He gave him a very high position and many gifts. The sentence about making him important means that he made him a great man, and the gifts are the many great gifts in the verse. The phrase about him being chief over the governors refers to the verse's words "chief of the governors over all the wise men of Babylon," meaning he was placed over the administrators and the wise men of Babylon.

Context: The narrator tells what happened after God showed Daniel the dream of the statue. The king, who was a pagan, recognized that Daniel's God is superior to all. This does not necessarily mean he gave up his gods; the Bible here only shows that he acknowledged the power of God.

For today: Daniel did not seek fame; he was faithful and gave God the credit. We can do our work with honesty and humility, trusting that God knows how to open doors in his time and that everything good comes from Him.
exp.2:0:
It says that King Nebuchadnezzar had a very large statue of gold made: sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. A cubit is about half a meter, so it would have been roughly 27 meters high and 3 meters wide. He set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. The word "set it up" simply means he erected it. Some think it may have been a statue with a base, or covered in gold, but the text does not make this clear.

Here the narrator of the book of Daniel is telling what the king did. It does not explain why he made it. The verses that follow show that he wanted to gather all the officials of the kingdom to give him honor. Later it will be seen that he demanded that they worship it, and that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego did not bow down.

For today: let us be on guard against the false gods that power, money or success ask us to worship. Even when they seem great and impressive, only God deserves our complete loyalty.
exp.2:1:
This verse tells how King Nebuchadnezzar summoned all the officials of his kingdom to the inauguration of the great statue. Several kinds of office are named: rulers, military commanders, judges, treasurers, counselors, and the administrators of the provinces. The word "dedication" refers to the ceremony that inaugurates the statue. The judges were probably the ones who heard cases, and the officials in charge of finances handled the money, although the exact meaning of some of these titles is debated.

Here the narrator speaks, and the protagonist is the king of Babylon. He wants to gather all his leaders in one public event, probably to display his power and to secure the unity and loyalty of the whole empire. What follows is an order to worship the statue.

For today: let us watch that no authority, social pressure, or custom takes the place that belongs only to God. Let us ask him for the courage to remain faithful.
exp.2:2:
This verse tells us that all the high officials of the kingdom gathered for the dedication of the great golden statue. They were rulers, judges, treasurers, and counselors, and all of them stood in front of the statue.

The narrator describes the event organized by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He gathered all the authorities to display his power and to secure the loyalty of the whole empire. What follows is the command to worship the statue, and that command sets up the test faced by Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.

For today: pressure to follow the crowd can come wrapped in official events and impressive ceremonies. Let us ask God for wisdom to recognize when something draws us away from worshiping him alone, and for steadfastness to obey him with humility and courage.
exp.2:3:
This verse tells of a herald, that is, an official announcer, who called out an order from the king in a loud voice. The word "herald" here means someone who makes a public proclamation. The order was addressed to people of every nation, language, and people group that made up the empire.

The herald speaks on behalf of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. He had set up a huge statue of gold and gathered all his officials for its dedication. The announcement sets up what follows: everyone was to bow down before the statue when the music sounded, or they would be thrown into a furnace of fire. The text does not explain in detail what the statue represented, and scholars interpret it in various ways.

Today, this passage reminds us that the world often demands loyalties that compete with God. We can ask Him for the courage to obey Him first, with respect and firmness, even when nearly everyone around us is doing something else.
exp.2:4:
It says that when the people heard the sound of the instruments (the horn or cornet, the pipe or flute, the small drum or tabor, the harp, the psaltery, the bagpipe, and all the rest), they were to fall down to the ground and worship the great golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. To fall down means to bow until your face touches the ground.

It is the king's herald speaking, announcing a command to people of every nation and language in the kingdom. All the officials had been gathered for the dedication of the image. The music served as the signal for everyone to worship at the same moment. The command came with a threat: whoever did not obey would be cast into a furnace of fire.

Today we may ask ourselves which kinds of "music" push us to follow the crowd, such as social pressure, fashion, or fear. God invites us to worship Him alone, even when it costs us to go against the current.
exp.2:7:
It says that, at that very moment, certain Chaldean men came forward to the king and accused the Jews. The word "accused" here means that they brought formal charges against them. The Chaldeans were the Babylonians, the people of the king.

The narrator tells us what happened right after everyone bowed down before the golden statue. These Chaldeans speak up to accuse the Jews, who had not obeyed the command. The Bible does not fully explain their motives; there may have been jealousy over the position the Jews held in the government (mentioned in verse 12), but the text does not say so clearly.

For today: when following God makes us different, some may criticize or accuse us. Let us ask God for the courage to be faithful with humility, without responding with hatred and without ceasing to do good.
exp.2:9:
Here some men of the Chaldeans remind King Nebuchadnezzar of his own decree. When the people heard the sound of the instruments, they were to bow down and worship the golden image. The horn is a trumpet or a cornet, the fife is a flute, the small drum is a little drum, and the bagpipe is a wind instrument like a bagpipe or a multi-pipe flute. The exact names of some of the instruments are uncertain.

The speakers are some Chaldeans who accuse the Jews before the king. First they flatter him with a wish for his long life, and then they repeat his law. In this way they prepare the accusation against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who did not worship the image.

Today, many voices push us to go along with the crowd, and sometimes they single out whoever thinks differently. Let us ask God for courage to be faithful to him with respect and humility, even when it costs us.
exp.2:13:
Nebuchadnezzar asks Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego directly whether it is true that they do not serve his gods or worship the golden statue he has set up.

The word "serve" here means to worship and honor. The king is asking whether these three men refuse to give that honor to his gods or to his statue.

The one speaking is the king of Babylon, and he is furious. Some Babylonian astrologers or advisers had accused these three young Jewish men, whom the king had placed in positions of importance. He gives them the chance to explain themselves before punishing them. The text does not say exactly which god the king worshiped or what the statue represented, and scholars interpret this in various ways.

For today: sometimes being faithful to God will put us under pressure from people who have power over us. We can decide in advance that God will have first place, and respond with respect and firmness, trusting that He sustains us, whatever the outcome.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that King Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury when he heard the young men's answer. His face changed, that is, his expression twisted in anger. Then he ordered that the furnace be heated seven times more than normal. The phrase about the furnace probably expresses extreme heat rather than an exact measurement.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. The three young Hebrews had just refused to worship the golden statue, and they said that God could deliver them, but that even if he did not, they would not give in. The king, accustomed to being obeyed, reacted with rage and punishment.

For today: when keeping your faith costs you misunderstanding or pressure, do not be surprised by the reaction of others. Choose to be faithful to God calmly and trust him, whatever the outcome.
exp.2:20:
This verse tells how Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego were bound while still wearing all their clothing and thrown into the blazing furnace. The long outer robes, the trousers or leg coverings, and the head coverings are named in the text, but scholars are not sure of the exact meaning of some of these words in Aramaic.

The narrator describes what happened after King Nebuchadnezzar, in a rage, ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter. The three young Jewish men had refused to worship the golden statue. The detail about their clothing sets up the story: later, nothing about them smelled of smoke.

For today: sometimes being faithful to God leads us through real trials, and God does not always spare us from entering the fire. But this account reminds us that He can be with us and care for us in the middle of it. Decide to obey Him today, even when it costs you.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego fell into the furnace of blazing fire while still tied up. The text does not show them safe yet; it only describes the moment they enter the danger.

The one telling the story is the writer of the book of Daniel. These three young Jews refused to worship the golden statue of King Nebuchadnezzar, and for that reason they were thrown into the furnace. The king had ordered it heated more than usual, and the fire killed the soldiers who threw them in. Soon after, the king will see four men walking loose and unharmed in the middle of the fire.

For today: obeying God does not always spare us from entering the trial, but God can be with us inside it. When you face pressure for being faithful, trust that you are not alone.
exp.2:24:
This verse says that the king saw four men walking free inside the furnace. Those who had been tied up were now loose, and the fire did them no harm. The phrase about walking calmly means they were strolling without anxiety. The fourth one had an appearance like the Son of God, that is, a divine or heavenly being.

King Nebuchadnezzar speaks here, astonished. He had ordered Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego thrown into the fire for refusing to worship the golden statue. He, a pagan king, describes what he understands. Some believe the fourth figure was the Son of God before becoming a man; others believe it was an angel, as the king says later (v. 28). The text does not make this clear.

For today: when you go through trials for being faithful to God, you are not alone. God does not always take the fire away, but he promises to accompany you in the midst of it. Trust his presence.
exp.2:26:
The verse tells how all the officials of the kingdom gathered to see the three young men who came out of the furnace. The fire had no power over them: not a hair of their heads was singed, their clothes were not changed, and they did not even smell of smoke. The phrase that the fire had no power over them means it did not overcome them, and the phrase that their coats were not changed means their clothing was not altered.

The narrator describes what happened after King Nebuchadnezzar had them summoned. The three had been thrown into the furnace for refusing to worship the golden statue. Now the high officials, who had earlier witnessed the king's command, become witnesses of the miracle. Afterward, the king himself will acknowledge their God.

For today: being faithful to God can be costly, but He cares for His own, whether by delivering them from the trial or by standing with them in the midst of it. Today you can stay firm in what is right, trusting that God is with you.
exp.2:28:
Therefore the verse says that King Nebuchadnezzar gives an order: anyone, of any people, nation, or language, who speaks against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego will be cut in pieces, and their house will be made a dunghill. The king gives the reason: no other god can deliver like this God.

King Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, speaks after seeing that the three young men came out of the fiery furnace without being burned. Before this, he had demanded that they worship a statue, and they refused. The decree is very harsh, typical of an ancient king; it is not a model for how to treat others, but it shows his amazement at the power of God.

For today: let us be faithful to God even when it costs us, and respect others with gentleness, trusting that God knows how to defend his name.
exp.2:29:
It says that King Nebuchadnezzar promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that is, he gave them greater honor and authority in the province of Babylon. The word "promoted" means that he raised them up and put them in a higher position.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Daniel. The three young Jewish men had refused to worship the golden statue and were thrown into the fiery furnace, but God protected them. After seeing them come out unharmed, the king acknowledged the power of their God and showed them favor. Some scholars point out that the text does not say the king was fully converted; it only acknowledges that this God is powerful.

For today: being faithful to God can be costly, but God knows how to care for his own. Sometimes he also honors them, though not always in the same way. We can obey with confidence, without depending on the applause of other people.
exp.3:0:
This verse is the greeting of a letter. King Nebuchadnezzar addresses all the peoples, nations, and languages of the earth over which he ruled. He wishes them peace that grows and overflows. In some Bibles, this verse appears as Daniel 3:31.

The one speaking is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He writes as a public letter, and the verses that follow say he wants to make known the signs and wonders that the Most High God worked for him. What follows in the chapter is his personal testimony, in which he acknowledges God's power after being humbled. The text gives no further detail about the exact nature of his faith, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

For today: when God works in your life, share it simply and with a good spirit, wishing peace on those who listen. Your testimony can be a gift to others, not a way of showing off.
exp.3:2:
He says that God's signs are great and his wonders mighty. His kingdom is everlasting, meaning eternal, without end. And his dominion, that is his authority as Lord, lasts from generation to generation, through all times.

The speaker is King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. It is a letter he sends to all peoples to tell what the Most High God did with him. According to the account, he himself acknowledges that God is greater than any king. Then he tells of a dream that frightened him and led him to that conclusion.

For today: our achievements and our power are passing, but God reigns forever. We can trust in him when everything seems uncertain, and count with gratitude what he has done in our lives, as this king did.
exp.3:7:
At last Daniel came into my presence. His name was Belteshazzar, after the name of my god, and in him is the spirit of the holy gods. Then I told him the dream.

Here the king, Nebuchadnezzar, speaks in his own account. He was troubled by a dream, and his magicians, astrologers, and diviners could not interpret it. He speaks from his pagan outlook: "holy gods" reflects the way he understood the divine. Some believe it refers to the Spirit of Daniel's God; others, that it is only his pagan way of speaking.

For today: when the answers of the world are not enough, seek out those who live close to God, and let your life reflect his character so clearly that others come to you in their need.
exp.3:8:
Nebuchadnezzar speaks to Daniel, whom he calls Belteshazzar, and asks him to explain the dream he had. He addresses him as master of the magicians, that is, chief of the wise men of the court. The phrase about the spirit of the holy gods reflects the way a pagan king would speak. The word "interpretation" means explanation of what the dream means.

The one speaking is the king of Babylon. He is troubled by a dream, and his counselors were unable to explain it. So he turns to Daniel, whose Babylonian name was Belteshazzar. The king recognizes that Daniel has an unusual ability, though he does not fully understand where it comes from. Later in the book, it becomes clear that the wisdom comes from the true God.

For today: when we have questions that no one can answer for us, let us seek God with humility. And if He gives us understanding, let us live in such a way that others can see His work in us and trust our testimony.
exp.3:9:
Here the king Nebuchadnezzar begins to tell his dream. He says that, while he was lying in bed, he saw in a vision a tree standing very tall in the middle of the earth.

The speaker is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He has just summoned Daniel, whom the Babylonians called Belteshazzar, because none of his wise men could explain the dream to him. Later on, Daniel explains that the tree represents the king himself: great, powerful, and a protector of many, but with the danger of pride.

For today: if God has given you success, influence, or possessions, remember that everything comes from Him. Use it to bless others, and do not think of your own greatness as something you own. Humility keeps us steady.
exp.3:10:
The tree in the dream kept growing and became stronger and stronger. It was so tall that it seemed to touch the sky, and it could be seen from the farthest edges of the earth.

King Nebuchadnezzar is the one speaking. He had a dream that troubled him, and he asks Daniel, whom he calls Belteshazzar, to explain it. Later Daniel will say that the tree represented the king himself, whose power and fame had spread enormously.

For today: success and influence can make us feel that everything depends on us. Take a moment to thank God for what you have and to recognize that all that we are and achieve is a gift from him. Humility keeps us steady as we grow.
exp.3:11:
It says the tree in the dream was beautiful and very fruitful. Its top, with the branches and leaves, is what it calls its crown. It gave food for everyone. The animals of the field rested in its shade, the birds made their nests in its branches, and every living creature, all flesh, was sustained by it.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, speaks, telling of a dream that troubled him. Daniel interprets it afterward: the tree represents the king himself, with his power and his great kingdom that protected and sustained many. But the dream announces that this tree will be cut down, to teach him that God rules over all kingdoms.

Everything good we have, whether authority, talent or resources, is meant to bless others, not to exalt ourselves. Ask yourself today: to whom can I give shade and sustenance? And remember that everything comes from God, who calls us to humility.
exp.3:12:
The king Nebuchadnezzar says that while he was lying in bed, he had a vision in his mind. He saw a watcher and a holy one coming down from heaven. The "watcher" is a heavenly being, a messenger of God who keeps watch and carries out his orders. "Holy" indicates that he belongs to God and serves him. This figure appears right after he sees the great tree.

The one speaking is King Nebuchadnezzar, recounting a dream that troubled him. The tree represented his power and his kingdom, which gave food and shelter to many. The watcher comes to give a sentence of judgment: to cut down the tree. Later Daniel explains that the dream announced the king's humiliation because of his pride.

For today: everything we have, whether power, success, or resources, we receive from God. If we use it with pride, we forget where it comes from. Today we can ask him for humility and use what we have to help others.
exp.3:15:
Here it is said that the king's mind would be changed: he would stop thinking like a person and would have a beast's heart, that is, he would act like an animal. This would last for seven periods of time. Many think the seven periods are seven years, though the text does not make this clear.

Nebuchadnezzar tells his dream of the great tree cut down. A watcher, a heavenly being, announces this sentence. Later Daniel will explain that the tree represents the king, who will be humbled until he recognizes that God rules over all kingdoms.

For today: everything we have, such as talents, work, or success, comes from God. We can live with humility and gratitude, and give glory to God instead of trusting only in our own strength.
exp.3:16:
It says that what will happen to the king was decided by messengers from heaven, called "watchers" and "holy ones," who are surely angels (as many understand, though not all). The purpose is that everyone may know that God, the Most High, rules over human kingdoms. He gives power to whomever he wills, even to the lowliest of men.

Nebuchadnezzar tells his dream of a great tree that is cut down. Here one of those watchers speaks within the dream. The message aims to humble the proud king and teach him who holds true authority. Afterward Daniel, with fear, prepares to explain it.

For today: do not trust in your power, your position, or your achievements as if they were yours alone. Everything you have is a gift from God. Live with humility and gratitude, and use your influence to serve others.
exp.3:17:
The king Nebuchadnezzar here finishes telling his dream and asks Daniel, whom he calls Belteshazzar, to explain it. He says that none of the wise men of Babylon could do so. He trusts Daniel because he believes that in Daniel there is the spirit of the holy gods, meaning something divine that gives him understanding.

The king speaks as a powerful and proud man, yet he is troubled by the dream. What he has just described says that the Most High rules over human kingdoms. Nebuchadnezzar speaks from his pagan outlook, which is why he speaks of gods; the Bible shows that Daniel's wisdom comes from the true God.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening, seek counsel from people who truly walk with God. And remember that human power is borrowed, for God is the one who governs.
exp.3:18:
Daniel, who was also called Belteshazzar, stayed silent for almost an hour, deeply troubled by what he was thinking. The king told him not to be frightened by the dream or by its meaning. Daniel answered with respect: "My lord, may the dream be for your enemies." That phrase is an old way of saying that the bad news should not touch you.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had dreamed of a great tree, and no wise man could interpret it. Daniel could, but he understood that its meaning was hard for the king: God would humble him because of his pride. That is why Daniel hesitated before speaking.

For today: sometimes we have to say difficult truths. We can do it as Daniel did: calmly, with prayer, with respect and with kindness, without hiding the truth, but caring for the person who hears it.
exp.3:19:
Daniel begins to explain the king's dream. He speaks about the tree the king saw: it kept growing and became strong. Its height reached up to the sky, meaning it was enormous, and it could be seen from far away across the whole earth. It is an image of great power and influence.

Daniel, who was called Belteshazzar in Babylon, speaks before King Nebuchadnezzar. The wise men of the kingdom had not been able to interpret the dream. Daniel took almost an hour before speaking, because the interpretation was hard: it announced a judgment against the king. In the verses that follow, he says that the tree is the king himself.

For today: everything we have, whether success, ability or influence, we receive from God. If we grow in something, let us remember to thank him and to use it for the good of others, not to show off.
exp.3:20:
This verse continues describing the king's tree in the dream. It had a beautiful crown, that is, its high and leafy top. It bore much fruit and fed everyone. The animals of the field rested in its shade, and the birds made their nests in its branches.

Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, explains to Nebuchadnezzar the dream that had troubled him. Daniel says the tree represents the king himself: his power was great, and it protected and sustained many peoples. But the dream also announces judgment for his pride, as the following verses show.

For today: if God gives us influence, work, or resources, it is to bless others, not to exalt ourselves. We can ask ourselves: does my life give shade and food to others? And remember that everything we have comes from God, so we should stay humble.
exp.3:21:
Here Daniel tells King Nebuchadnezzar that the giant tree in his dream is himself. His power had grown so great that it seemed to reach up to heaven, and his rule extended to the farthest corners of the earth.

Daniel speaks with respect but also with courage, to explain a dream that had troubled the king. Nebuchadnezzar ruled Babylon, a very powerful empire. Daniel explains that God sees his pride and that the dream is a warning before a judgment, so that the king will acknowledge that God rules over all.

For today: everything we have, whether talent, work, or influence, is a gift from God. We can be grateful for what we have achieved, but it is wise to live with humility, remembering that we depend on Him and that we should use what we have to bless others.
exp.3:22:
Daniel reminds the king of what he saw in his dream: a watcher and a holy one came down from heaven and ordered that the tree be cut down, but that its stump, with its roots, be left in the earth, bound with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field. There it would be wet with the dew of heaven and live like the beasts of the field until seven times had passed over him. Many understand these seven times as seven years, though the text does not specify this.

Daniel speaks before Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He explains that the tree is the king himself. The dream is a warning from God because of his pride, and the fact that the stump is left in place suggests that his kingdom would be returned to him.

For today: everything we have comes from God, so it is wise to live with humility and gratitude. If God corrects us, we can see it as an opportunity to return to Him and not as an end.
exp.3:23:
This verse is like the doorway into the verse of the dream. Daniel says that what follows is not his own opinion, but a declaration and a decree from the Most High, that is, a decree of God, which reaches King Nebuchadnezzar. He addresses the king as "my lord" out of respect, even though he has to give him a hard message.

It is Daniel speaking, the young Jew taken captive to Babylon. The king had asked him to interpret his dream of the great tree that was cut down. Daniel makes clear that the tree represents the king himself, and that the judgment comes from God because of his pride.

For today: when God corrects us, it is better to listen with humility. Everything we have, talents, work, or achievements, is a gift from him, and recognizing this protects us from pride.
exp.3:24:
It says that King Nebuchadnezzar will be driven away from people and will live with the wild animals of the field. He will eat grass like oxen and sleep outdoors, wet with the dew of heaven. This will last for seven periods of time (the Bible does not make clear whether these are seven years; many understand it that way). The meaning is that he will be made to know that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of men and gives them to whomever He wills.

Daniel speaks to the king and explains the dream of the great tree that was cut down. God warns him, through Daniel, that his pride will have consequences. The goal is not only to punish him, but to bring him to acknowledge that God is the one who gives and takes away power.

For today: everything we have, whether work, talents, or position, comes from God. We can thank Him with humility and use what we have to serve and help others, instead of boasting.
exp.3:25:
Here Daniel explains a detail of the king's dream. When they cut down the tree, they were to leave the stump with its roots in the ground. That means Nebuchadnezzar would not lose his kingdom forever. It would be kept for him until he acknowledged that the heavens rule.

Daniel speaks as a prophet and counselor before the king of Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar had dreamed of a huge tree that was cut down, and Daniel explains that God would humble him because of his pride. Even so, the sentence carried hope: there was a path to restoration.

For today: success and power are not ours; they come from God. If you notice pride in your heart, recognize it in time, humble yourself before God, and thank him for what you have. He can correct and also restore.
exp.3:31:
It says that Nebuchadnezzar will be driven away from people and will live with the animals of the field. They will give him grass to eat, like oxen. "Seven times" will pass over him, which probably means seven periods, perhaps seven years, although the text does not make this clear. All of this will last until he recognizes that God, the most High, rules over human kingdoms and gives power to whomever he wills.

A voice from heaven speaks, the voice of God. Nebuchadnezzar had just boasted about great Babylon, saying that he had built it by his own power and for his own glory. This sentence comes right at that moment, as a correction to his pride. Afterward, the king humbles himself and praises God.

Today we can remember that everything we have, such as talents, work, or achievements, is a gift from God. Before boasting, let us give thanks and use what we have with humility.
exp.3:36:
Nebuchadnezzar says that now he praises, exalts, and honors God, whom he calls the King of heaven. He affirms that everything God does is true, and that his ways are right. He also says that God is able to humble those who walk in pride, that is, with arrogance.

The king of Babylon speaks at the end of a personal testimony. According to the chapter, God humbled him because of his pride, and he lived for a time out of his right mind. When he acknowledged that God rules, he regained his reason and his kingdom. Some scholars debate the exact nature of his condition, but the text emphasizes the lesson: God is sovereign.

Today, we can examine where we place too much trust in our achievements or in our control. A simple practice is to thank God each day for what we have, and to recognize that everything is his gift. That attitude keeps us humble and grateful.
exp.4:2:
This verse tells that the servants brought to the banquet the golden vessels that had been taken from the temple in Jerusalem. The king drank from them, along with his nobles and officials, his wives and his concubines (secondary women who lived in the palace). Those vessels had been used for the worship of God, and now they were being used for a feast.

The narrator describes what happened in Babylon during Belshazzar's banquet. He was drinking wine and gave the order to bring the vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple. It was a sign of disrespect toward the God of Israel, and the account shows it just before the hand appears writing on the wall. There is discussion about how direct the family connection between Belshazzar and Nebuchadnezzar was, since the word for father can also mean ancestor.

For today: what belongs to God should not be treated lightly. We can ask ourselves whether we use with reverence our time, talents, and lives, which God has entrusted to us.
exp.4:3:
It says that King Belshazzar and his guests drank wine using the sacred vessels of the temple, and while they drank, they praised false gods. The list of materials (gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone) shows that these were idols made by human hands. Here, "praised" means they honored or exalted them.

Daniel recounts what happened at a royal banquet in Babylon. The vessels had been taken from the temple in Jerusalem years earlier. Using them at a party, and even to honor idols, was a mockery of the God of Israel. Right after this, a hand appears writing on the wall, as God's response to that contempt.

For today: God is not indifferent when what is holy is treated lightly. We can ask ourselves whether we honor God with what he has given us, or whether we place things, money, or pleasures in the place that belongs only to him.
exp.4:4:
It says that, at that very moment, fingers of a human hand appeared and began to write on the white plaster of the palace wall, opposite the candlestick, that is, the stand that held the lamps and gave light. The king could see the palm of the hand as it wrote.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Daniel. Belshazzar was holding a banquet and used the sacred vessels of the temple in Jerusalem to drink toasts and praise his gods. The hand appears as a response from God to that act of disrespect. Some scholars debate historical details of Belshazzar's reign, but the message of the text is clear.

Today we can remember that God sees what we do, and that what is holy is not a matter for mockery. It is wise to examine our hearts and turn back to God with humility before it is too late.
exp.4:5:
He says that when he saw the hand writing on the wall, King Belshazzar turned pale. His thoughts frightened him, his hips and loins seemed to go slack, as if his body were failing him, and his knees knocked together so badly that they struck one another.

The narrator describes what happened at a royal banquet. The king and his guests were drinking wine and praising false gods. According to the chapter, they had earlier used sacred cups taken from the temple in Jerusalem. Suddenly a mysterious hand appears and writes, and the king, who thought himself secure, is terrified.

For today: pride and mockery of what is holy may seem safe for a time, but they cannot stand before God. It is worth living with humility and reverence, and not waiting until fear arrives before taking God seriously.
exp.4:6:
King Belshazzar, terrified by the mysterious hand writing on the wall, shouts for his wise men to be brought in: the magicians, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers. He promises that whoever reads the writing and explains its meaning will be clothed in purple, given a gold chain around the neck, and made the third ruler in the kingdom. To "rule" here means to govern or hold authority.

The king speaks in the middle of a banquet, right after seeing the hand write. He is very frightened and looks for a quick answer with great rewards. As for the third ruler, it is usually understood as the third place of authority, after the king and another ruler, though the Bible does not explain the details.

For today: when fear shakes us, we often look for help anywhere, even in places that cannot answer. It is better to turn first to God, who gives true wisdom and peace.
exp.4:11:
It says that in Daniel was found an extraordinary spirit, knowledge and good understanding. He knew how to interpret dreams, to solve hard questions and to clear up doubts, that is, to explain what seemed a riddle. The word "found" in the verse is the one that matters here, and the word "interpretation" is what the verse calls the verse. Belteshazzar was the Babylonian name that had been given to him. The queen asks that he be called so that he may explain what was written on the wall.

The one speaking is the queen, probably the queen mother (it is not stated with certainty who she is), while King Belshazzar is terrified by a hand that wrote on the wall during a banquet. Not even the wise men of Babylon were able to read the message. She remembers Daniel, who had served in the time of Nebuchadnezzar.

For today: a faithful and steady life leaves a mark, even as time passes. Daniel was remembered in the crisis for his character and his relationship with God. Live today with integrity and trust in God; perhaps others will seek you out when their difficult moments come.
exp.4:14:
Here the king Belshazzar tells Daniel that he has already summoned the wise men and astrologers of the kingdom. He asked them to read the mysterious writing on the wall and explain its meaning, but none of them could.

King Belshazzar speaks, frightened because a hand wrote on the wall during a banquet. Since his experts had failed, he orders Daniel brought in, an exiled Jew who had a reputation for understanding hidden things. Belshazzar recognizes, perhaps without realizing it, the limits of human wisdom.

For today: there are problems that neither money, nor titles, nor experts can solve. When you reach that limit, do not despair. Seek God and people who live close to Him, and ask for wisdom with humility.
exp.4:18:
This verse says that God gave Nebuchadnezzar such greatness that all peoples, nations, and languages feared him and trembled before him. As king, he had absolute power: he could take a life or spare it, raise some to high positions and bring others down.

Daniel speaks before King Belshazzar, during a banquet where a mysterious writing appeared on the wall. Daniel refuses the king's gifts and reminds him of the story of Nebuchadnezzar, who, according to the text, received everything from God, but became full of pride and was brought low. In this way Daniel warns Belshazzar.

For today: everything we have, whether talent, work, or influence, is a gift from God. Use it with humility and gratitude, because pride makes us forget where everything comes from.
exp.4:21:
This verse says that Belshazzar did not humble himself, even though he knew very well what had happened to Nebuchadnezzar. To humble the heart means to recognize that you are not the center of everything and that God is above you. "His son" is understood as a descendant or successor on the throne; the word in Hebrew/Aramaic can include an ancestor.

The speaker is the prophet Daniel, who was called to interpret the mysterious writing on the wall during a royal banquet. Daniel reminds him how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar because of his pride. Belshazzar knew that story, but he ignored it and desecrated the vessels of the temple.

For today: learning from the mistakes of others spares us pain. If we know what God has done in the lives of others, or in our own, we should not harden ourselves. Today you can ask God for a humble heart, one that heeds his correction in time.
exp.4:26:
This verse says that God weighed Belshazzar like merchandise on a scale, and that he did not reach the weight he was supposed to have. "Tekel" comes from a word related to weighing. Being found wanting means he was lacking something and fell short.

Daniel is the speaker, a Jew taken captive to Babylon. King Belshazzar held a banquet and treated the sacred vessels of the temple in Jerusalem with contempt. Then a hand appeared and wrote on the wall. Daniel explains the message: God had seen the king's pride, and his kingdom was about to end.

For today: God looks at the heart with justice, not by appearances or by power. Today we can pause and humbly ask ourselves where we have lived with pride or without respect for God, and ask him for forgiveness and change while there is still time.
exp.4:28:
It says that, by order of King Belshazzar, they dressed Daniel in purple clothing, put a gold chain around his neck, and publicly announced that he would be the third ruler of the kingdom.

Daniel had just read the mysterious writing on the wall, which announced God's judgment on Belshazzar. Even so, the king kept his promise to honor whoever interpreted it. Daniel had not accepted gifts (v. 17), but the honor was given all the same. That very night the kingdom fell, so the position lasted only a very short time.

For today: let us not put our trust in honors or power, which pass quickly. Like Daniel, let us speak the truth with courage, without seeking reward, and trust that God sustains what truly endures.
exp.4:29:
That same night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), was killed. The text does not say who killed him or how; it simply announces the event with surprise and speed.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book of Daniel. That night Belshazzar was holding a feast and used the sacred vessels of the temple in Jerusalem. A hand appeared writing on the wall, and Daniel explained that God had judged his kingdom. The verse shows that God's word was fulfilled immediately. Historians debate some details of the fall of Babylon, but the book presents it as God's judgment.

For today: let us not live as if we had everything secured. Power, money and success do not last forever. Today is a good day to humble ourselves before God, live with reverence, and do what is right.
exp.5:3:
It says that the presidents and governors of the kingdom were looking for a reason to accuse Daniel about how he handled the affairs of government. But they found no pretext for accusing him, and no error or negligence. The reason is that Daniel was trustworthy, that is, reliable and honest, and no wrongdoing was found in him.

The narrator tells us that King Darius intended to set Daniel over the whole kingdom. This caused jealousy among the other officials, who wanted to remove him from the way. They examined his work, but found nothing. So, as the following verse shows, they would look for a different route: to use his faith in God against him.

For today: let us seek to live with such integrity in our work and in everyday life that, if anyone criticizes us, they will have no real grounds. Even so, honesty does not always prevent opposition, but it gives us peace and a good witness.
exp.5:6:
The chief officials of the kingdom come to Darius with a proposal. They say that all of them agree that the king should issue a firm decree: for thirty days, anyone who asks a petition of any god or any man, other than the king, will be thrown into the den of lions.

The ones speaking are the governors and presidents who wanted to destroy Daniel. Since they could not find any fault in his work, they decided to use his faith in God against him. Their claim that everyone agreed is doubtful, because Daniel, one of the three presidents, was not included. They also appealed to the king's pride.

For today: do not be surprised if your faithfulness to God brings opposition. Try to live with such integrity that, if you are accused, the only thing they can accuse you of is your faith.
exp.5:9:
Daniel learned that the decree had already been signed, and he went home. He opened the windows of his upper room, the ones facing toward Jerusalem, and he got down on his knees. He prayed three times a day and gave thanks to God, just as he always did.

Some men who were jealous of Daniel had tricked King Darius into forbidding anyone to pray to anyone but the king for thirty days. Daniel was a high official, and they were looking for a way to accuse him. He did not change his custom, even though he knew the risk. Facing Jerusalem recalls Solomon's prayer for the temple, though the text does not explain more.

Today, faith is strengthened by simple and steady habits. Choose a fixed time to pray each day, and do not drop it when pressure comes.
exp.5:11:
Daniel's enemies go before King Darius and remind him of the decree he signed: for thirty days, whoever made a request to any god or man other than the king would be thrown into the den of lions. Darius confirms that it is true and that the law of the Medes and Persians cannot be changed.

The ones speaking are the high officials who were jealous of Daniel. They saw him praying to God, as he always did, and now they use the decree to accuse him. With their words they trap the king: if he admits the law is firm, he will not easily be able to save Daniel.

For today: true faith holds firm even when remaining faithful costs dearly. Daniel did not hide his prayer or change his custom. We can ask God for courage to be constant in prayer, without boasting and without fear, trusting that he cares for us.
exp.5:13:
This verse tells us that King Darius was deeply distressed when he heard the accusation against Daniel. The quoted phrases in the source describe this: he was grieved greatly, he set his heart on helping Daniel, and he labored until sunset to rescue him. In other words, it hurt him deeply, he gave the matter his full attention, and he looked for a legal way to save him. He kept trying until the sun went down.

This is the narrator of the book describing what the king felt. The men who envied Daniel had tricked Darius into signing a decree that forbade anyone to pray to anyone but the king. Now Daniel was being accused for continuing to pray to his God. The king saw the trap, but the law of the Medes and Persians could not be changed.

For today: sometimes we recognize an injustice when it is already hard to correct. Let us learn to think before we commit ourselves, and to defend with courage those who suffer unjustly, without waiting until it is too late.
exp.5:17:
That night the king went back to his palace and spent the night without eating. No music or entertainment was brought before him, and he could not sleep. Explaining the verse's wording: the king's fasting means he went without food. The music that usually accompanied the king is referred to here as entertainment and the sounds of celebration that often filled his evenings. The phrase about his sleep leaving him means he suffered from sleeplessness.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. King Darius had been persuaded by his advisers to sign a law that condemned Daniel. Although he wanted to save him, he could not change the decree. His distress shows that he valued Daniel. The text does not say that Darius fasted for religious reasons, only that he spent the night without eating or sleeping.

For today: when an unjust situation takes away our peace, we should not ignore it. Let us bring our worry to God in prayer and act with courage on behalf of those who are suffering.
exp.5:18:
This verse says that King Darius got up very early, as soon as it was dawn, and went quickly to the den of lions. After a night without sleep or food, he did not want to wait; he went straight to see what had happened to Daniel.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. He tells how the king had signed a decree, deceived by officials who were jealous of Daniel, and could not change it. Although he had to put Daniel into the den, the king valued him. His haste and anguish show that he hoped, though with doubt, that the God of Daniel had protected him.

For today: when we go through a night of anguish, we can rise and draw near to God with hope, even if our voice trembles. He can act even when we cannot see how.
exp.5:22:
The verse tells us that King Darius was filled with joy when he learned that Daniel was alive. He ordered that Daniel be taken up out of the pit where the lions were. When Daniel was brought up, he had no wound at all. The text gives the reason: Daniel had trusted in his God.

Daniel had been accused by men who were jealous of his position, and the king, although he valued him, had to carry out a law that he himself had signed. He spent the night troubled. At dawn he hurried to the pit, and Daniel answered him that God had sent his angel. What follows shows that God did justice, and Darius publicly acknowledged the God of Daniel.

For today: trusting in God does not always spare us from trials, but He can take care of us in the midst of them. When you face something difficult, keep doing what is right, and bring your fear to God in prayer.
exp.5:23:
King Darius commanded that the men who had accused Daniel be brought, and they were thrown into the lions' den along with their children and their wives. Before they reached the floor, the lions caught them and broke all their bones.

It is part of the account in the book of Daniel. Daniel had been taken out of the den without any harm, because he trusted in God. The king then punished those who had plotted his death. Punishing the families as well was a harsh practice of that time and culture; the Bible records it, but does not present it as an example to follow.

For today: God cares for those who trust in him, even when they face injustice. We do not need to take revenge or scheme; we can remain faithful and leave justice in his hands.
exp.5:26:
This verse says that God saves and delivers his people, and that he performs signs and wonders both in heaven and on earth. As proof, it mentions that he rescued Daniel from the power of the lions. The "signs" are deeds that show God's power, and the "wonders" are extraordinary actions that cause amazement.

The speaker is King Darius, a foreign ruler. He had ordered Daniel thrown into the den of lions, and when he saw that God had protected him, he wrote this decree to all the peoples of his kingdom. His declaration shows how deeply impressed he was by what he saw. Scholars debate exactly who this Darius was, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: when you face a situation that seems hopeless, remember that God is still the one who saves and delivers. Trust him, and let your faithfulness, like Daniel's, be a visible witness to those around you.
exp.5:27:
This verse says that Daniel lived well and prospered during the reign of Darius and also during that of Cyrus, king of Persia. The word "prospered" here means that things went well for him, that he succeeded and kept his place.

Here the writer of the book is closing the story of the lions' den. Earlier, King Darius had acknowledged the God of Daniel. This verse shows that Daniel remained steady and respected after that event. Scholars debate exactly who Darius the Mede was, and the text does not fully clarify it.

For today: God can care for those who are faithful to him, even though he does not always do so in the way we expect. Keep doing what is right with steadiness, without depending on circumstances changing, and trust that God sustains your life.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that Daniel had a dream with visions while he was asleep, during the first year of Belshazzar's reign in Babylon. Afterward he wrote it down and recorded the main points of the matter. The quoted phrase about the summary and the quoted words about seeing are not explained further here; the sentence describing the images that passed through his mind while he lay in bed is the key point.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book, who tells what happened to Daniel, a Jew living in exile. Belshazzar governed Babylon, and Daniel was already an older man. This chapter marks a shift: from stories to prophetic visions. What follows, with the four beasts, has been interpreted in various ways, and scholars do not agree on all the details.

For today: Daniel wrote down what God showed him so that he would not forget it. We can note what we learn in prayer and in the Bible, and so remember more clearly what God is teaching us.
exp.6:1:
Daniel tells that, while he was asleep, he had a vision during the night. He saw that the four winds of heaven were striving upon the great sea, that is, they were crashing into and stirring up the great sea with force.

Daniel, now an old man, speaks in the time of King Belshazzar of Babylon. He wrote down what he saw. From that churning sea, four beasts come up right away. Many understand that they represent kingdoms that would rise in history, though interpreters disagree about exactly which ones they are. The winds and the sea are often seen as an image of nations in conflict.

Today we can remember that, even when the world seems like a turbulent sea, God remains in control of history. When the news troubles you, pray and trust that He has the final word.
exp.6:3:
He says that Daniel saw a first beast with the body of a lion and the wings of an eagle. While he watched, its wings were pulled off, it was lifted up from the earth, and it was made to stand on its feet like a man. Also, it was given a man's heart.

Daniel speaks, recounting a vision he had at night. He saw four beasts coming up out of the sea, and this is the first one. Many believe it represents the empire of Babylon, although some interpret it in another way. The central message of the chapter is that, however strong human kingdoms may seem, God still governs, and in the end he establishes his kingdom.

For today: human power, however impressive it may seem, is limited and temporary. If you feel intimidated today by people or situations that seem very large, remember that God has the final word. Trust in him and seek to live with humility.
exp.6:6:
In a night vision, Daniel saw a fourth beast, terrible and very strong. It had great iron teeth with which it devoured, broke into pieces, and trampled whatever was left. It was different from the beasts before it, and it had ten horns, which in the Bible often stand for power or rulers.

Daniel himself tells what he saw. This vision follows the visions of a bear and a leopard, which represent kingdoms that would come one after another. Many believe the fourth beast is Rome; others think of Greece or another empire. This is debated. The chapter shows that, even with so much human power, God sits on his throne and judges.

Today, when evil seems very great and strong, remember that it does not have the final word. Trust that God governs history, pray with calm, and remain faithful, even when the world seems out of control.
exp.6:8:
Daniel reports that he saw thrones or seats being placed, and that one called the Ancient of days, meaning someone eternal, sat down on one.
