His clothing was white as snow and his hair like pure wool, signs of purity and wisdom. His throne looked like a flame of fire, with wheels of burning fire, an image of his holiness and his judgment.

Daniel speaks in the first person and recounts a night vision. He had just seen a fourth terrible beast and a small horn that spoke with arrogance. Suddenly the scene shifts to heaven: God, the Ancient of days, sits down to judge. Most readers understand this "Ancient of days" to be God the Father.

For today: even when evil seems strong and arrogant, God remains on his throne and has the final word. You can rest in him and bring your injustices and fears to him in prayer.
exp.6:12:
Daniel sees in a night vision someone with the appearance of a human being coming with the clouds of heaven. He arrives before the Ancient of Days, that is, God, the Eternal, and they bring him near before him.

Daniel is the one speaking, recounting a vision about kingdoms that rule the earth, represented by beasts. After the judgment against the beast and its arrogant horn, this figure appears and receives the eternal kingdom. Many Christians understand him to be Jesus, who used this expression for himself. Some scholars also see a reference to God's faithful people; there are different interpretations.

For today: human powers may seem strong, but they do not have the last word. You can rest and obey God with confidence, because the kingdom of Christ is the one that endures.
exp.6:15:
Daniel says he went up to one of those who were standing near the throne. He asked him to explain with certainty the meaning of everything he had seen. That figure spoke to him and gave him the interpretation.

Daniel is the one speaking. He has just seen visions of four beasts and of someone receiving an everlasting kingdom. He was troubled and amazed, so he did not stay with his doubt. The one who explains to him is one of the beings who were there, probably an angel, though the text does not say so clearly. The verse follows at once: human kingdoms pass away, but the holy ones of the Most High will receive a kingdom that endures.

For today: when something in the Bible or in life confuses or troubles you, do not hide it. Come to God with your questions, in humility, and seek understanding in his Word and in wise counsel.
exp.6:18:
Daniel says that he wanted to know the truth about the fourth beast. It was very different from the others and caused great fear. It had teeth of iron and nails of bronze (here the word for metal refers to bronze or copper). It devoured, broke in pieces, and what was left over it trampled under its feet.

Daniel himself speaks. He had already seen four beasts in a dream, and an angel explained to him that they represent kingdoms. But the fourth troubled him more, and he wanted to understand it better. Scholars debate which empire it is: many think of Rome, while others propose other options. What is clear is that the message ends with the saints receiving the kingdom.

For today: when something frightens you or you don't understand what is happening in the world, don't keep it to yourself. Ask God for wisdom and seek his Word. He does not promise that there will be no hard powers, but he does promise that his kingdom remains forever.
exp.6:19:
Daniel continues asking about the fourth beast. Now he asks for an explanation of the ten horns on its head and of another small horn that came up after them, before which three of the others fell. This horn had eyes and a mouth that spoke boastful things, that is, it spoke with pride and arrogance. Moreover, it looked greater than the other horns.

Daniel speaks; he had received a vision of four beasts that represent kingdoms of the world. He is frightened and wants to understand what troubles him most: the fourth beast. Interpreters disagree about who this horn is; some think of a ruler from the past and others of one yet to come.

For today: proud and hostile power may seem enormous, but it does not have the last word. When you see injustice, trust that God will judge, and remain faithful with hope.
exp.6:20:
Daniel says that he saw how that small horn, which speaks with arrogance, was making war against the saints, that is, the people of God, and was defeating them. "Saints" means those who belong to God, not people who are special because of their fame.

Daniel is speaking, recounting a vision he had. He was frightened by the fourth beast and wanted to understand what it meant. Christian interpreters differ about who that horn is: some think of a historical ruler, others of a future power. What is clear is that the horn's victory is temporary. Soon the Ancient of Days arrives, that is, God, and judgment is given in favor of the saints, who receive the kingdom.

For today: if you suffer because of your faith, do not conclude that evil has the last word. Endure with hope, because God judges and keeps his promise.
exp.6:22:
The verse says that the fourth beast in the vision represents a fourth kingdom on earth, greater and stronger than all the ones before it. This kingdom will devour the whole earth, trample it down, and break it in pieces. It is an image of brutal domination and enormous reach.

Here an angel is speaking, the one whom Daniel asked to explain the vision of the four beasts, which had left him deeply troubled. Many believers see in this fourth kingdom the Roman Empire, though others interpret it differently. What is certain is that God shows that empires rise up and oppress his people, but they do not have the final word: in the end, judgment and the kingdom are given to the saints of the Most High.

For today: when evil or injustice seem enormous and unstoppable, let us remember that God still governs history and that his kingdom will endure. We can wait with patience and confidence.
exp.6:23:
This verse explains the vision of the fourth beast. The ten horns are ten kings that will arise from that fourth kingdom. After them another king will appear, different from the earlier ones and more powerful than they were, who will subdue three of them. To subdue means to bring them under his control or remove them from their place.

An angel speaks, explaining to Daniel the dream that had frightened him. Daniel was living in exile in Babylon, and this vision showed him that human empires pass away, and that in the end God judges and gives the kingdom to his people. Scholars disagree about who this king is: some think of Rome or Antiochus Epiphanes, others of a future ruler.

For today: even when evil seems to grow and hold power, it does not have the last word. We can remain faithful and at peace, because God governs history.
exp.6:25:
This verse says that God, as judge, will sit down to judge. Then he will take away the power of that wicked king. "Dominion" means authority or rule. The phrase about his power being destroyed and ruined to the very end means that his power will be brought to a complete end, with nothing left of it.

Here a heavenly being explains to Daniel the vision of the four beasts. The other king who speaks against the Most High and mistreats the holy ones is a figure that has been interpreted in various ways, and not everyone agrees on who he is. The central message is clear: his power has a limit, and God has the final word.

For today: when you see injustice seeming to win, trust that God is the final judge. You can rest in the fact that He has not lost control, and keep faithful, even in difficult times.
exp.6:26:
It says that in the end, the kingdom, the power, and the greatness of all the kingdoms of the earth will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High. "Dominion" means authority or rule, and "greatness" is majesty. That kingdom will have no end, and all the powers of the world will serve and obey it. Some understand that "him" refers to God, and others to the people of the saints.

An angel explains to Daniel his vision of four beasts, which represent kingdoms. An arrogant ruler will persecute the saints for a period of time, times, and half a time, a phrase that is interpreted in several ways. Then God judges and takes away his power. This encouraged a people who were suffering. Daniel was greatly troubled.

Today, when injustice seems to be in control, you can rest in the knowledge that God has the final word. Remain faithful and pray with hope, without ceasing to do good.
exp.7:1:
Daniel tells that, in a vision, he saw himself in Shushan, the capital or main city of the kingdom, in the province of Elam. There he was beside the river Ulai. The phrase about the chief city of the kingdom means the main city or capital. He repeats that he saw it in the vision to make clear that it was an experience given by God.

Daniel speaks as a Jew taken captive to Babylon. This is his second vision, in the third year of King Belshazzar. It is not known with certainty whether he was there in person or only in the vision. What follows, the ram with two horns, is the announcement of future kingdoms.

Today we can learn that God knows the future and holds it in his hands. Even when the powers of the world seem strong, God still governs. We can trust him when everything seems uncertain.
exp.7:2:
Daniel lifts up his eyes and sees a ram standing beside the river. It has two long horns, but one is higher than the other, and the higher one grew up after the other.

Daniel speaks, and he receives this vision in Susa, an important city in Persia, near the Ulai River. Later in the same chapter, the angel Gabriel explains that the ram stands for the kings of Media and Persia (Daniel 8:20). God shows Daniel what is to come so that he will know that God governs history.

For today: the empires and powers of this world may seem enormous, but God knows them and holds them in his hand. If today you feel small before your problems or before the news, trust that God is still in control.
exp.7:4:
He says that Daniel, while looking closely, saw a male goat coming from the west and crossing the whole earth so quickly that it seemed not to touch the ground. It had a large, striking horn between its eyes.

Daniel speaks here; he receives a vision while he is in Babylon. Later in this same chapter, the angel Gabriel explains that the ram represents Media and Persia, and the goat represents Greece, with its horn as the first great king. Many understand this to be Alexander the Great. The vision encourages God's people by showing that God knows the future.

Empires seem invincible, but none lasts forever. You can rest in the knowledge that God continues to govern history, even when the world seems to be in the hands of the powerful. Trust Him with your fears.
exp.7:6:
He says that the male goat came near the ram, attacked it in fury, and broke off its two horns. The ram had no strength to resist, so it was knocked down and trampled, and no one could rescue it.

He says that the male goat came near the ram, attacked it in fury, and broke off its two horns. The ram had no strength to resist, so it was knocked down and trampled, and no one could rescue it.

Daniel tells of a vision he received and describes it as he saw it. Later in the same chapter, the angel Gabriel explains that the ram represents the kings of Media and Persia, and the male goat the kingdom of Greece. Many understand that the great horn is Alexander the Great. God shows Daniel that empires rise and fall according to his plan.

For today: no human power lasts forever, however strong it may seem. We can trust that God still guides history, and rest in him when the world feels unstable.
exp.7:8:
Out of one of the four horns came forth another horn, small at first, but which grew very great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the pleasant land, that is, the beautiful land, which is probably Israel.

Daniel describes a vision he received in Babylon. The ram and the goat represent empires, and the angel Gabriel explains them later on (Medo-Persia and Greece). Many believe this little horn is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who oppressed Israel. Others also see a future fulfillment. The vision encouraged God's people in times of persecution.

For today: proud powers can grow very large and cause suffering, but they have a limit. God continues to govern history. When you see injustice, do not lose hope; trust in Him and remain faithful.
exp.7:9:
It says that the little horn became very powerful, so much so that it attacked the host of heaven. It threw some of that host and of the stars down to the ground and trampled them.

Daniel describes a vision he received. The male goat (Greece) had four horns after the great one was broken, and out of one came a little horn. Many connect it with Antiochus Epiphanes, who persecuted the Jews, and some also see a broader meaning pointing toward the future. The "stars" probably symbolize God's people. The vision comforted Israel: their suffering did not escape God's control.

For today: when evil seems to win and the powerful crush the weak, let us remember that their power has a limit. Let us be faithful and pray with confidence, because God still governs.
exp.7:21:
It says that the great horn of the male goat, which is the first king of Greece (Javan), was broken. In its place four horns came up, and this means that four kingdoms would arise from that same nation. But they would not have the strength and power that the first king had.

Here the angel Gabriel speaks, explaining to Daniel the vision of the ram and the male goat. Many understand that the first king is Alexander the Great, and that the four kingdoms arose after his death, when his empire was divided. This follows the line of the text, though the book does not give all the names. The message shows Daniel that empires change, and that God knows the future of his people.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever. If we see that the world changes and is shaken, we can rest in God, who remains the firm King.
exp.7:23:
It says that a cruel and arrogant king will become very powerful, but his strength will not really be his own. He will destroy in a way that is astonishing, which is to say in an amazing manner. He will succeed, doing whatever he wants without being held accountable, and he will attack powerful people and the people of God, the holy ones.

Here the angel Gabriel speaks, explaining to Daniel the vision of the ram and the goat. Many understand this king to be connected with Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who persecuted the Jews, and some see in it also a foreshadowing of a final oppressor. It is interpreted in several ways. God shows this to Daniel to encourage his people.

For today: unjust powers may seem unstoppable, but they have limits. Trust that God still governs, and remain faithful even when others prosper by doing wrong.
exp.7:24:
He says this wicked king will be clever and deceitful, and that his schemes will succeed. He will feel very important and will destroy many when they are unsuspecting, without them expecting it. He will even stand against the Prince of princes, who is God himself. But he will be broken, not by human strength, but by the action of God. The word "craft" in the verse means cunning, the skill of deception.

An angel, Gabriel, explains to Daniel a vision about a ram and a goat. Many believe this king refers to Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who persecuted the Jews; others also see a future figure. This is said to have comforted an oppressed people.

For today: the powerful who deceive and think themselves untouchable do not have the last word. We can remain faithful and trust that God judges with justice, even if it takes time.
exp.7:26:
Daniel says that he was left without strength and sick for several days. When he recovered, he went back to his duties in the king's service. But he was still astonished and deeply troubled by the vision, and no one could explain it to him.

Daniel himself is speaking, at the end of a vision about a ram, a male goat, and a cruel king who would arise. The angel Gabriel had explained part of it, but Daniel did not grasp everything. He had been told to keep the vision sealed, because it concerned many days to come. That is why he is left troubled, though obedient.

For today: we will not always understand everything God allows or reveals. We can, like Daniel, feel the weight of confusion, rest for a while, and then keep faithfully fulfilling our responsibilities, trusting that God knows more than we do.
exp.8:0:
In the first year of Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent, Daniel receives this scene. Darius was placed as king over the realm of the Chaldeans, that is, Babylon. The phrase about being placed indicates that he did not come to power merely by inheritance; someone gave him the office.

The writer is Daniel, a Jewish exile in Babylon. The passage marks the exact moment: Babylon had fallen and power was changing hands. Scholars debate the identity of this Darius, and there is no single certain answer. What matters here is that Daniel, in this time of change, turns to the Scriptures and prays for his people.

For today: when everything around you changes, return to the Word of God. Read it attentively and pray with humility. God remains faithful even when governments and circumstances change.
exp.8:2:
Daniel says that he turned toward God with his whole being. He sought him by praying and making supplication, and he also fasted. The rough cloth of mourning that was worn, and the dust that was placed on the head or used as a place to sit, were signs of humility and deep sorrow.

Daniel speaks as an old man in Babylon, during the first year of Darius the Mede. He had read in the writings of Jeremiah that the exile would last seventy years. When he saw that this time was being fulfilled, he did not simply wait, but turned to prayer. He immediately confesses the sins of his people, and his own sins as part of that people.

For today: when God shows you one of his promises, respond with sincere and humble prayer. Do not pray only to ask for things, but also to acknowledge your faults and to seek God with your whole heart.
exp.8:3:
Daniel says that he prayed to the Lord, his God, and confessed his sins. He begins by acknowledging who God is: great and dreadful, that is, he deserves deep respect and reverence. He says that God keeps his covenant (his solemn promise) and his mercy (his faithful love) toward those who love him and keep his commandments.

Daniel speaks as an older man who lived in exile in Babylon. He had read in the writings of Jeremiah that the destruction of Jerusalem would last seventy years. Seeing that this time was being fulfilled, he sought God with fasting and humility. Before asking for anything, he confesses the sins of the people, and includes himself among them.

For today: before asking God for anything, let us remember who he is and his faithfulness. Praying with humility and sincerity, without excuses, opens the heart to his forgiveness and his help.
exp.8:7:
Daniel tells God that the shame belongs to them. That shame reaches the kings, the princes, and the fathers, that is, every level of the people. The reason is clear: they sinned against God.

Daniel prays in Babylon, during the exile. He is reading the prophecies of Jeremiah and speaks to God on behalf of all Israel. Although he himself is presented as a faithful man, he includes himself in the people's guilt. He does not blame others or justify himself; he acknowledges that God was right to discipline Israel.

When we fail, healing begins with acknowledging it without excuses. Tell God the truth, without hiding or blaming others, because he is merciful and forgives.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that mercy and forgiveness belong to the Lord our God. What stands out is that he says this even though his people rebelled against him. Mercy is the love that does not give the punishment deserved, and forgiveness is wiping away the debt of sin.

The speaker is Daniel, a faithful man who lived in exile in Babylon. He is praying for his people and acknowledges that Israel deserved punishment. He does not defend himself or look for excuses; he confesses the sin of kings, princes, and ordinary people alike. His hope does not rest on the merits of the people, but on the character of God.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or justify yourself. Go to God with sincerity, because his heart is merciful. Confessing your wrong with humility opens the door to forgiveness and to a fresh start.
exp.8:10:
Daniel says that all of Israel broke God's law. They turned away so that they would not listen to his voice. Because of this, the curse and the oath fell upon them, that is, the consequences that God had warned about in the law of Moses for anyone who turned away from him.

Daniel is praying in Babylon, during the exile. He has read what the prophet Jeremiah said about the years of captivity. Although he himself lived faithfully, he confesses the people's sin as if it were his own, and he acknowledges that God was just in keeping his word.

For today: when we fail, there is no need to make excuses or blame others. We can speak with God honestly, admit our wrong, and return to him, trusting that he is merciful and forgives.
exp.8:12:
It says that all the disaster that fell upon Israel had already been written in the Law of Moses. Even so, the people did not seek the favor of the LORD with sincere prayer, turning from their wickedness and giving attention to His truth.

Daniel speaks while the Jews are in exile in Babylon. He reads that the time of the desolation of Jerusalem is drawing to its end, and he prays, confessing the sin of the whole people, including himself. He acknowledges that God was faithful to His word, both in the warnings and in the promises.

For today: do not wait until the consequences arrive to seek God. Today you can draw near to Him with humility, acknowledge your mistakes, and ask Him to teach you to live according to His truth.
exp.8:15:
Daniel asks God to turn away his anger and fury from Jerusalem, the city that belongs to him and his holy mountain. He acknowledges that God is righteous, and that because of the sins of the people and their ancestors, Jerusalem and Judah have become an object of mockery and shame in the eyes of all the nations around them.

Daniel prays while the people live in exile in Babylon. He had read in the Scriptures that the exile would last seventy years (Jeremiah 25 and 29). For this reason he confesses the sins of everyone as if they were his own, and he asks for mercy, relying on the character of God rather than on the merits of the people.

For today: when we have failed, we can draw near to God with sincerity, without excuses, and trust in his goodness rather than in our own achievements. Praying with humility for our family, church, or country is an act of love that God hears.
exp.8:17:
In this verse, Daniel asks God to hear him and to look closely at the ruin of Jerusalem, the city that bears God's name. He says that he does not pray trusting that his people are good, but in God's great compassion.

Daniel speaks on behalf of his people, who are in exile in Babylon. He had read that the desolation of Jerusalem would last a set amount of time, and so he prays confessing the sin of Israel. He acknowledges that the punishment was just, and yet he asks for forgiveness and restoration for the sake of God's name.

For today: when we pray, let us not come before God presenting our merits, but with humility, trusting in his mercy. We can be honest about our failures and still draw near with hope, because God is compassionate.
exp.8:18:
Daniel prays with great urgency. He asks God to hear, to forgive, and to act without delay. The request "act" means that God would step in and work. "Delay" means putting something off or holding it back. Daniel does not appeal to his own merits, but to the name of God, which is called over Jerusalem and over his people.

Daniel speaks on behalf of Israel, which was living in exile in Babylon. He had understood from the writings of Jeremiah that the desolation of Jerusalem would last for a set period of time. Because of this, he confesses the sins of the people as if they were his own. While he is praying, the angel Gabriel arrives with an answer.

For today: when you pray, do not rely on your own merits, but on the mercy and character of God. Be honest about your failings, ask for forgiveness, and pray with confidence that God will act according to his glory and his goodness.
exp.8:19:
Daniel says that he was still praying when what follows took place. As he spoke with God, he confessed his own sin and the sin of all Israel, and he presented his request before the Lord, his God. He had in mind the holy mountain, that is, Jerusalem, the place where the temple stood. Pouring out his plea means that he prayed with his whole heart, holding nothing back.

Daniel is the one speaking. He lived in exile in Babylon, and from reading Jeremiah he had understood that the time of the people's punishment was being fulfilled. For that reason he prayed with humility, without claiming to be righteous, and he asked for mercy for Jerusalem, which lay in ruins. While he was praying, God sent the angel Gabriel with an answer.

For today: when you pray, do not hide behind your merits. Speak with sincerity, acknowledge your failings, and trust in God's mercy. You can also pray for your family, your church, and your country, as Daniel did.
exp.8:23:
Daniel 9:24 says that seventy weeks have been decreed for your people, the people of Israel, and for your holy city, Jerusalem. Each "week" probably means a period of seven years. That time has goals: "transgression" is rebellion against God; "atonement" is covering or wiping away guilt; "everlasting righteousness" is a righteousness that lasts. To "seal up" means to confirm or close up, and "anoint the most Holy" may point to a holy place or to a holy person.

The angel Gabriel speaks with Daniel, who had prayed confessing the sin of his people. God answers with a plan for their future. Christians often see the Messiah here, although there are several interpretations about the dates and the details.

For today: God hears sincere prayer and has a plan to remove sin. Pray with confidence and humility, knowing that he keeps his promises in his own time.
exp.8:24:
Through the angel Gabriel, God tells Daniel to pay attention and understand. From the time the command goes out to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the coming of the Messiah the Prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. The word translated "weeks" most likely means groups of seven years. The city will be rebuilt, with its street and wall, though in troubled times.

Daniel was praying for his people in exile, and Gabriel arrives with the answer. Interpreters do not agree about which command is meant or how to calculate the years, but many Christians see Jesus as the Messiah in this passage.

For today: God has a plan with appointed times and purposes, even when we live through difficult seasons. We can pray with confidence and wait with patience, because He keeps what He promises.
exp.8:26:
It says that during one "week" (a period of seven years, according to most interpreters) someone will make a firm covenant with many. In the middle of that time, that person will stop the sacrifices and offerings. Then abominations that bring desolation will come, until the punishment already decided is poured out on the destroyed people. The word "Á" is "a," and "derramaráse" is "se derramará."

Gabriel speaks to Daniel, who had prayed for Jerusalem and its people. He explains to him what God has determined for them. There is discussion about who this person is: some see Christ and his sacrifice that brings an end to the temple sacrifices; others see an enemy ruler, either from the past or from the future. Christians do not agree on this.

For today: although we may not understand every detail, we can trust that God is in control of history. Like Daniel, let us draw near to Him in prayer with humility, knowing that his purposes are fulfilled.
exp.9:2:
Daniel tells us that for three weeks he kept a partial fast. He ate no fine bread, no meat, and no wine. He also did not anoint himself with oil, which was a scented oil used for cleansing and for lifting one's spirits.

Daniel, now an old man, speaks in the third year of King Cyrus. He had received a true revelation, but one that was hard and long to understand. He was troubled, and so he humbled himself and sought God with fasting and mourning. After this time, in the verse that follows, he has an impressive vision beside the river.

For today: when something weighs on you or you do not understand what God allows, seek His face with humility and perseverance. A simple fast, made with prayer and without seeking applause, can help you set aside distractions and listen to God with greater attention.
exp.9:4:
Daniel lifts up his eyes and sees a man clothed in linen, with his waist girded with fine gold of Uphaz. Linen suggests purity or a special service, and the waist is the part of the body where the belt or girdle is fastened. Where Uphaz was located is not known for certain; the words only indicate gold of very high quality.

Daniel speaks, beside the river Tigris (Hiddekel). He had just completed three weeks of mourning and fasting, seeking to understand what God had shown him. Many believe this man is an angel; others think he is an appearance of the Lord. The text does not fully settle the question.

For today: when we seek God with humility and perseverance, he can answer in ways that exceed what we imagine. Set aside a quiet time this week to pray and listen attentively.
exp.9:5:
He says Daniel saw a man with a striking appearance. His body shone like a precious stone, probably a gold or blue-green gem (no one knows for certain which). His face was like lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, and his arms and feet like polished brass. His voice sounded like the roar of a crowd or of an army.

Daniel himself tells what he saw beside the river Tigris (here called Hiddekel), after three weeks of fasting and prayer. Who this being is is not clear: some believe he is a powerful angel, like Gabriel, and others think it is an appearance of Christ before he was born. Christians have understood it in both ways.

For today: God is far greater and more glorious than we imagine. When we pray, let us do it with reverence and confidence, knowing that heaven is full of power and that our prayers do not fall into emptiness.
exp.9:9:
This verse says that a hand touched Daniel and helped him move, until he was resting on his knees and the palms of his hands. Daniel was lying on the ground, without strength.

Daniel had just seen an overwhelming vision and was left alone, weak, with his face toward the ground. The text does not say who the messenger is; many believe it is an angel, and others see it differently. What is clear is that he comes from God, because the passage then says that Daniel's prayers were heard.

For today: when you feel without strength or afraid, God does not leave you lying down. He touches you with gentle help, little by little, and raises you up. Ask him for that first step.
exp.9:10:
He tells me that a heavenly messenger speaks to Daniel and calls him a man greatly beloved, that is, a man who is highly loved and esteemed. He asks Daniel to understand his words and to stand upright, because he has been sent to him. Daniel was trembling while he listened.

Daniel had been praying and fasting for his people. The one speaking is a being sent by God; the text does not give his name, and some think he is an angel, such as Gabriel. Daniel sees an overwhelming vision and is left without strength. The messenger encourages him and prepares him to receive a revelation about the future.

For today: God sees those who seek him sincerely. When we pray, we can come near with reverence, but also with confidence, knowing that he hears us and can give us strength to rise and keep going forward.
exp.9:11:
A messenger from heaven tells Daniel not to be afraid. From the first day that Daniel set his heart on understanding and humbled himself before God, his prayer was heard, and that is why the messenger came.

The one speaking is an angel, whose name is not given, although some have identified him with Gabriel; the text does not state this. Daniel had been in mourning and fasting for three weeks, seeking to understand a vision about his people. He is trembling, and the messenger calms him by explaining that God heard his prayer from the beginning, even though the answer was delayed. The verses that follow describe a spiritual struggle that caused the delay.

For today: when it seems that God is not answering, remember that He hears you from the first word. The delay does not mean silence or abandonment. Keep praying with humility and confidence.
exp.9:13:
He says the heavenly messenger came to explain to Daniel what would happen to his people, Israel, in the latter days, that is, in times to come. The vision, he says, is still for many days, meaning that what he saw would be fulfilled later on, not right away.

The one speaking is a being sent by God, whose identity is not made clear. Some think he is an angel, others that he is a manifestation of the Lord. Daniel had been praying and fasting for three weeks in sorrow. The messenger says that God heard his prayer from the first day, but a spiritual struggle delayed the answer. The "latter days" are understood in different ways: as the times of Israel under future empires, or also as the end of the age.

For today: if your prayer seems slow to be answered, do not conclude that God has not heard you. He hears from the very first moment and works in his own time. Keep praying with patience and confidence.
exp.9:16:
Daniel says to the heavenly being standing before him: how can a mere servant talk with someone so great? He feels that he has no strength left and can hardly breathe. Here "breath" means breathing or courage. The phrase "my lord" is a respectful way of addressing him.

Daniel speaks as an old man, after three weeks of mourning and fasting. He has just seen an overwhelming vision and feels overcome. Someone with the appearance of a human touches him, gives him strength, and tells him not to be afraid. Scholars do not agree on who this messenger is; many think he is an angel.

For today: when you feel small or weak before God, or in a difficult situation, do not stay silent out of fear. Bring your weakness to him honestly. He often strengthens us so that we can listen and keep going.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that God's messenger is going to reveal to Daniel what has already been written down in the scripture of truth, something like a secure record of what God has determined. It adds that no one stands with him in this spiritual struggle except Michael, whom it calls your prince, that is, a leader or protector of Israel. The word "but" in the verse is the same as the word for "but" in the verse you are reading, and the phrase about helping him firmly means giving him strong support.

It speaks of a heavenly being who strengthened Daniel after he prayed and fasted. He has come to explain the future of his people. He speaks of a conflict with the princes of Persia and Greece, and many understand these to be spiritual forces behind the kingdoms, though some interpret it differently. The Bible gives no further detail.

For today: when you pray, trust that God works beyond what you can see. Keep praying with patience, because your hope rests in his truth, not in your circumstances.
exp.10:1:
Here the angel tells Daniel that he is going to show him the truth: there will still be three more kings in Persia, and a fourth who will be far richer than all of them. With that economic power, this king will stir up everyone against Javán, which is the biblical name for Greece.

The one speaking is a heavenly messenger who gives Daniel a revelation about the future. Many scholars think the fourth king is Xerxes, who attacked Greece, but some dispute this. The verses that follow announce a brave king, whom many identify with Alexander the Great, and whose kingdom would be divided into four.

For today: empires, money, and power may seem firm, but God knows the course of history and remains in control. When the world seems uncertain to you, rest in the knowledge that God sustains what is coming.
exp.10:2:
It says that after the kings of Persia a very strong king will appear. He will have a great empire and will do whatever he wants, with no one to stop him. The phrase about ruling means that he will dominate or govern with authority. The phrase about doing his will means that he will act as he pleases.

The one speaking is an angel who gives Daniel a vision of the future. Many scholars see Alexander the Great here, because the next verse speaks of a kingdom divided into four parts, and this fits the history. Even so, some prefer to see it in a more general way. The message seeks to show that God knows and directs history.

The great human powers seem firm, but they pass away. Today you can rest in the fact that God is still in control, even when the world appears to be dominated by the powerful. Trust in Him and serve with humility.
exp.10:3:
It says that the brave king of the previous verse will become very powerful, but his kingdom will be broken just when it is at its height. It will be divided toward the four winds of heaven. It will not pass to his children or keep the same strength, for it will be torn up and handed over to others.

An angel speaking to Daniel explains what is to come. Many scholars see here Alexander the Great, whose empire was divided among his generals and not among his descendants. Others read it differently, but this is the most common reading. God shows his servant that history is not beyond his control.

For today: do not place your security in power, money, or success, because all of that is temporary. Trust in God, whose kingdom never ends.
exp.10:7:
He says that the king of the south, who in the text is the one who rises up to take revenge, will carry off to Egypt the idols of his enemies, their leaders, and their valuable objects of silver and gold. "Precious vessels" are utensils and objects of value. Afterward, for some years, that king will leave the king of the north alone, that is, he will not attack him.

An angel speaks to Daniel and announces, in great detail, conflicts between two kingdoms neighboring Israel, the northern one and the southern one. Many scholars see here the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings, and Ptolemy III with his campaign. Others interpret it differently. The purpose is to show that God knows and directs history.

For today: kingdoms and their treasures pass away, and even their false gods cannot defend themselves. Entrust your life to God, who remains in control when the world seems chaotic.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that the king of the south is filled with fury and goes out to fight against the king of the north. He gathers a huge army, and the enemy army falls into his hands, meaning he wins that battle. The south is the direction the verse refers to, and the phrase about the army means that he organizes a force for war.

Here an angel speaks to Daniel, explaining what will happen in the future. Many scholars see in these verses the wars between the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt (the south) and the Seleucid kings of Syria (the north), after Alexander the Great. Some identify this battle with Raphia, in 217 BC, although this is an interpretation. The purpose is to show that God knows history and guides it.

For today: human powers rage, win and lose, but none of them controls history. You can rest in the fact that God remains faithful, even when the world seems chaotic.
exp.10:12:
This verse says that the king of the north will return and gather an army greater than the previous one. After a certain number of years, he will come quickly, bringing a great army and much wealth.

An angel speaks to Daniel and announces what will happen between two powers that surround Israel: the king of the north and the king of the south. Many scholars see here the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms, and in this verse, Antiochus III, although some interpret it in other ways. The purpose is to show that God knows history in advance.

For today: empires and wars may seem to control everything, but they do not have the last word. Trust that God continues to govern history, and rest in Him when the world seems confusing to you.
exp.10:13:
It says that in those times many will rise up against the king of the south. It also says that some men, violent and destructive ones from among your own people, will lift themselves up to bring about what was foretold, but they will fail and fall.

An angel speaks to Daniel and describes the conflicts between the king of the north and the king of the south, which many understand as the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms after Alexander the Great. Some interpreters see here Jews who attempted a rebellion and failed, but there is no complete agreement about who they were. The message is that God knows the course of history in advance.

For today: even when leaders and nations seem to control everything, God remains in control. You do not need to force His plans through pride or violence; trust Him and act with humility and patience.
exp.10:15:
This verse says that a powerful king, the king of the north, will advance against the king of the south and do whatever he wants, with no one able to stop him. He will establish himself in the land of Israel, which is often understood as the glorious land. There, the idea that the land would be destroyed or brought under his control is suggested, meaning he would ruin it or hold it under his power. Acting as he pleases is what the verse describes when it says he does according to his own will.

An angel explains to Daniel what will happen to the kingdoms that dominate the region. Many interpreters see here Antiochus III, the Seleucid king, conquering Israel around 200 BC. Others interpret it differently. God wants his people to know that history does not take him by surprise.

For today: when the powerful seem unstoppable, remember that God still governs history. Trust in him and stand firm.
exp.10:16:
The northern king arrives with all the strength of his kingdom. He makes an agreement that seems fair with the southern king, and he gives him a young woman to ruin his kingdom from within. The plan does not hold, and it does not serve him.

A heavenly messenger explains to Daniel what will come upon his people. Many understand that he is speaking of Antiochus III and the marriage of his daughter to the king of Egypt, but there are different interpretations. The deeper message is that God knows the history and governs it, even when kings scheme.

For today: do not trust in deception or crooked deals to get ahead. Act with integrity and rest in God, because plans without truth eventually collapse.
exp.10:19:
It says that after the previous king, another will come to take his throne. This one will send a raiser of taxes to collect money from the kingdom and keep up its splendor. But his reign will be short: within a few days he will be destroyed, and not by a fight or a war.

An angel explains to Daniel what will happen to the kingdoms that come after Persia. Many believe this verse speaks of Seleucus IV, who sent Heliodorus to collect taxes and died shortly afterward, apparently without battle. That is the most common interpretation, though not the only one.

For today: rulers and their projects are temporary, but God still guides history. When you see power and wealth that seem impossible to stop, remember that only God endures, and trust in Him.
exp.10:23:
It says that a king will enter a rich and peaceful region when no one expects it. He will do what neither his fathers nor his grandfathers did: he will distribute plunder, spoil and riches among his soldiers. He will also plan attacks against fortified cities, but only for a limited time.

An angel speaks with Daniel and reveals what will come between the northern and southern kingdoms. Many understand that this refers to Antiochus IV Epiphanes, although some also see in the passage a foretelling of a future tyrant. A deceptive power is shown, but one with limits.

For today: do not let yourself be fooled by someone who promises much and acts with cunning. The powers of this world have a set time, and God still governs history. Trust in Him and live with honesty.
exp.10:24:
It says that a king of the north will stir up his strength and his courage to attack the king of the south with a great army. The king of the south will also go out to fight with a very mighty army, but he will not prevail, because he will be betrayed.

An angel speaks to Daniel and announces future conflicts between two neighboring kingdoms. Many scholars see here the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings, and Antiochus IV and Egypt, though some interpret it differently. The message is that God knows history and directs it, and that everything happens at the appointed time.

For today: let us not trust only in strength, money, or human plans. Even the powerful fall through betrayal and deceit. We can rest in the knowledge that God is in control, and seek to live with honesty and loyalty.
exp.10:25:
They that eat of his table, his closest advisers and trusted people, will betray him and bring about his downfall. To "destroy" him here means to bring him to ruin. His army will be defeated, and many will be slain.

The one speaking is a heavenly messenger who explains to Daniel what is to come. Many understand this to be about the wars between the kings of the north and the south, and they often see in the king of the north Antiochus IV, although some interpret it differently. The message is that, even though kings plan and deceive, God still governs history and has an appointed time.

For today: trust and loyalty are worth more than power. Take care of your relationships, be faithful to those who trust you, and rest in the knowledge that God is in control.
exp.10:27:
It says that the king of the north returns to his own country loaded with riches, but with his heart set against the holy covenant, that is, God's people and their faith. He acts against that covenant and then goes back to his land.

It is part of a prophecy that an angel gives Daniel about conflicts between the kings of the north and the south. Many understand that it refers to Antiochus IV Epiphanes and his return from Egypt, when he attacked Jerusalem and the faithful Jews, although some also see a future fulfillment. The purpose is to show that God knows and controls history, and that everything happens according to his appointed time.

For today: when evil seems to triumph, do not lose hope. Remain faithful to God, because He governs time and cares for His people.
exp.10:28:
In the appointed time, the king of the north, as God had already set, will return and attack the south, which is Egypt. But this time the outcome will be different from the first campaign.

An angel explains to Daniel what will happen in the future with the kingdoms that would rule the region and with God's people. Many believe this refers to Antiochus IV Epiphanes and his second campaign against Egypt, which failed when the ships of Kittim, that is, the Romans, stopped him. Some also see a more distant fulfillment. Interpreters do not fully agree.

Even though the powerful make plans and seem to be in control, God governs the times. Today you can rest knowing that no abuse or injustice escapes his plan. Trust in him and remain faithful, even when everything seems difficult.
exp.10:33:
When they fall, they are given a little help, meaning a brief and limited aid. But many also join themselves to them with flattery, false praise and empty compliments. These people are not sincere; they come near out of convenience.

An angel speaks to Daniel, announcing what will come upon God's people. Many interpreters see here the persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, in the time of the Maccabees, although others also see a future application. The Maccabees may have been that little help, but it is not known that all of them were sincere. The purpose is to prepare and comfort the faithful.

For today: do not be surprised if in trial the help is small and some surround you with falseness. Be thankful for the simple support God gives you and seek sincere friendships. Remain firm, trusting in Him.
exp.10:34:
It says that some of the wise, that is, those who teach and guide the people, will stumble or suffer persecution. That trial will serve to purify them, as metal is refined or cloth is washed clean. This will last until the appointed time, the moment God has already set. The word "appointed" means a fixed limit.

An angel explains to Daniel what will come upon his people. He speaks first of persecutions, probably under foreign kings, and many interpreters see here Antiochus IV. Others also see a future fulfillment. The message is that God knows how long the trial will last.

For today: if you are going through a trial for remaining faithful, do not see it as abandonment. God can use it to purify you, and He holds control of the time. Hold on to Him with patience.
exp.10:35:
It says there is a king who does as he pleases. He is filled with pride and considers himself greater than any god. He even speaks astonishing and terrible things against the God of gods. He prospers for a time, until the indignation is finished, that is, God's judgment. Determination means something already decided by God.

Here an angel is explaining to Daniel what will come. Encouragement is given to God's people in times of persecution. Scholars disagree about who this king is: some think of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, others of a future antichrist, and others see both.

For today: human power and pride do not last forever. God still governs, even when the proud prosper. Trust in Him and stay humble.
exp.10:37:
This verse says that the king the prophecy speaks of will stop honoring the God of his fathers and will instead honor a god of fortresses (that means Mauzim). His ancestors did not know this god. He will honor it with gold, silver, precious stones, and very valuable things.

An angel speaks, revealing to Daniel what will happen in the future. The passage describes a proud and powerful king. Scholars interpret it in several ways: some see Antiochus IV Epiphanes, others a future ruler, the antichrist. There is no complete agreement, and so it is wise to be humble when interpreting it.

For today: when power, strength, or money take the place of God, the heart goes astray. Ask yourself what you trust in most, and put God first again.
exp.10:39:
It says that, at the appointed time at the end, the king of the south will clash with the king who is being described, like two bulls butting heads (that is what the idea of goring each other means). Then the king of the north will strike back with force like a storm, with war chariots, horsemen, and many ships. He will invade lands, overflow them like a flood, and keep advancing.

An angel speaks to Daniel and reveals future conflicts between the kings of the north and the south, which are probably set against the background of the kingdoms that followed Alexander the Great. Many believe this passage describes Antiochus IV, and others also see a reference to a final time. Interpreters do not agree on who "he" is. The purpose was to encourage God's people in times of persecution.

For today: powerful empires and leaders may seem to control everything, but God knows and governs history. When the world feels unstable, rest in the fact that his plan still stands.
exp.10:44:
He says this king will pitch his royal tents, that is, his camp with his command tent, between the seas and the pleasant holy mountain. Nearly everyone understands this to refer to Jerusalem, the holy mountain, and that the seas would be the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea. But in the end he will come to his end, and no one will help him.

An angel speaks to Daniel and reveals what will happen with powerful kings. This king is described as proud and violent. Interpreters do not agree on who he is: some think of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, others of a future ruler, the antichrist. What is clear is that the message aims to comfort God's people in times of oppression.

For today: no human power lasts forever, however strong it may seem. You can rest and remain faithful, trusting that God has the last word over history and over your life.
exp.11:0:
In a future time, Michael will stand up, the great prince or protecting angel of Daniel's people. It will be a time of distress such as never before in history, but God's people will be delivered, that is, everyone who is written in the book.

An angel speaks with Daniel at the end of his book, after visions about kingdoms and persecutions. He wants to encourage a people who will suffer. Some think he is speaking of the persecution under Antiochus IV, others of the end of time, and others of both. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: even when difficult times come, your security does not depend on circumstances, but on the fact that God knows his own and cares for them. Rest in him and keep doing good with hope.
exp.11:5:
This question is asked by one of the two beings who stood on the banks of the river. He directs it to the man dressed in linen, who was standing above the waters. He wants to know how much longer until the end of these wonders, that is, the astonishing and difficult events Daniel had just seen. The end refers to the fulfillment of everything.

Daniel receives a vision about times of great distress for God's people. One of the heavenly beings asks on behalf of everyone, and the man in linen answers with an oath: it will be a time, times, and half a time. Interpreters understand this in several ways. Daniel himself acknowledges that he heard, but did not understand.

For today: you do not need to understand everything to trust God. When there are questions without answers, bring them to Him honestly, and rest in the knowledge that He is in control of time.
exp.11:9:
This verse says that in the time of the end, many will be cleansed, made white, and purified, that is, made clean before God. By contrast, the wicked, those who live without wanting to obey God, will keep acting badly and will not understand. The ones who understand are the wise, those whose hearts are set on God.

The one speaking is the angel who reveals visions to Daniel about times of great trial. Daniel heard but did not comprehend, and he asked how everything would end. The angel answers that these words are sealed until the time of their fulfillment. The numbers of days that follow have been interpreted in several ways, and there is no single agreement.

For today: trial can purify us or harden us, depending on the attitude of the heart. If you do not understand everything, do not be discouraged. Seek God with humility, obey what you already know, and wait with patience.
exp.11:10:
It says that from the time the continual sacrifice (the daily offering presented to God in the temple) is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up (something detestable that defiles what is holy), there will be a thousand two hundred and ninety days, roughly three and a half years.

An angel speaks to Daniel at the end of the book, after visions about kings and persecution against God's people. Many believe it refers to the defiling of the temple under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and others also see a future fulfillment. Christians interpret it in different ways. What is clear is that the time of trial has a limit set by God.

For today: when you go through a difficult season, remember that God does not leave it without end or without control. Even if you do not understand everything, you can wait faithfully, trusting that he knows when it will end.
exp.10:30:
Armed forces will rise up to support this king. They will desecrate the temple fortress, and they will end the daily sacrifice. They will set up the abomination of desolation, an object or pagan worship that makes the holy place unclean.

An angel explains to Daniel what will come upon his people. Many scholars see here Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who in 167 B.C. desecrated the temple in Jerusalem. Others also see a future fulfillment, since Jesus mentioned this "abomination of desolation" (Matthew 24:15). Opinions vary.

For today: even when evil seems to win, God knows how things will end. The verses that follow say that the people who know their God will be strong. Knowing him each day in prayer and in his Word sustains us under pressure.
exp.8:4:
Daniel confesses the people's sin using several words that build on one another so their weight is felt. "Sinned and done wrong" points to falling short of what is right. "Acted wickedly" describes living without reverence for God. "Rebelled" means resisting his authority. Then comes "turned away from Your commandments and ordinances," which names the heart of the failure: the people turned their backs on the standards God had given them. Together these phrases end in a clear admission of turning away from what God commanded.

Daniel speaks as an elderly man in exile in Babylon. He had understood from the writings of the prophet Jeremiah that the time of the exile was drawing to an end. He then prays with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes, signs of humility and grief. He says "we have," even though his own life was faithful, because he identifies himself with his people.

For today: when we pray, let us not justify ourselves or blame others. Let us name our failures sincerely before God, trusting in his mercy.
exp.6:2:
This verse says that Daniel saw four huge beasts coming up out of the sea, with each one different from the others. The phrase "came up out of the sea" means they were rising from the waters, emerging into view.

Daniel is the one speaking, writing down what he saw in a dream at night, during the reign of Belshazzar in Babylon. The winds and the churning sea suggest confusion and conflict among the nations. Later the text explains that the beasts represent kingdoms. Scholars debate exactly which kingdoms they are, though many think of Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome.

For today: the powers of this world can seem huge and frightening, but Daniel reminds us that they do not have the last word. God is the one who governs history. When the news unsettles you, rest in the fact that He is still in control.
exp.6:13:
He says that the one who looks like "a son of man" was given authority, honor, and a kingdom. "Dominion" means power to rule. "Was given to him" is the sense here: the authority was handed to him. "Will not pass away" describes what does not come to an end. "Will not be destroyed" means it will never be ruined. People of every nation and language serve him, and his kingdom never ends.

Daniel speaks, recounting a vision he had at night. Earlier he saw beasts that represented kingdoms with limited power. Now he sees this figure come with the clouds before the Ancient of Days, that is, God. Christians see Jesus here, who used that title for himself. Some scholars also connect it to God's faithful people.

Today we can rest knowing that human governments pass away, but Christ's kingdom remains. When the news troubles you, pray and trust: the future is in God's hands, not in fear.
exp.9:14:
Daniel tells us that, while the angel was speaking these things to him, he lowered his gaze to the ground and was left unable to speak. The Berean wording describes him as becoming speechless, meaning he was struck silent. "These words" refers to what the messenger had just told him.

The one speaking is Daniel, now an old man, who has been praying and fasting. A heavenly messenger explains that a spiritual struggle had delayed his arrival, and that the vision concerns the future of his people. Daniel is overwhelmed before something so great. Afterward, someone with human appearance touches his lips and restores his ability to speak.

There are moments when, before God, the best thing is to be quiet, bow our heads, and listen. And if something overwhelms us, we can trust that God himself strengthens us and gives us words, as he did with Daniel.
exp.7:25:
It says that what the angel explained about "the evenings and the mornings" is true. It refers to the vision of the 2300 evenings and mornings (Daniel 8:14). Daniel is told to seal up the vision, that is, to keep it sealed and hidden, because it concerns the distant future.

The one speaking is the angel Gabriel, who has just explained to Daniel the vision of the ram, the male goat, and a fierce king who would oppress God's people. Interpreters disagree about the details, but many see here Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and others also see a future application. Daniel is left sick and confused.

For today: God is in control of history, even when we do not understand everything. We can trust Him, keep His Word in our hearts, and wait patiently, without being troubled by what we still cannot see clearly.
exp.4:0:
Here it says that King Belshazzar held a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and he drank wine with them.

Here the narrator of the book of Daniel speaks, and he opens the scene of a famous night in Babylon. Belshazzar appears as king, and the text calls Nebuchadnezzar his "father," something many understand to mean an ancestor or predecessor. The account sets up what follows: a feast of pride and excess that will end in judgment.

For today: be careful of a life of excess and of showing off before others. What looks like a grand celebration can hide a life without the fear of God. Let us ask him for humility and self-control, and remember that he sees everything, even when no one seems to be holding us accountable.
exp.3:6:
The verse says that the king called in his counselors: magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners. He told them his dream, but none of them could explain it to him. The king's own account of this moment is clear: he had been troubled by the dream, and he looked for answers among the wise men of his kingdom. The word "interpret" here means to explain what the dream means. The astrologers were men who studied the stars and claimed to read signs and omens.

The speaker is King Nebuchadnezzar, telling the story in his own words. The dream had frightened him, and he searched for answers among the wise men of his kingdom. When they failed, Daniel came in, and the king recognizes him as someone with a special spirit. Notice that the king speaks from his pagan point of view, which is why he refers to "the spirit of the holy gods."

For today: sometimes we turn to all kinds of human resources to calm our fears and doubts, and they do not bring us peace. This passage invites us to seek wisdom from God, through prayer and reading His Word, because only He truly knows the meaning of what we are going through.
exp.4:1:
Belshazzar, under the influence of the wine, gave orders to bring in the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar, his father, had taken from the temple in Jerusalem. He wanted the king to drink from them, along with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines. The verse names the nobles as the high officials of the court. The phrase "his father" probably means an ancestor, since in biblical usage "father" can also refer to a grandfather or a predecessor on the throne.

The narrator describes a lavish royal banquet. Those vessels had been set apart for the worship of God. Using them at a feast where idols were praised showed mockery and disrespect toward the God of Israel. Shortly afterward comes the judgment, with the writing on the wall.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we treat with respect what belongs to God: our time, talents, body, and worship. When pride or excess takes control of us, it is easy to make what is sacred ordinary.
exp.4:17:
Daniel tells King Belshazzar that the Most High God is the one who gave Nebuchadnezzar, his predecessor, the sovereignty, the greatness, the glory and the honor. The word "honor" means respect or dignity. Everything Nebuchadnezzar had came from God, not from his own power.

Daniel speaks before Belshazzar during a banquet at which a mysterious writing appeared on the wall. The king offers him gifts and power if he interprets it, but Daniel turns them down. Before reading the message, he reminds the king of Nebuchadnezzar's story. Daniel is preparing the king to understand that he himself did not learn that lesson.

For today: everything we have, whether work, talents or achievements, is a gift from God. Recognizing this protects us from pride and leads us to live with gratitude and humility.
exp.11:1:
This verse says that many of those who have died, who "sleep in the dust of the earth," will wake up, that is, be raised. Some will wake to everlasting life, but others will wake to shame and everlasting contempt. The word "contempt" here means scorn or disgrace.

An angel speaks to Daniel near the end of the book. He has just announced a time of great distress, but also the deliverance of those whose names are written in the book. It is one of the earliest clear statements in the Old Testament about the resurrection, given to encourage a people who were suffering.

For today: death does not have the final word, and what we do matters. You can live with hope in the midst of pain and entrust your life to God, who cares for his own.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that God sent a hand, only the palm with the fingers, and that this hand wrote the words Belshazzar saw on the wall. The verse calls it the hand that wrote the inscription. The writing is said to have been traced, or engraved, on the wall.

Daniel speaks to King Belshazzar during a banquet. A mysterious hand had just appeared and was writing on the wall, and no one knew what it said. Daniel explains that this sign comes from God in response to his pride, because he used the sacred vessels of the temple to drink and praised false gods.

For today: God sees how we use what we have and to whom we give honor. Today we can humble our hearts, thank Him for the life He gives us, and not put off turning back to Him until tomorrow.
exp.4:20:
This verse says that Nebuchadnezzar was driven away from people and lived like an animal. His mind was like that of a beast, meaning he lost his reason and acted as animals do. He lived with the wild donkeys and ate grass like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven. This lasted until he acknowledged that the Most High God rules over the kingdom of mankind and sets over it whomever He wishes.

Daniel speaks before King Belshazzar, during the feast at which a hand appeared writing on the wall. He reminds him of what happened to Nebuchadnezzar because of his pride, to show that Belshazzar had not learned that lesson.

For today: everything we have comes from God. We can ask Him for a humble and thankful heart, instead of boasting of our achievements or our power.
exp.4:13:
King Belshazzar says he has heard that the spirit of the gods is in Daniel, and that Daniel has insight, intelligence, and extraordinary wisdom. In other words, the king believes Daniel has a special ability that comes from a divine source.

King Belshazzar speaks in the middle of a banquet, when a mysterious hand wrote on the wall and no one in his court could explain it. On the advice of the queen, they summon Daniel, an exiled Jew. Note that Belshazzar speaks as a pagan, which is why he says "gods" in the plural. Daniel himself makes it clear in the book that his wisdom comes from the true God (Daniel 2:28).

For today: the people around us notice how we live, even if they do not share our faith. Let us strive for our character and wisdom to be so clear that, in moments of crisis, others know they can come to us, and so that we can point them to God as the source.
exp.4:12:
Here the account tells how Daniel was brought before King Belshazzar. The king asks him whether he is that Daniel who was one of the exiles from Judah, whom the king's father brought from Judah.

The one speaking is King Belshazzar. A mysterious hand had written on the wall during a feast, and none of his wise men could read it. The queen mother suggested he call for Daniel. From his question, it seems the king hardly knew him. Daniel was already an old man and had been away from the court for some time. The text speaks of "my father" Nebuchadnezzar; some scholars think it means an ancestor.

God can use people the world forgets. If you live faithfully before God, even when no one notices, He knows when to put you in the right place.
exp.8:25:
After sixty-two weeks, the Messiah will be cut off, meaning he will be put to death, and he will have nothing. Then the people of a coming prince will destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end will come like a flood, and there will be war until the very end, with desolations decreed.

The angel Gabriel speaks to Daniel, who was praying for Jerusalem and his people. The "weeks" are usually understood as periods of seven years. Many Christians see here Jesus and the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 A.D. Others also see a future fulfillment. The details are interpreted in various ways.

God had a plan from long before, and neither the death of the Messiah nor the ruins took him by surprise. When everything seems lost, we can trust that He still guides history.
exp.7:15:
And I heard the voice of a man calling from between the banks of the Ulai river. The voice called out, "Gabriel, explain the vision to this man." The idea of explaining the vision to Daniel is the core of the command.

Daniel had just seen a difficult vision, with a ram and a goat, and he was trying to make sense of it. Someone who looked like a man appears, and the command goes to Gabriel. This is the first time the Bible names Gabriel. Who the voice giving the command is, is not stated clearly; some think it is God himself, others a heavenly being.

For today: when you do not understand something in the Word of God, follow Daniel's example. Seek with humility and ask God for understanding. He knows how and when to help you comprehend.
exp.5:7:
Here, the high officials ask King Darius to put his official seal on the decree, so that it cannot be changed. The law of the Medes and Persians is described as one that cannot be repealed, meaning it cannot be undone once it is made.

The speakers are the governors and presidents, who envied Daniel and were looking for a way to accuse him. Since they could not find any fault in him, they used his faithfulness to God against him. They speak to the king with flattery, and the text does not say that Darius understood the trap. Daniel, when he learned of it, kept on praying as he always had.

Today we can learn from Daniel to keep our steadfastness with God, even when the environment presses us. A faithful and simple prayer, offered every day, gives us firmness when others try to silence our faith.
exp.1:19:
Daniel begins to praise God. He says that God's name should be blessed forever and ever, from eternity to eternity. The reason is that wisdom and power belong to God. Everything that is truly wise and strong comes from Him.

Daniel speaks as a young Jew exiled in Babylon. King Nebuchadnezzar had a dream that no one could tell or explain, and he had ordered the execution of all the wise men, Daniel included. After asking God for help along with his companions, God revealed the mystery to him in a night vision. The first thing Daniel does is give thanks, before presenting himself to the king.

For today: when God answers a prayer or gets you out of a difficult spot, do not walk past it. Stop first to thank Him and acknowledge that the help came from Him, not from your own cleverness.
exp.3:3:
This verse says Nebuchadnezzar lived at peace and prospering. "At ease" means without worries or threats. "Flourishing" is like a plant that grows and bears fruit: he felt strong and full of success in his palace.

The king of Babylon himself speaks, in a public letter to all the peoples. Before telling his story, he praises the Most High God for his signs. This verse begins the account: it describes his comfortable situation just before a disturbing dream frightened him. Many understand that the contrast prepares a lesson about pride and the power of God, although here only his tranquility is described.

For today: times of calm and success are also moments to thank God and not to trust in ourselves. Today, give thanks to God for what you have, and remember that everything comes from his hand.
exp.10:22:
He says this ruler will make alliances or treaties with others, but he will not keep them; he will act with trickery. Even though he will rise to power with only a few people behind him, he will keep growing stronger and will come out ahead.

The verse speaks of an alliance being made and of him acting deceitfully, so the idea is that the agreements are made, and the one making them works through deception.

An angel explains to Daniel what will happen in the future between the kings of the north and the south. Many scholars see Antiochus IV Epiphanes here, a Syrian king who persecuted the Jews, though some also see a broader prophecy. The message seeks to encourage God's people: none of this takes God by surprise.

Today we can remember that power gained through lies may look successful, but it is temporary. Let us keep our word and trust that God still rules, even when the cunning seem to win.
exp.4:25:
What it says: Daniel explains the meaning of the word "Mene." "This is the interpretation of the message" means "this is what the message means." "Mene means that God has numbered the days of your reign" means that God has counted the days of your rule. "And brought it to an end" means that God has put an end to it.

Context: Daniel, a Jewish prophet, speaks before King Belshazzar of Babylon. During a banquet, the king treated the sacred vessels of the temple in Jerusalem with contempt. Then a hand appeared and wrote on the wall, and no one could read it. Daniel interpreted it as God's judgment on the king for his pride. The text tells that that same night the kingdom passed into the hands of the Medes and Persians.

For today: Our life and our time are in God's hands. It is not wise to live with pride or to mock what is sacred. We can ask Him for humility, repent in time, and use well the days He gives us.
exp.3:4:
Daniel 4:5 says that King Nebuchadnezzar had a dream that frightened him. "Frightened him" means it alarmed him, and "alarmed" means it disturbed him deeply. The "images and visions in my mind" are the pictures he saw while he slept, and those images would not leave him alone, not even while he lay in his bed.

Here the king himself speaks, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, in a letter addressed to all the peoples. He tells how he was living at peace and prosperity when this dream shook him. Earlier he had praised the works of God, and then he relates how he came to that recognition. Next he asks his wise men to explain the dream, but none of them can.

For today: even when everything seems calm, a worry can shake us. When something unsettles us, let us not look for answers only in the voices of the moment; let us bring that unrest to God in prayer, for He gives peace and understanding.
exp.10:0:
In the first year of Darius the Mede, someone stood up to encourage him and give him strength. "Encouraging him" means cheering him on, and "strengthening him" means giving him support. The words "stood up" show a presence that helped.

The one speaking is the angel who gives Daniel his message, continuing what began at the end of chapter 10. It is not stated with certainty whom he helped: many think it was Darius, and others think it refers to Michael or to the angel himself. Then the angel promises to show him the truth about future kings and kingdoms.

For today: God works even behind what we cannot see, sustaining people in times of change. We can pray with confidence and also be someone who encourages and strengthens others.
exp.9:8:
Daniel tells us that he heard the sound of the words spoken by the being who appeared to him. As he listened, he was overcome and fell into a deep sleep, nearly unconscious, with his face to the ground.

Daniel is standing by the Tigris River, after three weeks of fasting and mourning (Daniel 10:2-4). He sees a glorious messenger, and his companions flee in fear. The Bible does not say with certainty who this being is; some believe he is an angel, others believe he is an appearance of Christ. What is clear is that Daniel is left without strength before the holiness of what he sees and hears.

For today: when God seems great to you and you feel small or weak, do not run away. Daniel was touched, lifted up, and strengthened. Come near with humility and prayer, and let God raise you up.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that Arioch quickly brought Daniel before King Nebuchadnezzar. The verse describes Arioch hastily taking Daniel to the king, and his words present Daniel as one of the exiles from Judah who will be able to tell the king the interpretation of the dream.

Arioch is speaking, the officer in charge of putting the wise men of Babylon to death. The king had ordered them killed because no one could tell him his dream or its meaning. Daniel had just prayed, and God revealed the mystery to him. Arioch presents himself as the one who found Daniel, although it was Daniel who asked to see the king.

God can use people who seem to be in the lowest place, such as an exile, to bring light and hope. If God entrusts you with something, do it with humility and do not seek your own fame. Pray first, as Daniel did, and trust that God works even in difficult situations.
exp.3:27:
It says that everything Daniel had announced in the interpretation of the dream about the cut-down tree happened to King Nebuchadnezzar. The verse uses the plain word "this" to point back to all of that announcement. It marks the shift from the warning to its fulfillment.

The one telling the story here is the narrative of the book, which begins to recount how the dream was fulfilled. Daniel had already advised the king to leave his sins behind and show mercy to the poor. The verse serves as a bridge: the warning was real, and what follows shows what happened when the king did not change. The text does not explain here why the punishment took twelve months to arrive.

For today: when God warns us through his Word or through a wise person, it is not wise to delay the change. His patience is an opportunity to humble ourselves, correct our course, and help the one who needs it.
exp.2:27:
Nebuchadnezzar praises the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He recognizes that God sent his angel and rescued his servants, who trusted in him. They disobeyed the king's command and risked their lives rather than serve or worship any god except their own God.

The one speaking is the king of Babylon. He had ordered everyone to worship a great golden statue and had thrown these three young Jewish men into the furnace for refusing. Seeing them come out unharmed, he is amazed. His praise is remarkable, although the text does not say that he stopped worshiping other gods; it only acknowledges the unique power of this God to deliver.

For today: trusting God and remaining faithful to him may cost us something, but he does not abandon us. Decide today to be faithful in small things, even when no one else is.
exp.11:7:
