Daniel says that he heard the words of the man clothed in linen, but he did not understand them. So he asks respectfully, "My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?" The word "outcome" here refers to how everything will finish or what result it will have.

Daniel speaks at the end of his book. He has just received very profound visions about times of persecution and of the end. The angel had sworn that everything would happen "for a time, times, and a half," an expression that scholars interpret in several ways. Daniel receives no further explanation; instead, he is told that the words are sealed until their appointed time.

For today: you do not need to understand everything in order to keep trusting God. You can ask him sincerely, as Daniel did, and then go on living with faith, purity, and patience, knowing that God knows the outcome.
exp.11:4:
Daniel says that he looked up and saw two other beings, one standing on this bank of the river and one on the opposite bank. The words "one on this bank" refer to the bank nearest to him, and "one on the opposite bank" refers to the figure on the far side. In other words, Daniel sees two figures, one on each side of the river, and the man clothed in linen stands above the waters between them.

Daniel is speaking after receiving a long vision about times of great distress and the hope of the resurrection. He has been told to seal the book until the time of the end. These two beings appear as witnesses, and one of them will ask the question: "How long will it be until the end of these wonders?" The text does not say clearly who they are; many think they are angels, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God does not leave his people without answers or without witnesses. When you do not understand how long a trial will last, you can bring your questions with humility and trust that time is in God's hands.
exp.1:39:
It says that the fourth kingdom will be as strong as iron. Just as iron shatters and crushes everything, this kingdom will crush and shatter the others. "Shatters" means breaking into pieces, and "crushes" means overpowering and bringing everything under its control.

Daniel is speaking to King Nebuchadnezzar and explaining the dream of a great statue made of several materials. Each part represents a kingdom that would come. Many think the fourth kingdom is Rome, though some understand it differently, and it is debated exactly which one is meant. Daniel makes clear that God is the one who gives and takes away power from kingdoms.

For today: the strongest empires also pass away, but God remains in control of history. When the world seems ruled by force, you can rest and trust that your life is in the hands of the One who governs over all.
exp.1:12:
This verse says that the king's order had already been issued. The wise men of Babylon were being taken away to be executed. Since Daniel and his companions were also counted among the wise men, men went looking for them so that they too would be put to death along with the others. The verse says the order was given, and it describes the search for Daniel and his friends as the next step in carrying it out.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. King Nebuchadnezzar had had a dream that troubled him. He demanded that his wise men tell him the dream and its meaning. They said it was impossible, and the king, in a rage, ordered all of them put to death. Daniel and his friends had not been consulted, yet they were still in danger.

There are times when we suffer the consequences of other people's decisions without any fault of our own. Daniel did not panic: according to the next verse, he spoke with prudence and sought to understand the situation. When a crisis comes, let us ask God for calm and wisdom before we react.
exp.0:4:
It says that King Nebuchadnezzar assigned these young men a daily portion of the royal food and the wine. They were to be trained for three years, and after that they would enter the king's service.

The narrator tells how Babylon carried off young Jewish men from prominent families into exile. The king wanted to train them in his language and culture so that they would serve in his court. The king's food was a gift, but it was also a way of binding them to Babylon. The book does not explain everything here, but the next verse sets up Daniel's decision in verse 8.

Today, what the world offers us sometimes seems generous and convenient, but it comes with a hidden price. Let us ask God for wisdom to be thankful for what is good, to discern what shapes our hearts, and to remain faithful with humility.
exp.6:7:
Daniel tells us that, while he was watching the horns of the fourth beast, another horn came up among them, a little one. Three of the first horns were uprooted before it. This horn had eyes like those of a man, which suggest intelligence or cunning, and a mouth that spoke words of arrogance, words full of pride.

Daniel, who receives this vision at night, is the one speaking. The horns represent kings or powers. Interpreters disagree about who the little horn is: some think of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, others of a future power or antichrist, others of Rome and its successors. The vision ends with God as Judge, and that brings comfort to the oppressed people.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed by powers that boast and speak with arrogance. None of them has the last word. Trust that God judges with justice and, in the meantime, live with humility and faithfulness.
exp.2:11:
They say that certain Jews, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, whom the king had placed in important positions in the province of Babylon, have ignored him. The phrase "have ignored you" means that they did not give the king their attention and did not obey his command. They refused to serve his gods or worship the golden statue he had set up.

The ones speaking are Chaldean astrologers or wise men, who accuse the three young men before King Nebuchadnezzar. The text presents them as accusers, and it shows that they resented foreigners holding high posts. They remind the king that he himself had appointed them, in order to provoke his anger.

For today: being faithful to God can bring misunderstanding, criticism, or pressure. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego did not go along with the crowd. We can ask God for the courage to obey him with respect, even when others do not understand.
exp.9:19:
He says that the heavenly messenger asks Daniel whether he knows why he has come. The messenger explains that he must soon go back to fight against the prince of Persia, and that once he has left, the prince of Greece will come.

A heavenly messenger is speaking, the one who has just strengthened Daniel, who had become very weak because of the vision. Earlier he explained that his answer was delayed by a spiritual struggle. The "princes" are usually understood as spiritual powers linked to nations, although some scholars see them differently. The passage shows that there is an unseen battle behind the course of history, and that Michael helps in it.

Today we can pray with persistence, even when the answer takes a long time. God works in things we do not see, and we are neither alone nor forgotten.
exp.11:12:
This verse tells Daniel to keep going on his way until the end of his life. It says he will rest, which is a way of speaking about death, and that afterward he will rise to receive his inheritance at the end of the days. The word "inheritance" here refers to the share that God has set aside for him.

The one speaking is the angel who has explained to Daniel visions about times of great distress, and who closes the book with a personal promise. Daniel did not understand everything he had been told, and he is simply asked to keep trusting. The numbers of days in this part of the book have been interpreted in several ways, and there is no single explanation that everyone accepts. Many readers see here a hope of resurrection.

For today: even when we do not understand everything God is doing, we can stay faithful day after day. Our rest and our future are in his hands, and that gives us peace to live with confidence.
exp.5:21:
Daniel says that God sent his angel to shut the mouths of the lions and so protect him. He explains that God found him innocent, meaning he was without guilt before God. He also affirms that he had done nothing wrong against the king. The word "innocent" here means that Daniel was upright and without fault.

Daniel speaks after spending the night in the lions' den by order of King Darius. His enemies accused him of praying to God, although he had done no wrong. In the morning the king, distressed, ran to the den and called out to him. Daniel answers the king with respect and testifies that God looked after him.

Living with integrity gives us peace, even when others accuse us without reason. We can keep doing what is right and trust that God cares for us, although he does not always do so in the same way he did with Daniel.
exp.2:6:
This verse tells us that, as soon as the sound of the instruments was heard, people from every nation and language bowed down to the ground and worshipped the king's golden statue. The "horn" is the wind instrument, the "flute" and "zither" and "lyre" and "harp" are the stringed and wind instruments that played together, and "all kinds of music" shows how much sound filled the plain. "Fall down" means they threw themselves to the ground.

The narrator describes how Nebuchadnezzar's command was carried out, since he had threatened the furnace of fire for anyone who did not worship. The text stresses that people from every nation and language took part, with no one left out. Fear and social pressure weighed heavily. Still, the scene sets up the contrast with Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.

Today we also feel pressure to follow the crowd in what gets applauded or what is feared. Before going along with the current, ask yourself: whom am I really worshipping?
exp.6:24:
This verse describes a king or power that will rise up in arrogance. He will speak against God, the Most High, and will oppress his faithful people, called "the saints of the Most High." He will also intend to change the appointed times and the laws, that is, the dates and rules God has set. The saints will be handed over to his power "for a time, and times, and half a time," which is commonly understood as three and a half years, though some read it as a symbolic period.

The angel who interprets the vision of the four beasts for Daniel is the one speaking. Daniel is frightened and wants to understand. Interpreters disagree about who this "other horn" is: some think of Antiochus Epiphanes, others of a future antichrist.

For today: even when evil seems to be winning, God has the last word. Remain faithful and hopeful, because the eternal kingdom will belong to God and to his people.
exp.1:46:
The king Nebuchadnezzar tells Daniel that Daniel's God is truly the God of gods and the Lord of kings, meaning greater than all the gods and all the rulers. He also calls him the Revealer of Mysteries, because he uncovers hidden things. The word "mystery" in the verse itself means a hidden thing.

The king of Babylon speaks after Daniel has told him and explained his dream, something none of the wise men of his court could do. Daniel had said that the credit belonged to God, not to himself. The king acknowledges God's power, although the text does not say he fully gave up his own gods; that remains open.

When God acts in our lives, we can bear witness with humility, as Daniel did, and point to God instead of seeking praise. In this way others can see who He is.
exp.9:17:
It says that the one who had the likeness of a man touched Daniel again and strengthened him. The phrase "the likeness of a man" means that he had a human form. "Strengthened" here means giving him strength, not just comforting him.

Daniel is speaking. He had just received a vision so overwhelming that he felt weak and nearly out of breath. He had been fasting and praying for his people. The one who touches him is a heavenly messenger; the Bible does not give his name here, and some identify him as an angel, though there are different opinions. His touch prepares Daniel to hear the message.

For today: when you feel exhausted or speechless before God, do not be afraid or pull away. God knows how to give you strength for the moment. Ask him simply to strengthen you, and trust that he often does so with tenderness and at the right time.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that the God whom Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego serve has the power to save them from the blazing fiery furnace, and also from your hand, O king. "Exists" points to the reality of God as the foundation of their confidence. "Deliver" means to rescue them or bring them out safely.

These three young Hebrews, taken captive to Babylon, are the ones speaking. King Nebuchadnezzar had set up a statue and demanded that everyone worship it, under threat of death. They answer calmly and firmly. They affirm that God is able to save them, but in the following verse they make clear that even if He does not, they will not bow down to the statue.

Today we can trust that God has the power to help us in our trials, and still be faithful if the answer does not come as we hope. Our obedience does not depend on the outcome, but on who God is.
exp.8:21:
He instructed me and spoke with me, saying, "O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding." The angel Gabriel came to Daniel, spoke to him, and explained that he had come with a clear purpose: to give him understanding about the vision. The phrase "made me understand" means that he helped me grasp what was being shown. The "insight" refers to the verse of the message that God wanted to give him.

Daniel is praying and confessing his sins and the sins of Israel, while the people live in exile in Babylon. It is the time of the evening sacrifice when Gabriel arrives. Gabriel speaks, sent by God, and answers Daniel's prayer with a message about the future of Israel and its city. How the "seventy weeks" are to be interpreted is something Christian scholars understand in various ways.

For today: when we pray with humility and sincerity, God hears us and can give us light and understanding in his time. Pray with a willing heart, and trust that God answers.
exp.1:43:
It says that God, the God of heaven, will set up a kingdom of his own in the days of those kings. That kingdom will never be destroyed, and it will not be handed over to another people. Instead, it will shatter all the earlier kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it will itself stand forever. The word "shatter" means to break into pieces, and "bring to an end" means to finish them completely.

Daniel speaks to King Nebuchadnezzar and explains the dream of a great statue made of several metals. The feet of iron and clay represent divided and weak kingdoms. Many Christians see here the kingdom of Christ; others see it as a kingdom that will be fully revealed in the future. Interpreters do not agree on every detail.

For today: human powers, however strong they may seem, are temporary. We can trust that God has the final word and live with hope and peace, without placing our security in governments or in riches.
exp.1:21:
This verse says that God reveals the deep and hidden things. He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him. Nothing is hidden from Him. The word "dwells" means lives or remains with Him.

Daniel is speaking in a prayer of praise. He has just received from God, in a night vision, the dream of King Nebuchadnezzar and its meaning. That mystery put the lives of all the wise men of Babylon at risk, including Daniel and his friends. For this reason he gives thanks and acknowledges that wisdom comes from God, not from himself.

For today: when you face something you do not understand or a dark situation, ask God humbly for light. He knows what you cannot see. And if He gives you understanding, just as He did for Daniel, give thanks to Him.
exp.10:18:
He says that this king, after his conquests in the islands, will turn back toward the fortresses of his own land. There he will fail: "he will stumble and fall and be no more" means that he will vanish and no longer be seen. It is the end of his power.

The angel gives Daniel a detailed prophecy about the kings of the north and the south who would come after the Persian empire. Many scholars see here Antiochus III the Great, who died after a defeat and an attempt to plunder a temple, though some interpret it differently. The central point is that God knows history and directs it, even when kings seem all-powerful.

The powerful of this world pass away, and their plans do not last forever. Today we can rest in the fact that God still governs, even when we see injustice. Therefore, instead of placing our security in money, prestige, or power, let us trust in the One who remains forever.
exp.10:29:
Daniel 11:30 says that ships from Kittim will come against a king of the north, and he will lose heart. Kittim is usually understood to mean the west, near Cyprus. Then he will turn back and rage against the holy covenant and do damage. He will return and show favor to those who abandon the holy covenant.

The angel gives this message to Daniel in a vision about the conflicts between the kings of the north and the south. Many understand it to speak of Antiochus IV Epiphanes and of Rome, which forced him to withdraw from Egypt in 168 B.C. Some also see a more distant fulfillment in view. The purpose is to warn God's people of the persecution that was coming.

For today: do not lose heart when evil seems strong. God knows the times and sustains those who are faithful to Him. Remain firm in Him, even when others give way.
exp.8:6:
It says that God is righteous and that the people have good reason to feel shame. Being covered with shame, with no way to lift up one's eyes, describes the people's condition. That shame reaches everyone: Judah, Jerusalem, and all Israel, both those who are near and those scattered far away among the nations.

The reference to being driven away means that God scattered them because of their unfaithfulness to Him.

Daniel speaks in prayer on behalf of his people. The Israelites were living in exile in Babylon, and Daniel had come to understand from the writings of Jeremiah that the time of punishment was nearing its end. Although he himself is presented as a faithful man, he includes himself in the confession, saying "we." After this, he prays for mercy.

For today: when we fail, we can stop making excuses and sincerely acknowledge that God is righteous. That humility does not take us away from Him but brings us closer to His mercy.
exp.6:11:
As for the other three beasts in the vision, their power to rule was removed, but they were granted an extension of life for a fixed time. "Dominion" means authority or rule. "An extension of life" means that they did not disappear right away.

Daniel speaks, recounting a night vision. The beasts represent kingdoms that dominate the world. Many understand them to be ancient empires, though scholars debate exactly which ones they are. God, as Judge, removes the power of the last beast, and then the "son of man" receives an everlasting kingdom. Christians often see Jesus there.

For today: the powers of this world seem enormous, but they have limits and God governs them. You can rest and pray calmly, trusting that the kingdom of Christ is the one that endures.
exp.3:28:
This verse says that twelve months had passed since the dream and Daniel's counsel. King Nebuchadnezzar was walking calmly on the roof of the royal palace in Babylon. The verse's wording "twelve months later" means that the king was walking after the full year had gone by, and he was strolling without any sense of hurry.

The king himself is the one telling the story. Daniel had warned him to change his life and to deal with justice and mercy toward the poor. A full year went by, a time of waiting and of opportunity. This verse sets the scene for the moment when the king, full of pride, will speak about his own greatness.

For today: do not confuse God's patience with his silence. If He has given you time to correct something, do not let it pass. Use today to act with humility and to help those in need.
exp.3:29:
As he walks through his palace, Nebuchadnezzar looks out over the city and takes pride in it. He exclaims that it is Babylon the Great, which he himself built as a royal residence by the might of his power and for the glory of his majesty. The phrase "the glory of my majesty" refers to his own splendor and greatness.

The one speaking is the king of Babylon. A year earlier, God had warned him in a dream that he should give up his pride and act with justice. Twelve months later, he had not changed. While he was still speaking, a voice from heaven announced that he would lose his kingdom and live like an animal until he acknowledged that God rules over all.

Everything we have, our talents, our work, and our achievements, is a gift from God. When you accomplish something, give thanks and share it with humility, without believing that you did it all by yourself.
exp.2:15:
Daniel 3:16 says that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answer King Nebuchadnezzar calmly and firmly. Their words, "we have no need to answer you in this matter," mean that they feel no pressure to explain or defend themselves to him on this point.

The king has just threatened them with the furnace of fire if they do not worship his golden statue. These three young Jews, who served in Babylon, had already decided to be faithful to God. That is why they need no time to think it over. Some understand their answer as great trust in God; others see it as a decision already made. Both ideas fit with what they say afterward.

For today: if you have already decided in your heart to obey God, you will not have to be anxious when the pressure comes. Decide today, in prayer, what you will not compromise on.
exp.0:15:
The passage says that the steward, the official who looked after Daniel and his friends, kept withholding the king's rich food and the wine they were supposed to drink, and gave them vegetables instead. A "portion" is the daily amount assigned to them. The "vegetables" were plant foods that grew from the ground, such as seeds like lentils or beans; some believe the term covered other plant foods as well.

The story then moves on to the ten-day test that Daniel proposed. Daniel did not want to defile himself with the king's food, probably out of faithfulness to God; the text does not explain every detail. When the steward saw the good result, he agreed to keep the change permanently.

For today: Daniel did not rebel with pride, but asked respectfully and proposed a reasonable test. When you want to stay faithful to God in a difficult environment, act with humility, wisdom, and trust that He can take care of you.
exp.1:2:
Here the king Nebuchadnezzar tells his wise men that he has had a dream, and his mind is anxious to understand it. The word "spirit" refers to his mind and his inner state, and "anxious" describes a restless mind that has no peace. He wants to know the meaning of the dream, but later it becomes clear that he no longer remembered the dream itself, or that he wanted to test his wise men (the text allows both readings).

The speaker is the king of Babylon, the most powerful man of his time. He had called together magicians, astrologers and Chaldeans, his advisers, because he felt the dream was important. With this opening, the chapter sets the stage for God, through Daniel, to show that only He reveals what is hidden.

For today: when something takes away our peace, let us not rely only on human resources or on people famous for their wisdom. Let us bring that unrest to God in prayer, for He knows what we do not understand and can give us direction and calm.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that King Belshazzar was terrified when no one could read the mysterious writing. "Became even more terrified" means his fear grew stronger and deeper. "His face grew even more pale" means his face lost its color, showing how shaken he was. "His nobles were bewildered" means his leaders were also confused and unsettled.

This happens during a great banquet, when a hand appeared writing on the wall. The narrator of the book describes the king's reaction. The wise men of Babylon failed, despite the reward offered, and the fear grew. Shortly afterward, the queen suggests calling for Daniel, a man of God.

For today: power, wealth, and experts cannot calm a heart that faces God without peace with Him. When we feel fear or lack answers, we can stop trusting only our own resources and seek God's wisdom in prayer and in His Word.
exp.1:3:
Here the wise men of Babylon, called astrologers, answer King Nebuchadnezzar in Aramaic. They say to him, "O king, may you live forever!" a respectful greeting typical of the court. They ask the king to tell his dream to them, his servants, and they promise to give the interpretation.

The king is troubled by a dream that has disturbed him. He has called his advisers, and they speak with confidence, thinking it is enough to hear the dream. From this verse the book shifts from Hebrew to Aramaic, and many scholars think this is because of the setting of the court; there is no full agreement on the exact reason.

For today: the astrologers spoke with great assurance, but they soon discovered their limits. We can learn to be humble before our own limitations and to seek the wisdom that comes from God, who is the one who reveals what is hidden.
exp.0:20:
It says that Daniel remained there, serving in the court of Babylon, until the first year of King Cyrus. The word "remained" here means that Daniel stayed in his place and kept serving, and this marks how long his service lasted. It does not say that he died that year, but that his service reached to that time.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. He closes the first chapter, which tells how Daniel and his friends were chosen and stood out for their wisdom. Cyrus came after the fall of Babylon, so this sentence shows that Daniel lived through the change from one empire to another. Even so, the book also mentions a third year of Cyrus (Daniel 10:1), so this sentence does not mark the end of his life.

For today: faithfulness to God is not just one brilliant moment but a steadiness across the years, even when everything around us changes.
exp.5:5:
So the governors and satraps gathered together before the king and greeted him with a formula of respect: "O King Darius, may you live forever!" The phrase "went together" means they came as a group, as if they were one.

The ones speaking are the senior officials who envied Daniel. They had not been able to find any fault in him, so they planned to use his faith against him. Notice that their flattery of the king hid a trap: they wanted him to sign a decree that, without his realizing it, would put Daniel in danger. The verses that follow say they presented the idea as if all the leaders agreed, though the text does not make clear whether Daniel was consulted.

For today: let us be wary of flattery that comes with hidden motives, and let us seek to live with as much integrity as Daniel, so that if anyone attacks us, they will find nothing real to accuse us of.
exp.10:17:
He says that a king will turn toward the coastlands and capture many of them. But a commander will put an end to his reproach and will turn it back upon him. The verse of the word "turn" means "pay back."

An angel speaks to Daniel and reveals what will happen to the kingdoms after him. Many believe this refers to Antiochus III, the king of the north, who was defeated by the Romans. Some details are debated, but the message is clear: powerful kings do not have the final word.

Today it reminds us that pride and unlimited ambition end badly, while God continues to govern history. We can rest in Him and ask Him for humility so that we do not trust in our own achievements.
exp.8:16:
Daniel asks God to hear his prayer and his pleas. He also asks God to cause his face to shine upon the sanctuary, the temple in Jerusalem, which lies in ruins and abandoned. He asks this for the sake of the Lord, that is, for the sake of God's name and honor.

Daniel speaks after reading in Jeremiah that the exile would last seventy years. He confesses the sins of his people as if they were his own. He does not rely on his own merits, but on the mercy of God. Some believe that "the Lord" here refers to God himself; others see in this a foreshadowing of the Messiah, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: when you need to ask for forgiveness or help, pray with humility. Do not present your achievements, but the goodness of God, and ask him to let his glory be seen in your situation.
exp.4:22:
Daniel confronts Belshazzar over his pride against God. He reminds the king that the sacred vessels from the house of God were brought out so that he, his nobles, his wives, and his concubines (secondary wives of the king) could drink wine from them. The king also praised gods made of silver and gold, bronze and iron, wood and stone, which cannot see, hear, or understand. Yet he did not glorify the God who holds his very breath in His hand and directs all his ways. The phrase "you have exalted yourself" describes a heart filled with arrogance.

Daniel speaks to the king in the middle of a banquet, at the very moment a mysterious hand wrote on the wall. He reminds Belshazzar how Nebuchadnezzar was humbled by his pride until he acknowledged God. Belshazzar knew that story and still did not change. That is why Daniel is about to explain the message of judgment.

For today: God calls us to honor Him with humility rather than pride. Let us learn from what He has already shown us and not treat what is holy with careless disregard. We can thank Him today for the breath of life He sustains in us.
exp.5:20:
Daniel answers the king with a respectful greeting: "O king, may you live forever!" It was a common courtesy formula in the courts of that time. "Then Daniel replied" simply means that he answered him.

Daniel is speaking, having just spent the night in the den of lions. King Darius, who had reluctantly condemned him under a law the king himself had signed, came very early and anxious. Daniel bears him no grudge and makes no accusation; he treats him with honor and at once explains that God shut the lions' mouths.

For today: even when someone has treated us unjustly, we can respond with respect and calm. A kind response opens the way for others to see God's faithfulness in our lives.
exp.10:42:
He says that this king of the north will gain control of the gold, the silver, and all the riches of Egypt, and that the Libyans and Cushites will also submit to him. "Gain control of" means he will take hold of these things for himself. "Treasures" are stored-up wealth. The idea of the Libyans and Cushites submitting is understood as they will be under his rule as he passes through their lands.

An angel explains to Daniel what will happen to the kingdoms that would oppress Israel. Many see here Antiochus IV Epiphanes, while others also see a prophecy of a future ruler who is an enemy of God. Scholars do not agree, so it is wise to speak with humility. The central message is that no human power is eternal; verse 45 says that this king will come to his end.

Today we can remember that riches and power do not give lasting security. Let us trust in God, who governs history.
exp.11:11:
Blessed, or happy, is the one who knows how to wait with patience and manages to reach the end of the 1,335 days. The verse's note on the word for "blessed" means very happy and blessed by God. The word for "waits" carries the sense of patient, faithful waiting, and "reaches" means arriving at the end of that time.

This is the end of the book of Daniel. An angel gives Daniel the final revelation about times of great trial for God's people. The verse before this one speaks of 1,290 days, and this one adds 45 more days. The Bible does not explain the reason for that difference, and interpreters understand it in several ways. What is certain is that the message aims to encourage the faithful to persevere, and then God promises Daniel rest and an inheritance in the end.

For today: when you go through a difficult wait, do not obsess over dates or calculations. Trust that God keeps his promises and remain faithful day after day.
exp.10:4:
The king of the South will grow strong, but one of his commanders will grow even stronger and will rule his own kingdom with great authority. The phrase "rule his own kingdom" shows that this commander will not simply serve the king but will govern a realm of his own, and "great authority" describes the scale of his power.

Here a heavenly messenger gives Daniel a vision of the future. It comes after the description of a powerful king, whom many understand to be Alexander the Great, whose kingdom was later divided into four. Many scholars see in the king of the South Ptolemy I and in the commander Seleucus I, but not everyone interprets it the same way. God shows that he knows history in advance.

For today: human powers rise and fall, so let us not place our security in them. Let us trust in God, who rules over all.
exp.4:15:
Here King Belshazzar speaks to Daniel and says he has heard that Daniel can give interpretations and solve difficult problems. If Daniel can read this inscription and explain its meaning, he will be clothed in purple, a sign of royal honor, have a gold chain placed around his neck, and be made the third highest ruler in the kingdom.

Belshazzar is frightened because a mysterious hand wrote on the wall during a banquet. His wise men could neither read the message nor explain it, so he calls for Daniel. Daniel refuses the rewards, since he does not serve for payment, but he will speak on behalf of the Most High God. Some scholars think "third ruler" means third in command, although the exact meaning of the title is understood in several ways.

For today: God's wisdom is not bought with prizes, nor does it rest on status. We can ask God for understanding and serve with honesty, without being swayed by money or power.
exp.7:13:
Here the question of the holy ones is answered: how long will this vision last? The answer is 2,300 evenings and mornings, and after that the sanctuary will be properly restored.

Daniel has just seen a horn that attacks God's people, takes away the daily sacrifice, and tramples the sanctuary. An angel answers the question of another. There are several interpretations: some understand 2,300 literal days, others 1,150 days (counting each evening and morning as a separate unit), and others a longer prophetic period. For this reason it is wise to speak with humility about the details.

For today: even when evil seems to win for a time, God sets a limit and promises to restore what is his. We can wait with patience and trust that he has the final word.
exp.6:17:
This verse says that, after the violent kingdoms of the earth have passed away, the saints of the Most High, that is, the people of God, will receive the kingdom and possess it forever. "Forever" here means "for all eternity," and the phrase "yes, forever and ever" stresses that this lasts without end.

Daniel has just seen in a vision four great beasts that represent four kings or kingdoms. Frightened, he approaches one of those standing there, probably a heavenly being, and asks for the verse. That figure answers him with this message of hope. Scholars debate exactly which kingdoms the beasts represent, but the central message is clear: God has the last word.

Today, when the world may seem dominated by injustice, we can rest in the fact that the final kingdom belongs to God and to his people. That hope encourages us to remain faithful, with patience and without fear.
exp.6:14:
Daniel says that his spirit was grieved within him, and that the visions in his mind alarmed him. "Was grieved" means he was deeply distressed and unsettled. "In my spirit" points to the inner core of who he is, the place where he felt the weight of what he had seen.

The one speaking is Daniel, now an old man, who has just seen four beasts and then a scene from heaven, where someone like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom. Daniel does not understand everything he saw, and he feels shaken. For that reason, right after, he goes to one of those standing there and asks him to explain the meaning.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be calm when something about God or the world confuses or unsettles you. Do as Daniel did: be honest, seek answers with humility, and ask God in prayer and in his Word.
exp.4:27:
It says that Belshazzar's kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians. "Peres" is the third word written on the wall, and it sounds like "Persians," which makes a play on words. Some scholars also see in it the idea of being divided.

Daniel, a Jewish prophet, speaks during a banquet of King Belshazzar in Babylon. A mysterious hand wrote on the wall, and no one could read it. Belshazzar had mocked and used the sacred vessels of the temple in Jerusalem. Daniel interprets the message as God's judgment. According to the text, that very night the king died.

For today: our power, success, or security are on loan, not eternal. It is wise to live with humility, respecting God and what is holy, without waiting until it is too late to correct course.
exp.2:8:
These men, Chaldeans, approach Nebuchadnezzar and greet him with a words of respect: "O king, may you live forever!" This was a common way of honoring a ruler in that time.

The speakers are Chaldean men, probably officials or people close to the court. They have just seen that everyone was bowing down to the golden statue, and they are about to accuse the Jews Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Some interpreters see jealousy or rivalry here, since those Jews held important positions, but the text does not state this clearly.

Today we can notice that kind words sometimes hide bad intentions. Before we let ourselves be carried away by a compliment or an accusation, it is wise to ask what lies behind it. As believers, let us seek to speak the truth without envy.
exp.5:16:
They brought a stone and placed it over the mouth of the lions' pit. The king sealed it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles. To seal meant to press a mark into wax or clay, like a signature. The pit is a deep hole, and the phrase "so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed" means that nothing could be altered in what had been decided about Daniel.

The account tells what King Darius did. His advisers had deceived him into signing a law against praying to anyone other than himself, and Daniel kept praying to God. Darius wanted to save him, but the law could not be changed. With the seal, no one could take Daniel out or alter the outcome.

For today: when a situation seems closed and without a way out, remember that God is not limited by sealed doors. Keep faithful and trust in Him.
exp.3:26:
Daniel asks King Nebuchadnezzar to accept his advice. He tells the king to break away from his sins by doing what is right, and from his wrongdoing by showing mercy to the oppressed. The phrase "break away" here means to end something and set it right through good deeds. The words "perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity" mean that God might extend the king's peace. Daniel does not promise this; he says "perhaps."

Daniel has just interpreted the dream of the tree that was cut down. He announces that God will humble the king for his pride. Daniel speaks with courage, but also with care for the king, and he offers him a way out before the judgment comes. Scholars understand "break away" as a real change of conduct, not as a way of buying forgiveness.

Today, God invites us to turn back with concrete actions. Think of an injustice or neglect toward someone in need, and do something practical this week to set it right.
exp.5:2:
Daniel rose above the other administrators and satraps because of his extraordinary spirit, a quality of character and mind that went beyond the ordinary. For this reason King Darius planned to set him over the whole kingdom. "Extraordinary spirit" means that he distinguished himself from the others, and "planned to set him over" means that the king intended to appoint him.

The narrator describes how Darius organized his government with one hundred and twenty satraps, supervised by three administrators. Daniel was one of them. Some understand "spirit" as a spirit given by God; others understand it as his character. This reputation aroused the envy of the others, and that prepares the trap that comes later.

For today: do your work with excellence and honesty, even when no one notices. An upright life speaks more loudly than words, and God can use it to bear witness.
exp.5:25:
Darius orders that in every part of his kingdom people are to tremble in reverence before the God of Daniel. Here, "tremble in fear" means deep respect and awe, not only fear. A "decree" is an official order from the king. A "kingdom" is a ruler's realm, and "dominion" refers to the authority that ruler holds. The verse says this God is living, endures forever, and that his kingdom will never be destroyed and his rule will never end.

King Darius speaks after Daniel was rescued from the den of lions. He writes to all the peoples under his rule to make known what has happened. Historians debate exactly who this Darius was, but the text presents him as ruler of the Median and Persian kingdom. His decree comes from having seen with his own eyes that God cared for Daniel.

For today: governments and fashions change, but God remains. When you face pressure or fear, remember that your life rests in a living God whose kingdom does not end. May your faithfulness, like Daniel's, be a visible witness to others.
exp.5:24:
Then King Darius wrote to the people of every nation and language in his kingdom. His greeting was: "May your prosperity abound," that is, "may you have great well-being." The wording here is simple and direct, and it carries the same sense of wishing people good things in abundance.

The king speaking here is Darius, the Median ruler. He had just seen that Daniel came out alive from the den of lions, because he trusted in his God. After that, the king wanted his whole empire to know what had happened and to respect Daniel's God. Some scholars debate the exact identity of this Darius, and the question is not fully settled.

For today: a person's firm faith can bear witness even to those who do not believe. Live with integrity and trust in God, even under strong pressure; your example can bring peace and hope to others.
exp.8:11:
He says that God carried out what he had warned. He had announced a punishment for the people and for their rulers, and he made it happen. The verse's wording is that he "carried out the words" spoken against them, which means God followed through on what he had said. The disaster that fell on Jerusalem was so great that nothing like it had ever been done under all of heaven, a way of saying across the entire known world.

Daniel is praying in confession for his people, who are living in exile in Babylon. He acknowledges that the destruction of Jerusalem was not an accident, but the result of disobeying the law of Moses, which had already warned of these consequences. Daniel does not blame God; he declares that God is righteous.

When God warns us, he speaks in earnest, but he also invites us to return to him. We can imitate Daniel's prayer: honestly acknowledge our failures, without excuses, and ask him for help to change.
exp.6:21:
The horn that made war against the saints would have power only until the Ancient of Days arrived, that is, God himself, as the eternal Judge. Then judgment would be pronounced in favor of the saints, that is, God's faithful people. "Pronounced judgment in favor of" means they would be declared in the right. When the appointed time came, they would take possession of the kingdom.

Daniel recounts a vision he had of four beasts. Here he describes what he saw concerning the horn that persecuted the saints. An angel will later give him the verse. The message encouraged God's people in the midst of persecution. Interpreters disagree about who that horn is, but all agree that its power has a limit.

For today: if you suffer injustice or pressure because of your faith, remember that God has the final word. Remain faithful and wait with confidence for his time.
exp.5:1:
This verse says that Darius appointed three administrators over the hundred and twenty satraps, and that Daniel was one of them. The satraps were to be accountable to these three, so that the king would not suffer loss. The loss in view would be things like tax revenue or the kingdom's property.

The narrator is the author of the book of Daniel, who tells how Darius the Mede organized his government. Who exactly this Darius was is debated among scholars. What is clear is that the king wanted an orderly and honest system. Daniel already holds a position of great responsibility, and this sets up the account of the jealousy that will come later.

For today: if you have authority or handle resources, do so with transparency and give account willingly. Like Daniel, whose faithfulness no one could question, make your work honest and trustworthy.
exp.10:6:
Someone from the queen's own family line, "one from her family line," will rise up in his place. He will come against the army of the king of the north, enter his fortress, and fight and prevail.

A heavenly messenger speaks with Daniel and explains what will happen to his people in the future (Daniel 10:14). Many scholars see here the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt and the Seleucid kings of Syria, and they think this person is the brother of the princess mentioned earlier. Others interpret it differently, since the text gives no names.

Powerful kingdoms rise and fall, but God continues to guide history. When the world seems unstable to you, rest in the knowledge that his plan does not break.
exp.1:0:
In the second year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams that troubled his spirit, and sleep escaped him. "Troubled his spirit" means that he was disturbed and filled with anguish. "Sleep escaped him" means that he lost his sleep and could not rest.

The narrator tells the story from Daniel's perspective. He presents the most powerful king of his time, restless because of a dream. This prepares the account in which God, and not the wise men of Babylon, reveals what is to come. Some wonder about the date, because Daniel had been there for several years. Different explanations have been proposed, but there is no certainty.

For today: power, money, or success do not give true peace. When anxiety takes away your sleep, bring your worries to God, who knows what is coming and cares for you.
exp.0:12:
Daniel asks Melzar to make a comparison. The words "compare our appearances" mean that the young men should be looked at and examined, and "appearances" refers to how they look, including how healthy they seem. "The royal food" is the food the king provided each day. "According to what you see" means "based on what you see." Daniel is saying: look at how we appear compared with the other young men, and decide based on that. "Your servants" is a humble way of speaking.

Daniel speaks with the official in charge of the eunuchs, who was looking after him and his three friends in Babylon. They wanted to avoid the king's food, probably so as not to defile themselves (the text suggests this in verse 8). Daniel does not rebel; he proposes a test of ten days, with respect, and lets the result speak.

For today: when you want to be faithful to God in a difficult setting, act with respect, humility and good reasons, without fighting or forcing yourself on others. Trust God and let your conduct speak.
exp.1:48:
This verse tells us that Daniel asked the king for a favor, and the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon. The phrase "to manage the province" refers to overseeing the business and running of the province. "While Daniel remained in the king's court" means that Daniel stayed at the court, close to the king, in a position of influence. Some believe this indicates that he held a role as a judge or an important official.

Daniel had just revealed and interpreted the dream of King Nebuchadnezzar, and the king acknowledged that Daniel's God is the God of gods. The king had already promoted Daniel, and now Daniel uses his influence, not for himself, but to benefit his three friends.

For today: if God gives you influence, work, or recognition, think about how you can open doors for others. Serving and remembering those who walk alongside you is a humble way to honor God.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that Nebuchadnezzar, the great king of Babylon, became arrogant and stubborn in his pride. Because of this, God removed him from the throne and took away the glory He had given him. "Became arrogant" means that his heart was filled with haughtiness. "Was deposed" means that he was removed from power. "His glory was taken from him" means that his honor and greatness were stripped away.

The prophet Daniel is speaking before King Belshazzar during a banquet in Babylon. A mysterious hand had just written on the wall, and Daniel is interpreting the message. He reminds Belshazzar of what happened to Nebuchadnezzar, to show him that he too has been proud and has not learned the lesson.

For today: everything we have, our talents, our work, or our achievements, is a gift from God. When we remember this, the heart stays humble and thankful.
exp.7:20:
This verse says that the shaggy goat in the vision represents the king of Greece. The large horn between its eyes is "the first king," that is, the first great king of that empire. Many scholars identify him with Alexander the Great, although the text does not give his name.

The one speaking is the angel Gabriel, who explains to Daniel the vision of the ram and the goat. The ram had already been identified with Media and Persia. Now Gabriel shows how power would pass from one empire to another. God reveals to Daniel that history is not out of control and that it has an appointed time.

For today: when the world seems dominated by powers that rise and fall, remember that God still guides history. You can rest in the knowledge that your life and your future are in the hands of the One who knows the end from the beginning.
exp.10:43:
A powerful king will receive news from the east and from the north that will alarm him and deeply unsettle him. He will then set out in a great rage to destroy many people and bring them to ruin.

An angel speaks to Daniel and explains what will happen in the future. Chapter 11 as a whole describes conflicts between the kings of the north and the south. This "king" is understood in several ways: many think of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, while others see a figure of the end times. There is no complete agreement, so it is wise to read it with humility. The next verse says that his power will come to an end with no one to help him.

For today: human kingdoms may seem strong, but they have limits. If we see violence or unjust power today, we can rest in the knowledge that God governs history. Let us pray with confidence and seek to do good with peace.
exp.1:26:
Daniel tells the king that no one in his court can explain the mystery he is asking about: not the wise men, the enchanters, the mediums, or the magicians. The king has asked for the mystery itself, and Daniel says plainly that these advisors cannot make it known to him.

Daniel speaks to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The king had a dream that troubled him and demanded that his advisors tell him both the dream and its meaning. They could not, and the king ordered the wise men put to death. Daniel, a young Jewish exile, first makes clear that no human resource is enough. He will soon point out that only God reveals mysteries.

For today: Daniel does not boast of his own ability, but acknowledges human limits and directs our attention to God. When we face questions or situations that are beyond us, we can humbly admit that we do not have all the answers and ask God for wisdom, while still acting with honesty.
exp.10:32:
This verse says that the wise among God's people, those who understand his will, will teach and give understanding to many. But this will come at a cost: for a time, some will fall by the sword or by fire, others will be taken captive, and others will have their goods taken from them. To be plundered means to have what you own seized by force. The words "for a time" indicate that the suffering will not last forever.

Here an angel speaks, revealing to Daniel what is to come. Interpreters often see in this the persecution of the Jews under Antiochus IV Epiphanes in the second century B.C., although some also see an echo of the end times. The message was meant to encourage the faithful in the midst of suffering.

For today: teaching God's truth with love and courage can bring rejection or cost. Even so, it is worth remaining faithful, because God uses our witness to bless others and knows how long each trial will last.
exp.1:10:
What it says: The wise men of Babylon tell the king that what he asks is so difficult that no one can explain it to him except the gods, who do not live among mortals. Here "request" means what the king is asking for, and "difficult" means beyond what ordinary people can do. "Mortals" refers to human beings.

Context: The speakers are the Chaldeans, the wise men of King Nebuchadnezzar. He demands that they tell him the dream and its meaning, and they cannot. They admit that their gods are far removed from people. This sets the stage for Daniel, who trusts in a God who does reveal secrets, to step onto the scene. That is why the king becomes furious and orders them put to death.

For today: When we face something beyond our ability, we should not rely only on our own wisdom. We can turn to God in prayer, for He is near and gives direction to those who seek Him with humility.
exp.1:7:
Here King Nebuchadnezzar answers his wise men, telling them that he knows for sure they are stalling for time. "You are stalling for time" means that you are putting off or stretching out the matter. "My word is final" means that the king's decision is settled and cannot be changed.

The king is troubled by a dream that has disturbed him. He asks the magicians and astrologers to tell him the dream and its meaning. They ask him to tell them the dream first. He suspects they want to invent a false answer while time passes, and so he demands a real proof of their power.

For today: when something is beyond us, it is better to admit it with humility than to pretend we know. Only God reveals what is hidden, and to Him we can come with sincerity.
exp.1:4:
King Nebuchadnezzar answers the wise men of Babylon, who are called Chaldeans here. He tells them: "My word is final." He means that his command is firm and settled, and it cannot be changed.

If they do not tell him the dream and its interpretation, they will be cut into pieces, that is, torn apart, and their houses will be reduced to rubble.

The king speaks, troubled by a dream that has disturbed him. The wise men asked him to tell them the dream first so they could interpret it, but he demands that they themselves tell him what the dream was. With this he wants to test whether their interpretations are true and not just empty words.

For today: human power and the wisdom of the world have limits. In the face of life's deepest questions, it is wise to turn to God, who reveals what is hidden, as this chapter will show.
exp.10:41:
The king of the north will keep on conquering. "He will extend his power over many countries" means he will use his power to dominate other territories. And Egypt, which was a strong nation, will not escape being taken either.

An angel speaks to the prophet Daniel, now an old man, and reveals what will happen to powerful kingdoms that would affect Israel. Scholars are divided: some see Antiochus IV Epiphanes here, others a future ruler, and others a mixture of both. There is no single certain interpretation. The purpose was to encourage God's people in difficult times.

Empires and rulers may seem invincible, but none of them is eternal. God continues to guide history. When you see injustice or abusive power, rest in the knowledge that God has the final word and trust in Him.
exp.11:6:
Daniel heard the man dressed in linen, who was above the waters of the river. This man raised both his right hand and his left hand toward heaven and swore by God, the one who lives forever, that it would last "for a time, and times, and half a time," a period that many understand as three and a half years, though it is interpreted in several ways. "Shattered" means broken or scattered. "The holy people" refers to God's people as a group. When their power has been completely broken, all these things will be completed.

A voice asks the man dressed in linen how long it will be until the end of these wonders, and he answers with a solemn oath to give full assurance. Daniel is receiving a vision about times of great trial for the people of God.

For today: even when we do not understand God's timing, we can trust that He has set a limit on every trial and will keep His word. Rest in His promise, not in your calculations.
exp.2:5:
This verse is the threat that goes with the king's command. Whoever does not fall down and worship the golden statue will be thrown immediately into a furnace of blazing fire. The phrase about falling down means dropping to the ground, and "immediately" means at once, with no lengthy trial and no second chance.

The speaker is the herald, the official messenger of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. He announces to all the peoples that when the music sounds, they must worship the statue. The punishment seeks to ensure total obedience and unity under the king. Later, this command will put the faithful Jews who serve God in a difficult position.

For today: sometimes there will be pressure to give in on what we know pleases God, because "everyone is doing it." We can decide in advance to be faithful to God with respect and firmness, trusting that He sustains us even when it costs us.
exp.1:35:
This verse marks a change in the scene. Daniel has finished telling the king about his dream, and now he announces that he will give its meaning. When he says "we will tell," he includes his companions along with himself, and "the king" is the one who will hear the verse.

Daniel speaks to the king of Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar had had a dream that troubled him, and no one in his court could tell it back to him or explain it. Daniel, after asking God for help, described the statue and the stone. Now the interpretation begins, and he makes clear that it is not his own invention, but something God revealed to him.

For today: when we do not understand what is happening in the world or in our lives, we can do as Daniel did: pray first and ask God for wisdom. And if He gives us light, let us speak with humility, giving Him the credit.
exp.7:10:
This verse says that the little horn made itself so great that it set itself against even the Prince of the host, meaning the commander of the heavenly army, who is God himself. Because of this horn, the daily sacrifice was removed, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown.

Daniel recounts a vision he received in Babylon, with a ram, a male goat, and a little horn. Many connect it with Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who defiled the temple in Jerusalem; others also see a future fulfillment. It was given to encourage a people who would suffer persecution.

For today: when evil seems powerful and faith seems trampled, remember that God remains the Prince and that his power is greater. Keep your life of prayer constant.
exp.2:25:
Nebuchadnezzar comes near to the door of the blazing furnace and calls out to the three young men: "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out!" They come out of the fire.

The king of Babylon is speaking. He had ordered these three Hebrews thrown into the furnace because they refused to worship his golden statue. Now, astonished, he sees four men walking loose and unharmed in the middle of the fire. The text does not say who the fourth figure is: the king speaks of someone who looks like a son of the gods, and later says that God sent his angel. There are different interpretations.

God can be with us and care for us in the middle of trial, even when he does not immediately bring us out of it. Trust in him and remain faithful, even when doing so is costly.
exp.9:1:
It says that Daniel was very sad and troubled for three full weeks. The verse simply says he was mourning for three full weeks, and the phrase points to a stretch of time that went on without a break, about twenty-one days.

It is Daniel himself who speaks, now an old man, in the third year of King Cyrus of Persia. He had received a true but difficult revelation, one that spoke of a long period of conflict. The verses that follow show that Daniel went on a partial fast. The Bible does not state exactly why he was grieving; many believe the suffering of his people and what lay ahead weighed heavily on him.

For today: when something weighs on your heart, do not ignore it or hide it. Pause, pray earnestly, and seek God steadily, even when the answers take time and the situation is hard to understand.
exp.0:16:
God gave these four young men, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, knowledge and understanding to grasp every kind of literature and learning. The word "literature" points to the writings and culture of their day, and "knowledge" refers to wisdom and learning in general. Daniel was also given insight to understand visions and dreams of all kinds.

The narrator of the book is the one speaking. These young Jews lived in Babylon as captives and were being trained to serve the king. They had resolved not to defile themselves with the king's food, and the text makes clear that their wisdom did not come only from their own effort but was a gift from God.

For today: do your study and your work well, but recognize that your abilities are a gift from God. Ask him for wisdom and use it with humility, even in settings where few share your faith.
exp.1:22:
Daniel gives thanks and praise to God, whom he addresses as the God of his fathers, meaning the God of his ancestors. He acknowledges that God has given him wisdom and power, and that God has now answered the request he and his friends made. In the Berean Standard Bible, the dream is described as "the dream of the king," so the answer God gave is the revealing of that dream.

Daniel speaks after God revealed the king's dream to him in a vision at night. The king had ordered that all the wise men of Babylon be put to death because none of them could tell him his dream. Daniel and his friends prayed asking for mercy, and God answered them. Before going before the king, Daniel pauses to give thanks.

When God answers a prayer, it is worth stopping to thank him before moving on to what comes next. Daniel did not take the credit for himself but recognized that everything came from God. Today we can do the same: thank him by name for what he has done.
exp.1:30:
Daniel tells King Nebuchadnezzar that in his dream he saw a great statue. It was enormous, it gleamed with a dazzling brightness, and it stood right in front of him. Its appearance was awe-inspiring, meaning it filled him with fear and wonder.

Daniel speaks as a young Jewish man taken captive to Babylon. The king had a dream that troubled him, and none of his wise men could tell him what it was or what it meant. Daniel makes clear that he is not wiser than others, but that God, who reveals hidden things, showed him the dream. He then explains that the statue represents human kingdoms that follow one another.

For today: what the world presents as great and impressive is not permanent. When you feel overwhelmed by human power, remember that God governs history. And if He gives you understanding, let it be used to serve with humility, not to boast.
exp.5:12:
Daniel's enemies go before King Darius and bring their accusation. They describe him as one of the exiles from Judah who shows no regard for the king or for the decree the king has signed, because he keeps making his request to God three times a day. "Makes his request" means he prays. "One of the exiles from Judah" refers to the Jews who were taken as prisoners to Babylon.

The ones speaking are the high officials who, driven by envy, persuaded the king to sign a law forbidding prayer to anyone but him. They knew Daniel would not stop praying. Their accusation sounds like loyalty to the king, but in truth it aims to destroy an upright man.

For today: Daniel kept up his habit of prayer, even knowing the risk. We can ask God for steadiness to keep our faith constant and simple, without hiding it out of fear of what others may say or do.
exp.10:36:
This verse says that this king will show no regard for the gods of his fathers. He will also show no regard for "the one desired by women," a phrase that is understood in several ways: some think it refers to the natural desire for a wife and family, and others think it refers to a god that women worshiped. He will not regard any other god, because he will set himself above them all.

The angel speaking to Daniel is showing him what is to come. Here he describes a proud king who puts himself above every god. Scholars disagree about who is meant: many think of Antiochus Epiphanes, while others see here a future antichrist. What is certain is that the text shows that God knows and controls what will happen, until his appointed time is fulfilled.

For today: let us guard against the pride that makes us live as if we did not need God. Let us follow the God of our fathers with humility and put him first.
exp.7:12:
Daniel hears two holy beings, that is, angels, speaking together. One asks how long the vision will last. The question concerns the daily sacrifice being taken away, and the rebellion that causes desolation. It is why the sanctuary and the people are trampled underfoot.

Daniel has just seen a horn that attacks God's people and takes away the daily worship. Many connect it with Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and some also see a future fulfillment. The two thousand three hundred days are understood in several ways: as literal days, or as evenings and mornings of sacrifice. The question is a cry: how long will this suffering last?

For today: when pain or injustice seems long, you can honestly ask God how long. He sets a limit to evil and promises to restore what was destroyed.
exp.3:35:
At the same time, my sanity was restored to me. My honor and splendor returned to me for the glory of my kingdom. My advisers and nobles sought me out, I was restored to my throne, and surpassing greatness was added to me.

The king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, speaks in his own personal testimony. Earlier, his pride led him into a terrible humiliation, a time when he lost his sanity and lived like an animal. When he lifted his eyes to heaven and acknowledged that God rules over everything, his mind returned to him. Scholars debate exactly what his illness was, but the text emphasizes that it was a judgment from God.

For today: God resists the proud, but welcomes the one who humbles himself. If you recognize today that everything you have is a gift from God, you can begin to live with more peace, gratitude, and simplicity.
exp.8:20:
Daniel says that he was still praying when Gabriel, the same angel he had seen earlier in a vision, came to him. He describes Gabriel as coming "in swift flight," meaning quickly, and says that Gabriel arrived at about the time of the evening sacrifice, meaning around that hour. Here "man" simply refers to a figure who looked like a man.

Daniel speaks in the first person. He was confessing his sins and the sins of Israel, and he was pleading for Jerusalem while the people lived in exile in Babylon. The hour of the evening sacrifice was a time of prayer in Israel. Gabriel comes to give him understanding about what would come.

For today: pray with sincerity and humility, without rushing. God hears from the very first moment you cry out, and he may answer in ways you did not expect.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that the people did not listen to God or pay attention to Him. "Obeyed the voice" means heeding what He says and putting it into practice. "Walk in His laws" means living according to His commandments. God had spoken to them clearly through His servants the prophets, but they did not follow them.

Daniel is praying in Babylon, during the exile. Although he himself was faithful, he includes himself in the confession, saying "we." He acknowledges that the whole nation rebelled, and that the hardships they were living through were connected to that disobedience, just as Moses had warned. Even so, Daniel relies on the fact that God is merciful and forgives.

Today we can learn to listen to God with humility. If we have ignored what He tells us in His Word, we can confess it sincerely and turn back to Him, trusting in His mercy.
exp.11:3:
Daniel is told to keep the message he received safe: to shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end. The text says "many will roam to and fro," a phrase that can be understood as many people moving back and forth, searching or investigating. "Knowledge" here means understanding or insight, and it will increase.

An angel speaks, the man clothed in linen, after the vision about times of great distress and the resurrection. The book is sealed to preserve it, and because its full fulfillment was reserved for later. Some think the knowledge refers to understanding the prophecy; others, to a general increase of learning. It is not clear what the exact idea is.

Today, God keeps his promises even when we do not understand everything. He invites us to know him with humility through his Word, and to trust him where mystery still remains.
exp.11:8:
God tells Daniel to go on his way, because the message he has received is kept shut up and sealed until the time when it will be fulfilled. Behind this picture stands the image of a rolled-up document protected by a seal, one that has not yet been opened. "Fulfillment" refers to the time of the end, when everything comes to pass.

The one clothed in linen, a heavenly figure who appears in this vision, is the speaker. Daniel has just said that he heard but did not understand, and he asks how these things will end. The answer gives him no further details; he is asked to trust. Interpreters differ on how these prophecies are fulfilled, and it is honest to acknowledge this.

For today: you do not need to understand everything in order to keep trusting God. There are things He does not yet explain, and still He invites us to live with faithfulness, patience, and hope, knowing that He holds the future in His hands.
exp.10:31:
It says that a powerful king will corrupt with smooth talk and flattery those who had already broken the covenant with God, and will lead them into even greater sin. The word "flattery" refers to the flattering speeches used to win someone over. Those who violate the covenant are the ones who break faith with it. By contrast, the people who know their God will firmly resist him and act with courage.

An angel speaks to Daniel and announces what will come upon his people. The passage describes a king of the north who persecutes the Jews, defiles the temple, and takes away the daily sacrifice. Many interpreters connect him with Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and some also see a projection toward the final time. The message seeks to encourage the faithful in the midst of the trial.

For today: knowing God truly, through prayer and reading his Word, gives us steadfastness when the world flatters us to make us give in. Whoever knows him is not easily deceived and dares to obey.
exp.7:7:
This verse says the male goat, which represents a powerful kingdom, became very great. But at the height of its power, its large horn was broken off, and four prominent horns came up in its place, pointing toward the four winds of heaven. The verse uses the same idea in its own words, so no separate note is needed here.

Daniel describes a vision he received. Later, the angel Gabriel explains that the goat is the kingdom of Greece and the large horn is its first king (Daniel 8:21). Many understand this to refer to Alexander the Great and the division of his empire into four parts after his death. God shows this to Daniel to announce that He knows the future.

Today we can learn that no human power lasts forever, not even at its best. Let us trust in God, who governs history, and not place our security in what passes away.
exp.9:18:
He says to Daniel with tenderness, "Do not be afraid, you who are highly precious." He tells him he is deeply valued and gives him peace. "Be strong now; be very strong" means to regain strength. While the messenger was speaking, Daniel felt his strength return and asked him to keep speaking, because he had strengthened him.

Daniel has just seen a vision so overwhelming that he was left without strength and without breath. The one speaking is a heavenly messenger in human appearance; the text does not give his name, and people have debated who he is. He touches Daniel, calms him, and then explains the spiritual struggle behind the kingdoms of this world.

For today: when fear or weariness leaves you without strength, do not stay silent. Draw near to God, listen to His Word, and let His peace lift you up. Very often He strengthens us while He speaks to us.
exp.9:12:
A heavenly messenger explains to Daniel why he was delayed in arriving. The prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed him for twenty-one days. Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help him, for the messenger had been left there with the kings of Persia. "Opposed me" means that he resisted him.

Daniel had been in three weeks of mourning, prayer and fasting. From the first day God heard his plea and sent the messenger. Many understand that the "prince of Persia" is a spiritual power behind that empire, though some think of a human ruler. The text gives no further detail, so it is wise to speak with caution.

For today: when it seems that God is slow to answer, this does not mean that he has not heard you. There are things we do not see. Keep praying with patience and trust, knowing that God listens from the first day.
exp.8:14:
Daniel reminds God that he brought his people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and that by doing so he made a name for himself that is renowned to this day. Then he confesses: "we have sinned; we have acted wickedly." The word "wickedly" here means that they acted with evil, showing no respect for God.

Daniel prays in Babylon, during the exile of the people. He has read that Jerusalem would lie in ruins for a time, and so he prays with humility. He includes himself in the guilt of the people, although the Bible does not accuse him of that sin. To ask for forgiveness, he relies on what God has already done in the past.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or make excuses for yourself. Acknowledge your sin honestly and turn to God, remembering how he has helped you before. He is faithful and listens to the humble heart.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that on the twenty-fourth day of the first month, Daniel was standing on the bank of a great river, the Tigris.

Daniel, now an old man, speaks from Persia, during the reign of Cyrus. He had spent three weeks in mourning and fasting, likely troubled about his people and their future. That fast ended around the time he reached the river. There he had an impressive vision of a heavenly being. The text does not say why he went to the river; it is best not to invent a reason.

For today: when you are worried about something that weighs on your heart, keep praying faithfully. Daniel waited three weeks and God did not forget him. Sometimes the answer takes time, but God listens and acts in his own timing.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that Daniel's enemies looked for something to accuse him of, but they could find no fault in his work. So they concluded that the only way to attack him was through his faith. The phrase "any charge against" means a reason to bring an accusation against someone. "The law of his God" refers to the way he lived and worshiped God.

The ones speaking are the governors and presidents of Darius's kingdom. They were envious, because Daniel was outstanding and the king intended to set him over the whole kingdom. Since they could not prove any wrongdoing, they planned a trap with a decree that would force him to choose between obeying the king or continuing to pray to God.

For today: let us strive to be people of integrity at work, in study, and in the family, so that our conduct speaks well of our faith. And if we are ever criticized for following God, let it not be because we were careless or unjust.
exp.4:7:
This verse tells us that all the wise men of King Belshazzar came into the hall, but none of them could read the mysterious writing that had appeared on the wall. They also could not explain to the king what it meant. The word "interpret" here means to explain the meaning.

Here the narrator of the book of Daniel is speaking. The king was terrified because, in the middle of the feast, a hand wrote on the wall. He had offered great rewards to anyone who could decipher it, but the experts of Babylon failed. In this way the scene is set for Daniel to be called upon to give the interpretation.

For today: human wisdom has its limits, and there are situations where neither money, titles, nor experts give us answers. When you find yourself with no way out, humble yourself and seek God in prayer and in his Word, for he gives light and understanding to those who seek him.
exp.8:22:
As soon as Daniel began to pray, God sent an answer. The angel Gabriel came to explain it to him. He calls Daniel "highly precious," meaning a man who is deeply loved and valued by God. Then he asks Daniel to think carefully about the message and understand the vision.

The angel Gabriel is speaking to Daniel. Daniel was praying and confessing the sins of his people, who lived in exile in Babylon, and he asked for mercy for Jerusalem. God answers him with the prophecy of the seventy weeks, which many Christians connect with the coming of the Messiah, although there is debate about how to interpret those periods of time.

God hears our sincere prayers from the very first moment. Pray with confidence, and then take time to read his Word so that you can understand what he wants to teach you.
exp.3:34:
Before God, all the peoples of the earth are counted as nothing, which means no one can be compared to Him. He does as He pleases with the armies of heaven and the peoples of the earth. No one can restrain His hand or say to Him, "What have You done?"

The one speaking is King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. He had grown proud, and God humbled him: he lost his reason and lived like an animal for a time. When he lifted his eyes to heaven and regained his understanding, he acknowledged that God alone truly rules. These words are his confession after being corrected.
