For today: when you feel insecure or want to control everything, remember that God rules over all. Hand Him your plans with humility and trust that His work is just and good, even when you do not always understand it.
exp.4:30:
Daniel 5:31 tells us that Darius the Mede received the kingdom of Babylon at the age of sixty-two. The word "received" here means that he took over the government, right after the fall of Belshazzar.

This is the end of chapter 5. God had announced, through the writing on the wall, that Belshazzar's kingdom would be given to the Medes and Persians. The narrator, who is Daniel, describes how that word was fulfilled that very same night. Historians do not agree on exactly who "Darius the Mede" was; some connect him with a governor under Cyrus, others with Cyrus himself. For that reason it is wise to speak with humility on that point.

For today: human powers can seem firm, but they change in a single night. God remains. Trust in Him more than in any authority, wealth, or passing stability, because his word always comes to pass.
exp.7:18:
Here Gabriel tells Daniel that he is going to explain what will happen in the latter time of wrath, that is, in a later period of God's judgment and anger. The phrase "because it concerns the appointed time of the end" means that all of this will unfold at the moment God has set. "I will make known to you" means "I will help you understand."

Daniel has just seen a vision of the ram and the goat. He was so frightened that he fell face down to the ground and fell asleep. The angel Gabriel lifts him up and explains the meaning. Interpreters disagree about what "the end" refers to: some think of the persecution under Antiochus IV, others of a more distant final time, and others of both.

God does not leave his children without an answer when they do not understand. Even if there are things about the future we cannot grasp, we can trust that he is in control and knows the exact time. Bring your doubts to him in prayer today and rest in the fact that he carries out his plans in his time.
exp.1:18:
This verse says that God showed Daniel the secret of the king's dream, and He did it during the night, in a vision. The word "mystery" appears in the verse itself, so no further explanation is needed. The phrase "was revealed" means that God made it known to him. When he received the answer, Daniel praised God.

King Nebuchadnezzar had a dream that troubled him, and he demanded that the wise men tell him both the dream and its meaning. No one could, and the king ordered all the wise men put to death. Daniel asked for time, sought out his three friends, and together they prayed, asking God for mercy. This verse is the answer to that prayer.

When you face a problem that is bigger than you are, pray with other believers and ask God for help. And when the answer comes, do not forget to give thanks right away, as Daniel did.
exp.7:11:
This verse says that the "small horn" of the vision was handed power over God's people, the host, because of rebellion. This power stopped the daily sacrifice, flung the truth to the ground, and prospered in whatever it did. The rebellion is the reason the host and the daily sacrifice were given over to the horn.

Daniel recounts a vision he received about a ram and a male goat. Many understand that the small horn refers to Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who defiled the temple in the second century B.C. Others also see a future fulfillment. An angel explains the vision afterward, and the message seeks to comfort a people who were suffering.

For today: when wickedness seems to triumph, remember that it has limits and that God has the final word. Remain faithful in your worship and in your love for the truth, even when others despise it.
exp.10:20:
It says that after one king will come another who is "despicable," a person who does not deserve to be king. No one will give him the royal honors that go with the position. Even so, he will arrive "in a time of peace," meaning without any open war, and will seize the kingdom by "intrigue," which means secret scheming and smooth talk meant to win people over to his side.

An angel speaks to Daniel and foreshadows for him the story of the kingdoms that would come. Many scholars see here Antiochus IV Epiphanes, king of the Seleucid empire, who rose to power through cunning. Some also see a foreshadowing of a future oppressor. Interpreters do not agree on everything.

For today: let us be wary of anyone who comes to power with nothing but clever words. Let us ask God for discernment to see whether a person's character and actions match what they say. And let us remember that God continues to rule above every leader.
exp.11:2:
This verse promises that those who are wise, meaning people who are sensible and have spiritual understanding, will shine like the brightness of the heavens. It also says that those who lead many toward righteousness, meaning those who guide others toward what is right, will shine like the stars forever.

A heavenly messenger speaks to Daniel about a final time of great distress and of resurrection. After mentioning those who will rise to life or to shame, the message comforts the faithful: their faithfulness is not forgotten. Interpreters differ on the details of when and how this will be fulfilled, but all see here a firm hope.

Today we can be encouraged to live with wisdom and to guide others toward God with patience, even when no one notices. God does see it, and He values it.
exp.1:29:
Here Daniel says that God revealed to him the secret of the king's dream, but not because he is wiser than other people. "Any man alive" means every person. "Made known" means told or shared, and "interpretation" is the meaning of the dream. God did this so that the king would be given the meaning and so that he would understand the thoughts of his mind.

Daniel speaks before King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. The king had a dream that troubled him, and his wise men could tell him neither the dream nor its meaning. Daniel first makes clear that the answer comes from the God of heaven, not from his own talent. Then he begins to describe the great image the king had seen.

For today: if God gives you a skill, knowledge, or an opportunity, do not think yourself superior. Use it with humility to serve others and to give glory to God.
exp.3:1:
It says that King Nebuchadnezzar feels he should tell everyone about the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for him. The verse uses the words "I am pleased to declare," which show that he is glad to make these things known publicly.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon speaks in a letter addressed to all the peoples of his empire. After a humbling experience, which the chapter recounts right after, he acknowledges that the Most High God rules over everything. His testimony begins with praise and gratitude.

For today: when God works in your life, do not keep the testimony to yourself. Share it simply and humbly with your family, your friends, or your coworkers, so that they too may come to know the greatness and goodness of God.
exp.1:36:
Daniel tells King Nebuchadnezzar that he is "the king of kings," meaning the most powerful ruler of his time. But he makes clear that the king did not earn this position on his own: the God of heaven gave him the sovereignty, the power, the strength, and the glory.

Daniel is speaking before the king of Babylon after recalling the king's forgotten dream and explaining it to him. In the dream there was a great statue, and Daniel now begins to interpret it. Nebuchadnezzar is the head of gold. Daniel wants the king to understand that his authority comes from God, not from himself.

Everything we have, whether abilities, work, influence, or authority, is a gift from God. That invites us to live with humility and gratitude, and to use what we have received to serve others well.
exp.8:5:
This verse says that the people did not listen to or heed the prophets, who were God's servants. They spoke in the Lord's name to everyone: kings, leaders, ancestors, and ordinary people. The "leaders" were the heads or rulers, and the "fathers" were the ancestors.

Daniel speaks here, praying and confessing the sin of his people, though he himself is presented as a faithful man. He identifies with Israel and says "we have sinned." He is in exile in Babylon and acknowledges that the punishment came because of rebellion, not because they had not been warned. God had spoken to them many times through his prophets.

For today: God still speaks, above all through his Word. Today we can ask ourselves which biblical truth we have heard and not put into practice, and ask God for forgiveness and help to obey it with humility.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that only Daniel saw the vision of the glorious being. The men who were with him did not see it, but a great terror fell on them, and they ran off and hid themselves.

Daniel is the one who recounts what he experienced on the bank of the Tigris River, after three weeks of prayer and fasting. The text does not say who the man is; some believe he is an angel, and others think he is an appearance of Christ before his coming. The companions felt something without understanding what it was, while Daniel did see the vision.

God reveals himself to those who seek him sincerely. If we pray with persistence, we may receive more than others notice. And when we feel fear in the presence of what is holy, let us remember that God knows how to lift up his own, as he did with Daniel.
exp.4:9:
She entered the banquet hall after hearing the uproar from the king and his nobles. She greeted the king with the words "O king, may you live forever!" and told him not to let his thoughts terrify him or his face grow pale. A pale face here points to fear.

She speaks as the queen, probably the queen mother, since the king's wives were already present at the banquet. It is not known for certain who she was. Belshazzar was terrified because a hand had written on the wall and none of the wise men could read it. She seems to calm him and to remind him of Daniel.

For today: when fear overwhelms us and human answers fail, it is wise to listen to someone who has God's wisdom, and to remember those who have been faithful, even when others have forgotten them.
exp.1:15:
Daniel went before King Nebuchadnezzar and asked him for some time. He said that he would then give the king the interpretation of the dream. The verse uses the word "interpretation" for this idea, meaning the verse of what the dream meant.

The king had a dream that troubled him, and he demanded that the wise men tell him both the dream and its meaning. Since they could not do so, he ordered that all of them be put to death. Daniel, who was also one of that group, spoke calmly with Arioch, the captain of the guard, and learned what was happening. Then he asked the king for time. The Bible does not say how he got the king to grant it.

When you face great pressure, do not rush or give in to panic. Ask for time, breathe, seek counsel and pray, as Daniel did with his companions, before you respond.
exp.2:12:
Nebuchadnezzar was furious with rage when he was told that three young Jewish men had not bowed down before his statue. He summoned Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and they were brought before him right away. The word "then" here signals that this happened immediately after the report reached the king.

The narrator of the book of Daniel is speaking. Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon, and he had set up a golden statue and ordered everyone to worship it. Some astrologers accused Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who were officials of the kingdom. For the king, not worshiping the statue was an offense against his authority. For these three men, worshiping it would have meant disobeying God.

Today, being faithful to God can bring pressure or anger from others. We can respect people, yet decide beforehand whom we will worship, and trust that God is with us, even when we do not know how everything will turn out.
exp.0:10:
This verse is only the introduction to what Daniel is going to say. Daniel speaks to the steward whom the chief official had appointed over him and his three friends: Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The word "eunuchs" here refers to the officials of the king's court. Some scholars think "Melzar" may be a title rather than a personal name, but there is no certainty.

Daniel and his friends were young men taken captive to Babylon. The chief official feared that the king would punish him if the young men looked weak. That is why Daniel does not argue, but seeks out another overseer and speaks to him with respect, proposing a test.

For today: when you want to remain faithful to God, you do not need to be aggressive. Speak with respect, offer a reasonable proposal, and trust that God can give favor before those who have authority over you.
exp.0:3:
The verse says that the king of Babylon wanted young men without any flaw in their bodies, handsome, gifted in all wisdom, knowledgeable, quick to understand, and qualified to serve in his palace. They would also be taught the language and literature of the Chaldeans. "Blemish" means a defect or stain. "Qualified" means suitable or capable for the task.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling what Nebuchadnezzar commanded Ashpenaz, the chief of his officials (or chamberlains; the term is understood in several ways). Judah had just been defeated, and Babylon sought young men of noble birth to train them and put them into its service. Many understand that it was also a way of integrating them into Babylonian culture.

For today: God can use us even in places we did not choose. Learning, preparing ourselves, and working well are valuable, but we must take care that what we learn does not displace our faith and faithfulness to God, as Daniel and his friends will do.
exp.9:15:
Daniel says that suddenly one with the likeness of a man touched his lips. Then he was able to open his mouth and speak. He said to the one standing before him, "My lord, because of the vision, I am overcome with anguish, and I have no strength." The phrase "I am overcome with anguish" describes a very deep distress that Daniel felt in the presence of the vision.

Daniel is beside the river Tigris, after three weeks of mourning and fasting. He has seen an impressive vision, and the messenger announces to him what will come upon his people. Daniel was left speechless and with his eyes cast to the ground. The text does not say with certainty who this being is; some think he is an angel, and others that he is a special appearance of God.

When we feel without strength or words before what God reveals, we are not alone. God knows how to meet our weakness, give us a voice, and strengthen us. We can draw near to Him with sincerity, just as we are.
exp.1:14:
Daniel asks Arioch, the captain of the king's guard, why the king's decree was so harsh. The word "harsh" here describes how severe the order was, so Daniel is asking why the king had issued such a severe command. Arioch then explained the situation to Daniel, that is, what was happening and why.

Daniel speaks here after King Nebuchadnezzar ordered that all the wise men of Babylon be put to death, because none of them could tell him his dream or its meaning. Daniel and his companions were going to be included in the sentence. Instead of reacting with fear or anger, Daniel answered calmly and with sensible questions, and in this way he learned the facts.

For today: before reacting to a crisis, it is wise to ask questions calmly and understand the situation well. A calm and respectful attitude opens doors, and it prepares us to seek God with clarity, as Daniel did right away.
exp.5:10:
This verse tells how a group of men came together and caught Daniel petitioning God. He was asking for help and speaking with God, as he always did. "Went as a group" means they came together as one body, and "petitioning and imploring" means asking earnestly and urgently.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The other officials, jealous of Daniel, had persuaded King Darius to sign a law forbidding anyone to pray to any god or person other than the king for thirty days. They were looking for an excuse to accuse Daniel. He knew about the law, but he kept praying with his windows open toward Jerusalem.

For today: make prayer a firm habit, not something that depends on circumstances. If God holds first place in your daily life, you can remain faithful with peace even when there is pressure around you.
exp.0:6:
He says that the chief official, the king's officer in charge of the young men, gave new names to the four Hebrew friends. Daniel was renamed Belteshazzar, Hananiah was given the name Shadrach, Mishael was given the name Meshach, and Azariah was given the name Abednego. The phrase "chief official" here refers to the one in charge of the court's young men, and the word "official" describes his role in the king's service.

The narrator tells how Babylon took these young men from Judah to train them for service to the king. Their Hebrew names pointed to the God of Israel, since Daniel means "God is my judge." The new names are connected to Babylonian gods and customs, although the exact meaning of some of them is debated. It was a way of shaping their identity.

Today we may also find that our surroundings try to change who we are. Even if others call you by another name or treat you differently, your worth and your identity come from God. Like Daniel, decide calmly and respectfully to remain faithful to him.
exp.6:10:
Daniel says that he kept watching the vision because the horn would not stop speaking arrogant words. Then he saw that the fourth beast was slain, its body was destroyed, and it was thrown into the blazing fire. "Kept watching because of the words" means that he kept paying close attention to what the horn was saying. "Destroyed" means that it was torn down.

Daniel himself tells of a vision he had at night. The beasts represent kingdoms, and the little horn is a proud ruler who speaks against God. Interpreters disagree about exactly who it identifies. What is clear is that, after the Judge sits down and the books are opened, that power is judged and comes to an end.

For today: proud powers may seem strong and speak with great arrogance, but they do not have the last word. God is the just Judge. You can entrust to him the injustices you see and live with humility and hope.
exp.3:33:
At the end of that time, Nebuchadnezzar says, he looked up to heaven and his sanity was restored to him. Then he praised, honored and glorified the Most High, the one who lives forever. He declared that God's dominion is an everlasting dominion and that his kingdom endures from generation to generation.

The same king of Babylon speaks here, describing in his own words what he went through. God had warned him, through a dream that Daniel interpreted, that he would be driven away from people for seven periods of time because of his pride. Scholars debate what illness or condition it may have been, and it is not known for certain how long those "times" lasted; many think of seven years.

For today: when pride makes us feel we own everything, looking up to God brings our humility back. Today you can pause for a moment and thank God, acknowledging that everything you have comes from Him.
exp.4:24:
This verse repeats the mysterious words that a hand wrote on the palace wall: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN. Here "written" means that the writing was left engraved or traced on the wall. They are Aramaic words that seem to be terms for weights and measures, and that is why no one in the court understood their meaning.

The prophet Daniel speaks to King Belshazzar during a banquet. The king had used the sacred vessels of the temple in Jerusalem to drink and to praise idols. Daniel explains to him that this writing is a judgment of God against his pride. The verses that follow explain that his kingdom would be counted and brought to an end.

For today: God sees how we use what he has given us. Today you can stop and ask yourself whether you are honoring God with your life, your time and your decisions, or whether you live only for yourself. Repenting in time is better than ignoring his voice.
exp.0:7:
Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king's food or wine. The word "defile" is the verse's own word, so it stays as it is. The king's food here is the daily ration from the king's table. The "chief official" was the one in charge of the young men at the palace. Daniel did not rebel; he asked for permission with respect.

The book tells how Daniel and his companions were taken to Babylon and given Babylonian names. They were to be educated in the style of that court. The text does not say with certainty why the food would have defiled him; it has been explained by Jewish law about foods, by the offering of food to idols, or by both. Even so, the text shows that God gave him favor before the official.

For today: decide in advance what your convictions are, before the pressure comes. And when you must defend them, do so with respect and humility, trusting in God.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that when the tree is cut down, the stump, meaning the trunk with its roots, must be left in the ground. It would be bound with a band of iron and bronze, out in the tender grass of the field. It would also be drenched with the dew of heaven, and it would live among the animals, grazing on the grass of the earth like them.

In the dream, Nebuchadnezzar tells what he saw. A watcher, a heavenly being, announces a judgment on the tree. Later, Daniel explains that the tree is the king, proud of his power. Leaving the stump shows that he would not be destroyed forever, but humbled and then restored.

For today: God corrects pride, but He also leaves a hope. Recognize that everything you have comes from Him, and live with humility and gratitude.
exp.6:9:
Daniel sees God on his heavenly throne. A river of fire flows out from his presence, and a vast multitude of attendants serves him and stands before him. "Thousands upon thousands" and "myriads upon myriads" are ways of saying they cannot be counted. The court is convened and the books are opened, meaning a judgment begins in which everything is brought into the light.

Daniel himself recounts this vision he had in a dream. He sees four beasts that represent kingdoms, and a little horn that speaks with arrogance. This scene of the heavenly court shows that this proud power does not have the final word. Interpreters disagree about which kingdoms each figure corresponds to, but the central message is clear: God governs and judges.

For today: when you see injustice or arrogant people who seem to be winning, rest in the knowledge that God sees everything and will do justice in his time. Live honestly today, as one who knows that nothing is hidden before him.
exp.7:16:
Daniel tells us that Gabriel, God's messenger, came near to the place where he was standing. When Daniel saw him coming, he was terrified and fell facedown on the ground. Gabriel speaks to him: "Son of man," he says, and he tells Daniel to understand that the vision concerns the time of the end, that is, the time set by God.

Daniel had seen a vision of a ram and a male goat, and he did not understand it. While he was pondering it, a voice commanded Gabriel to explain it to him. Interpreters debate exactly which period the "time of the end" points to, but all agree that God controls the times of history.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows or promises, draw near to Him with humility and keep seeking His Word. He has a time for everything, and He does not forget you.
exp.0:8:
It says that God caused Daniel to be well liked by the chief official, that is, by the official in charge of the young men taken to Babylon. The words that your verse renders as "favor" and "compassion" mean favor and kindness, and this favor is shown to come from God.

The passage tells the story of Daniel, a young Jew taken captive to Babylon. Daniel had just asked not to defile himself with the king's food and wine. The Bible does not explain here in detail the exact reason; some think of foods forbidden by the law, others of his concern about offerings to idols. Even so, the official was afraid of the king, and this verse shows that God was working in his heart.

When you want to be faithful to God in a difficult place, do it with respect and humility, and trust that He can open doors and soften hearts. It will not always happen in the same way, but God cares for His own.
exp.9:7:
Daniel tells us that he was left alone and saw this great vision. No strength remained in him, and his face grew deathly pale, so that he was powerless.

Daniel speaks as an old man, after praying and fasting for three weeks. He sees a glorious being beside the river Tigris. His companions see nothing, but they feel terror and flee. Daniel is left alone before that overwhelming presence. Interpreters disagree about who this being is: some think it is an angel, like Gabriel, and others think it is an appearance of Christ before he was born. The text does not make this entirely clear.

Before something so great, our strength runs out. But God does not leave us on the ground: in the next verse a hand touches Daniel and raises him up. When you feel weak, come to God with humility. He knows how to sustain you.
exp.1:9:
The wise men of Babylon tell the king that no one on earth can do what he asks. He wants them to tell him a dream he has already forgotten and also explain what it means. They add that no king, however great and powerful, has ever asked anything like this of any magician, enchanter, or astrologer.

The speakers are the astrologers, advisers to King Nebuchadnezzar. The king is troubled by a dream and suspects they are stalling for time. They object because, from their experience, the request goes beyond all human ability. Their answer shows the limits of human wisdom and sets the scene for Daniel to turn to God.

For today: there are things we cannot solve with our own cleverness or our own resources. Recognizing this is not weakness. It is the first step toward coming to God in prayer, with humility, and asking him for wisdom.
exp.8:1:
In the first year of Darius's reign, Daniel says he carefully studied the sacred books. There he found the number of years that the LORD had spoken to the prophet Jeremiah: the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. "Desolation" means complete ruin and abandonment.

Daniel speaks as an elderly Jew taken captive to Babylon. Babylon had just passed into the hands of the Medes and Persians. As Daniel read the Scriptures, he understood that the time of Jeremiah's prophecy (Jeremiah 25 and 29) was drawing near its end. This moved him to pray, to fast, and to confess the sins of his people.

For today: God's Word is not only to be read; it also leads us to prayer. Daniel trusted God's promises, but he did not sit idle; he embraced them with humble prayer. Before you ask for anything, let the Bible direct your heart.
exp.6:5:
Daniel sees a third beast, similar to a leopard. It has four wings like a bird's on its back, four heads, and it is given authority to rule. The phrase "was given authority" simply means that authority was given to it.

Daniel speaks, recounting a vision he had at night. The four beasts represent kingdoms that rise one after another. Many believe this third one is Greece, with the speed of Alexander the Great and his empire later divided, but some understand it in a different way. What matters is that the authority "was given" to it: God remains the one who allows kingdoms to rise and fall.

For today: when the powers of this world seem enormous or threatening, remember that none of them is eternal or escapes God's control. You can pray calmly and trust that He sustains history and your life.
exp.10:38:
He says that this king will attack the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god, whom he acknowledges, and will greatly honor those who acknowledge that god. He will make them rulers over many people and distribute the land for a price. "Rulers" here means those who govern, and "a price" points to payment or profit.

An angel explains to Daniel what is to come, in a prophecy about the kings of the north and the south. This passage speaks of an arrogant king who exalts himself above everything. Many believe it refers to Antiochus IV Epiphanes; others also see a future fulfillment in the antichrist. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: when power, money, or success becomes our god, we end up using others. Let us ask God for a humble heart that puts Him first.
exp.1:5:
This verse says the king promises rewards to whoever tells him his dream and what it means. The words "gifts and rewards" refer to favors and presents, and "great honor" refers to a place of high respect. The king ends with a direct command: tell him the dream and its interpretation.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon speaks to his wise men. He is troubled by a dream that he cannot remember, or that he does not want to reveal. Earlier he threatened them with punishment, and now he adds rewards. He wants to be sure that their interpretation is true and not something they have made up.

For today: when someone pressures us with rewards or threats, let us remember that only God gives true wisdom. Before promising what we cannot deliver, we can ask God for help with humility.
exp.5:15:
This verse says that King Darius gave the order, and they took Daniel and threw him into the den of lions. Before this happened, the king spoke to Daniel: "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!" The king's words show his hope that the God Daniel faithfully serves would rescue him. Some words to note: "gave the order" means commanded, "den" means a deep pit or cave, and "continually" means all the time.

King Darius speaks here. His advisers, out of jealousy, had tricked him into signing a law that forbade praying to any other god for thirty days. Daniel kept praying to God as he always did. The king was distressed and tried to save him, but the law of the Medes and Persians could not be changed. So he had to carry it out, though he did not want to.

For today: serving God faithfully, in small things and in hard ones, leaves a witness that others notice, even those who do not believe. Today you can keep your habit of praying and obeying God even when no one applauds you, trusting that He cares for you.
exp.7:22:
In the later part of the kingdoms that followed Alexander, when the rebellion has reached its full measure, an insolent king will rise to power. This is someone bold and shameless. Those who turn against God and his law are the ones the verse describes as rebels. The description of this king as "skilled in intrigue" points to someone clever at schemes and at deceiving others.

Here the angel Gabriel speaks, explaining to Daniel the vision of the ram and the goat. The goat represents Greece. Many interpreters see in this king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who persecuted the Jews; others also see in him a foreshadowing of a future oppressor. The passage is understood in several ways.

For today: clever people in power may prosper for a time, but they do not have the final word. Trust in God, remain faithful, and do not be deceived by the apparent success of evil.
exp.2:19:
Here the account tells how King Nebuchadnezzar commanded some mighty men of valor in his army to tie up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and throw them into the blazing fiery furnace. The phrase "tie up" means to bind them securely, and "mighty men of valor" refers to strong, capable soldiers.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. The king was furious because these three young Jewish men had refused to worship the golden statue. They had already said that God could deliver them, and that even if he did not, they would not bow down. The king answered with great force and anger.

For today: sometimes being faithful to God will cost us discomfort or rejection. Decide ahead of time to obey him, trusting that he is with you, even if you cannot yet see how he will sustain you.
exp.8:13:
It says that the LORD kept the calamity in store and then brought it upon the people, just as he had said he would. The word "kept" in the verse above means that God held the disaster back, ready for the right time. Daniel confesses that the LORD is righteous in all that he does, and that the people had not obeyed his voice.

Daniel is praying in Babylon, during the exile. He looks at the law of Moses and understands that the destruction of Jerusalem was not chance, but the result of the disobedience the law had already warned about. He does not blame God; he joins the confession of the people and asks for mercy.

For today: when we face the consequences of our mistakes, we can stop making excuses for ourselves and speak with God honestly. Acknowledging his justice does not sink us in guilt; it opens the door to asking for forgiveness and returning to him, who is faithful and compassionate.
exp.0:13:
Daniel 1:14 tells us that Melzar, the official in charge of the young men, agreed to Daniel's proposal and tested them for ten days. The verse of this verse says that Melzar agreed to the proposal of Daniel and his friends. He ran the test with them for ten days. "Agreed" means that he was in accord, and "tested" means that he put them to the test. The "vegetables" were food of plant origin, and perhaps included grains and seeds.

Daniel and his companions were in Babylon, far from their homeland, and the king gave them food from his own table. Daniel decided not to defile himself with it (v. 8), but he spoke with respect. Melzar was afraid of the consequences, and Daniel proposed a simple and reasonable plan. Here the writer of the book narrates how God gave them favor.

For today: when you want to be faithful to God in a difficult environment, act with respect, wisdom and humility. Trust God and take concrete steps, without fighting or despising others.
exp.10:11:
It speaks of a great army, or of its king, who wins a battle and becomes full of pride. The words "the king of the South will be proud in heart" describe his arrogance, and "will cast down tens of thousands" means he will bring down a vast number of enemies. But "he will not triumph": his victory will not last, nor will it give him lasting rule.

The one speaking is a messenger sent by God to Daniel, who reveals to him what will happen to his people. This chapter describes wars between the king of the north and the king of the south. Many scholars relate them to the Syrian and Egyptian kingdoms after Alexander the Great, and this verse to the Egyptian victory at Raphia. The details are interpreted in several ways.

For today: success can tempt us to believe we are invincible. Give thanks for your achievements with humility, remembering that God governs history and that only his kingdom endures.
exp.0:14:
After the ten days of testing, Daniel and his three friends looked healthier and better nourished than the young men who were eating the king's food. "Looked" refers to their overall appearance. "Better nourished" means they appeared healthy and well fed. "Food" is the daily share assigned to them.

This is part of the story in Babylon. Daniel, a young Jew taken into exile, did not want to defile himself with the king's food. He asked the chief of the eunuchs for a ten-day test with vegetables and water. The text does not explain why that food was a problem; some think it was because of Jewish laws about food, others because of its connection with offerings to idols. The narrator shows that God honored his faithfulness.

For today: Daniel chose, with respect and without rebellion, to be faithful to God in a concrete matter. We can do the same in our work or studies: live with integrity, ask with humility, and trust God with the results.
exp.6:16:
These four great beasts represent four kings, and this verse says so. When it says they "arise from the earth," it means they are powers that will come up on the earth, one after another. In the Bible, "king" sometimes refers to a single person and sometimes to a whole kingdom.

Here the heavenly helper whom Daniel asked is speaking, since Daniel was frightened and wanted to understand his vision. Scholars disagree about which empires the four are: many think of Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece and Rome, while others propose a different list. What is certain is that the next verse ends with the kingdom given to the saints of the Most High.

For today: when the world seems dominated by frightening powers, do as Daniel did. Ask God, seek to understand, and remember that human kingdoms pass away, but the kingdom of God remains.
exp.7:0:
This verse says that Daniel received a new vision in the third year of King Belshazzar's reign. It describes the vision as coming "subsequent to the one that had appeared to me earlier," that is, after the vision of the four beasts recorded in chapter 7.

The one speaking is Daniel, a Jew living in exile in Babylon. Belshazzar was ruling there, and this vision came a few years after the earlier one. Daniel makes the timing clear so the reader understands that God continues to reveal to him what will happen to the kingdoms of this world. From here on, the language of the book returns to Hebrew.

For today: God does not forget his people even when they live through hard times. If you feel far from home or confused by what you see, seek God in prayer and in his Word, and trust that he still has control.
exp.5:8:
This verse says that King Darius put his signature on the written decree that had been presented to him. The decree is the official document that stated the king's command, and everyone was required to obey it. With his signature, the order was put into force.

The high officials of the kingdom, who envied Daniel, proposed this law to the king. For thirty days no one could ask anything of any god or man, only of the king. Darius signed, and according to the law of the Medes and Persians, a decree once signed could not be changed. The Bible does not say that Darius saw the trap; the text suggests that he was moved by flattery.

Be careful with hasty decisions, especially when we are flattered. Before we commit ourselves, it is wise to stop, think, and pray. Daniel, on the other hand, did not change his faithfulness to God, even though this cost him dearly.
exp.10:40:
He will enter the Beautiful Land, which is the land of Israel, and many countries will fall under his power. But Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites, peoples east of the Jordan, will be delivered from his hand. The countries in this verse are the lands he conquers, and the words "delivered from his hand" mean that these peoples will be saved.

An angel speaks to Daniel and reveals, in prophetic language, future conflicts between the kings of the north and the south. Many believe this describes Antiochus IV, and some see a final figure as well. Interpreters do not agree on every detail. The purpose is to encourage God's people: history is not chaotic, and God knows it.

Today we can live without fear in the face of news about powers and wars. God remains in control and cares for his own. Trust in him with calm and prayer.
exp.7:19:
This verse is a direct explanation of the vision. The two-horned ram that Daniel saw represents the kings of Media and Persia. Here the horns stand for the power and authority of those kingdoms.

The one speaking is the angel Gabriel, who explains to Daniel a vision that left him deeply troubled. Daniel had fallen asleep face down on the ground, and the angel raised him up to show him what would come at the appointed time of God's wrath. The verses that follow show that Greece (Javan) would come afterward, and the text presents this as something God already knows.

For today: empires may seem strong, but none of them lasts forever. God knows how history ends. When news or circumstances unsettle you, rest in the fact that He still governs and cares for His people.
exp.7:14:
Daniel describes what happened while he was watching the vision and trying hard to understand it. Suddenly, standing before him, was someone who looked like a man.

Daniel himself is the one speaking. He had just seen a puzzling vision about a ram, a goat, and a sanctuary being trampled, and he had heard the question, "How long?" He did not understand any of it. Right away the passage makes clear that this being is Gabriel, sent to explain the vision to him. Interpreters differ on some details of the two thousand three hundred days, but the passage makes clear that God responds to the one who seeks to understand.

For today: when you do not understand something in the Bible or in your life, do not give up. Think, ask, and ask God for light with patience. He knows how and when to give you understanding.
exp.3:32:
This verse says that God's sentence was carried out at once on Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven away from mankind, ate grass like an ox, and was left out in the open, drenched with the dew of heaven. His hair grew until it was like the feathers of an eagle, and his nails like the claws of a bird. The phrase "driven away from mankind" means that he lost his place as king and lived apart from other people.

Here the narrator of the account speaks, and earlier a voice from heaven spoke. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had filled himself with pride over his power. God had warned him in a dream, and now judgment arrives. Many understand that he suffered a mental illness, although the text does not name it. The punishment lasted for "seven times," and the text does not make clear how long that was.

For today: pride deceives us, because it makes us believe we achieved everything by ourselves. Recognize God in your successes and thank him with humility. He himself restored the king when he acknowledged him.
exp.1:37:
This verse says that God has placed both people and the beasts of the field and the birds of the air into the hands of King Nebuchadnezzar, and has made him ruler over them all. The word "ruler" here means one who governs or holds authority. That is why Daniel tells him, "You are that head of gold," meaning the most precious part of the statue the king saw in his dream.

Here Daniel speaks, a young Hebrew taken captive to Babylon. The king had a dream that troubled him, and Daniel explains it. His central point is that Nebuchadnezzar's power did not come from himself, but from the God of heaven. Other kingdoms follow, so no empire lasts forever. Scholars disagree about which later kingdoms are meant.

For today: everything we have, such as work, influence, or abilities, is a trust from God. We should use it with humility and gratitude, not with pride.
exp.4:10:
Here the queen tells the king that there is a man in your kingdom who has the spirit of the holy gods in him. In the days of your father, Nebuchadnezzar, he was found to have insight, intelligence, and wisdom like that of the gods. Your father appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners.

The one speaking is the queen, probably the queen mother, though it is not known for certain who she was. Belshazzar is terrified because a hand wrote on the wall during his feast, and no one can explain the message. She calms him and advises him to call for Daniel, whom he had already forgotten.

For today: a life faithful to God leaves a mark, even when others forget it for a time. Live with integrity and wisdom, and God can use you when you are needed most.
exp.9:0:
In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, God gave a message to Daniel, who was also called Belteshazzar. The message was true, and it concerned a great conflict. The words "was revealed" mean that it was shown to him. The verse begins its next thought with "and," which joins the message to what Daniel understood about it. Daniel understood the message, and the understanding came to him in a vision.

The writer is Daniel, a Jew who lived in exile in Babylon and later under Persian rule. This was around 536 B.C. Some understand the great conflict to be a prolonged struggle; others see it as a period that would stretch on until its fulfillment. The verses that follow show that Daniel fasted and prayed in sorrow.

For today: God keeps what He says, even when it takes a long time. When the answer is slow, we can keep praying, keep seeking to understand His Word, and trust that His timing is better than ours.
exp.3:30:
This verse says that King Nebuchadnezzar was still speaking when a voice came from heaven and interrupted him. The voice speaks to him directly: "It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, that the kingdom has departed from you."

Here God speaks from heaven. The king had just boasted about great Babylon, saying that he had built it by his own power and for his own glory. God answers that pride at once. The verses that follow explain that Nebuchadnezzar would be humbled until he acknowledged that the Most High rules over men.

For today: when we achieve something, it is wise to give thanks to God rather than boast. Everything we have, our talents, our strength and our opportunities, comes from Him. Humility keeps us grounded.
exp.10:5:
After some years, the king of the south and the king of the north will form an alliance. The daughter of the king of the south will go to the king of the north to seal the agreement. But she will not keep her position of power, and his strength will not endure. At that time she will be given up, along with her royal escort, her father, and the one who supported her.

An angel speaks to Daniel, a prophet in exile, to announce what would happen. Many scholars see here the Hellenistic kingdoms of Egypt (the south) and Syria (the north), and a political marriage like that of Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, although some interpret it in other ways. The message is that God knows history.

Human alliances and power are fragile. Today we can place less trust in influence or convenient arrangements, and more in God, who sustains all things.
exp.7:3:
Daniel describes seeing a ram charging toward the west, the north, and the south. No animal could stand against it, and there was no escape from its power. It did as it pleased and became great.

Daniel recounts a vision he had in Susa, beside the Ulai river. Later in this same chapter, the angel Gabriel explains that the two-horned ram represents the kings of Media and Persia (Daniel 8:20). That empire expanded greatly. God shows this to Daniel so that he will know that the powerful kingdoms of history do not escape His knowledge.

For today: human powers may seem unstoppable, but they have a limit. Trust that God remains in control, and seek your security in Him rather than in those who dominate.
exp.2:17:
What it says: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego tell the king that even if God does not rescue them from the furnace, they will still refuse to serve his gods or worship the golden statue he has set up. "But even if He does not" means the same as "even if he does not." "Worship" here means to honor and give reverence.

Context: The speakers are Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, Jews who had been taken captive to Babylon. King Nebuchadnezzar had commanded everyone to worship his statue, and the penalty for refusing was being thrown into a blazing furnace. They answered calmly and respectfully, but without giving in. They trusted that God was able to save them, but they did not assume that he would.

For today: Our faithfulness to God should not depend on everything going our way. We can pray in faith asking for help, and still decide to obey him if the answer does not come as we hope. Today, this may mean acting honestly even when it costs us, or keeping our faith even when others mock us.
exp.10:26:
It says that two kings, the one from the north and the one from the south, will sit at the same table as if they wanted peace, but each will have evil intentions toward the other in his heart. They will speak lies to each other's faces. "But it will not succeed" means that their deceptions will not achieve what they seek, because "the end" (the appointed time) has not yet come.

An angel explains to Daniel, through a vision, what will happen between two rival kingdoms. Many scholars see here the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings, although some interpret it in other ways. The central message is that God governs the times, and human intrigues cannot hasten or change his plan.

For today: lying, even when disguised as courtesy, builds nothing lasting. Let us be sincere in our words and trust that God works in his time, even when we see deceit around us.
exp.3:13:
This verse describes a loud command given from heaven: the great tree must be cut down. Its branches are to be chopped off, its leaves stripped away and its fruit scattered, and the animals and birds that lived in its shade are to flee from it.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, tells his dream. A watcher, meaning a holy messenger from heaven, gives this order in a loud voice. Later, Daniel explains that the tree represents the king himself: his power protected many, but his pride would be brought low until he acknowledged that God rules over all kingdoms.

For today: whatever we have, whether work, talent or influence, is a gift and not a credit to ourselves. We can use it to give shade and food to others, and to thank God with humility, for he raises up and can also bring low.
exp.7:17:
Daniel tells us that while the angel Gabriel was speaking to him, he fell into a deep sleep with his face to the ground. Then the angel touched him, helped him to his feet, and Daniel was able to stand again.

Daniel is the one speaking. He has just seen a very powerful vision, and Gabriel comes to explain it to him. Daniel had already bowed down in amazement, and now he is nearly without strength. Gabriel lifts him up so he can listen and understand what follows about the future, which begins with the ram, identified as the kings of Media and Persia.

For today: when we feel weak or overwhelmed by what God shows us or by what we are living through, we can remember that He sustains and strengthens us. We can come near with humility, ask Him for help, and rise to listen to His Word.
exp.10:9:
His sons will stir up strife and gather a great army. One of them will advance forcefully, sweeping through like a flood, and will again carry the battle as far as his fortress.

Here the angel speaks, revealing to Daniel what is to come. It is a prophecy about the wars between the king of the north and the king of the south. Many believe it refers to the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms, which arose after Alexander the Great. The details of who these kings are are interpreted in various ways, but the central message is clear: God knows history.

For today: even though the world may seem full of conflict and human ambition, you can trust that God remains in control. Rest in Him when the news troubles you, and seek peace in your relationships.
exp.4:16:
Daniel tells King Belshazzar that he does not want his gifts. "You may keep your gifts for yourself" means "keep your gifts," and "give your rewards to someone else" means "give them to someone else." Even so, Daniel promises to read the inscription and explain its meaning.

During a banquet, a hand appeared and wrote on the wall, and the king was terrified. The wise men of Babylon could not interpret the message, so they called for Daniel. He speaks freely because he does not serve the king for money or power, but serves God. Soon he will remind Belshazzar of what happened to Nebuchadnezzar.

Today we can learn that God's truth cannot be bought or sold. When we have to speak or act with honesty, it is good to do so without being moved by rewards, pressure, or fear of losing something.
exp.2:21:
This verse tells us that the king's command was so urgent, and the furnace so hot, that the fiery flames killed the men who carried up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. The word "urgent" here means that the command demanded speed. The phrase "carried up" means they had lifted and carried the men to throw them in.

The narrator of the book of Daniel relates what happened after Nebuchadnezzar, in his rage, ordered the furnace heated more than usual because the three young Jewish men would not worship the golden statue. The soldiers died, but the three young men fell into the fire, and what follows shows that God took care of them.

For today: sometimes anger and haste lead to harm, even to one's own people. Before acting in anger, it is wise to stop and think. And if you suffer for remaining faithful to God, remember that danger does not have the final word, for He can be with you in the midst of the trial.
exp.2:14:
Nebuchadnezzar gives three young men one last chance. If they bow down and worship the statue when they hear the music, they will be spared. If they refuse, they will be thrown at once into a blazing fiery furnace. The instruments named are the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, and pipes.

The one speaking is the king of Babylon, angry because Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, Jews who served in his government, would not worship his golden statue. He feels so powerful that he defies God: "Then what god will be able to deliver you from my hands?"

Today too there are pressures to give in on what we believe, out of fear of losing something. This passage invites us to decide ahead of time to be faithful to God, trusting Him no matter the threats or the cost.
exp.7:5:
He says that the male goat, the animal with a notable horn, rushed at the ram with two horns, the one that was standing beside the canal. He did it with furious power, that is, with enormous rage and force. The description of him rushing at the ram portrays a swift and violent attack.

Daniel speaks, telling of a vision he received. Later the angel Gabriel explains that the ram represents the kings of Media and Persia, and the male goat the kingdom of Greece (Daniel 8:20-21). Many understand the great horn to be Alexander the Great, which the text suggests, though it does not name him directly. The vision shows that God knows the course of empires.

For today: human powers may seem invincible, but none lasts forever. You can rest in the fact that God still governs history, so do not place your security in what is falling apart, but in Him.
exp.6:27:
Here Daniel says that the verse of the vision has come to an end. The word translated here means an account or a message, and the end of the verse is the end of what the angel told him. Daniel admits that his thoughts troubled him greatly and that his face turned pale. Even so, he kept the matter to himself, meaning he held onto what he had heard and thought it over in silence.

The same Daniel speaks, a man who had just seen four beasts representing kingdoms, a judgment in heaven, and an everlasting kingdom given to the saints of the Most High. The images were powerful, and the interpretation spoke of terrible powers and a final judgment. That is why he was deeply shaken, though there was also hope.

For today: when something in God's Word unsettles you or you do not fully understand it, you do not have to resolve it right away. You can keep it in your heart, pray, and meditate on it calmly, trusting that God's kingdom endures.
exp.5:19:
King Darius came near the den and called out to Daniel in a voice full of anguish. He asked whether Daniel's God, the one he serves faithfully, had been able to rescue him from the lions.

The king called out in a distressed voice, and he hurried to the den. Here is what the wording means: "in a voice of anguish" means he cried out in deep distress; and "the den" is the pit where the lions were kept.

Here the king speaks. He had signed a decree that, through the scheming of other officials, led to Daniel being thrown into the den for praying to God. The king did not want this, and he spent the night without eating, without music, and without sleep. His question shows fear and a little hope. We do not know how much he believed at that moment, but he calls God "living."

For today: serving God faithfully, even when it costs us, can be a quiet witness. Others are watching us, and sometimes in their hardest moments they remember how we lived.
exp.2:10:
This verse repeats the penalty of the king's law: whoever did not bow down and worship the golden statue when the music sounded would be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. The phrase "does not fall down and worship" describes the act of bowing down, and "blazing" describes the furnace being lit.

The speakers are some Chaldeans, officials or wise men of the kingdom, who address King Nebuchadnezzar. They remind him of his own law in order to accuse Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, three Jews with authority in Babylon. The accusation probably contains envy, although the text does not say so in so many words.

For today: the pressure to obey others against our conscience can be strong. Before the difficult moment arrives, it is wise to decide in prayer that God holds first place, and to ask him for the courage to be faithful to him with respect and firmness.
exp.3:5:
Nebuchadnezzar gives an order: all the wise men of Babylon are to be brought before him. He wants them to interpret the dream that frightened him. The phrase "I issued a decree" refers to the order he gave, and "interpret the dream" means explaining what the dream means.

The speaker is King Nebuchadnezzar, in a letter that tells what he went through. He was calm and prosperous, but a dream filled him with fear. As was customary in ancient courts, he first turned to his advisers and specialists. The verses that follow show that they were unable to give him the answer.

For today: when something troubles us, we usually look for help in the sources we know best. Yet sometimes they fall short. We can bring our worries to God in prayer and seek wise counsel from people who know Him, trusting that He gives the light we need.
exp.6:4:
It says Daniel saw another beast, a second one, that looked like a bear. It was raised up on one of its sides, and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth. Then it was told, "Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!"

Daniel himself recounts this vision he had at night. There are four beasts, which represent kingdoms that would dominate the world. Many believe the bear is Medo-Persia, though others propose different identifications. The three ribs could be conquests, but this is not certain. The underlying message is that God knows the course of empires, and He announced it to His people to give them hope.

Human powers may seem enormous and devouring, but they do not have the last word. When news from the world frightens you, remember that God governs history. Rest in Him and keep doing good with confidence.
exp.5:0:
King Darius decided it made good sense to appoint one hundred and twenty satraps to rule throughout his kingdom. The verse says it "pleased" him, meaning he judged the plan to be fitting, and the word "appoint" simply means he chose and placed these rulers in their posts.

The narrator of the book of Daniel tells this account after the fall of Babylon. Darius organizes the government so that the kingdom runs in an orderly way. Scholars do not agree on who this Darius exactly was, and that question is still debated. What the text highlights is that, within this new system, Daniel stands out for his character.

For today: Darius sought order and accountability to avoid losses. Let us do the same in our work or family: let us be responsible and honest, even when no one is watching us, as Daniel was.
exp.5:14:
They say that Daniel's enemies came back to press the king. They reminded him that, by the law of the Medes and Persians, no decree or ordinance the king had established could be changed. The idea of a decree being changed or revoked is what the law forbade.

These were the high officials who had tricked Darius into signing a ban on praying to anyone other than the king. Daniel kept praying to God, and they accused him. The king wanted to save him, but these men used the law to force his hand. The text tells us how rigid that law was; we don't need to add more historical details.

For today: be careful with decisions made out of pride or in a hurry, because they can later bind us. And if you find yourself called to be faithful to God under pressure, remember that Daniel trusted God without relying on the way out that the men offered.
exp.10:21:
Daniel 11:22 says that a flood of forces will be swept away before the powerful king and destroyed, along with a prince of the covenant. The great armies are pictured as a flood that is overwhelmed and broken before him.

An angel reveals to Daniel what will happen to the kingdoms of the north and the south after Alexander the Great. The "vile" person in the context is usually identified with Antiochus IV Epiphanes. About the "prince of the covenant" there are several views: some think of the high priest Onias III, others of an allied leader, and others see a look forward to Christ. There is no single certain answer.

For today: human powers may seem unstoppable, but they do not have the final word. God continues to govern history, so we can rest in Him when the world feels unstable.
exp.10:14:
This verse says that the king of the North will come, build up a siege ramp against the walls, and capture a well-defended city. The forces of the South will not stand, and even their best troops will not be able to resist. A siege ramp is a raised earthen structure built up against the walls so that attackers can reach the top, and a fortified city is one that has strong defenses.

An angel speaks to Daniel and announces, in great detail, the conflicts between two kingdoms that surrounded Israel. Many scholars see in this the wars between the Seleucid kings (north) and the Ptolemaic kings (south), though not all agree on identifying every event. The purpose was to show that history does not escape God's control.

For today: when the world seems dominated by powers that no one can stop, remember that no human force is final. Trust in God, who sustains his people and knows the end.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that the king of the south will invade the realm of the king of the north, but afterward he will return to his own land. The phrase "invade the realm" is the reader's wording here, and it shows that the king of the south is entering his enemy's territory, and that he will not stay there.

The one speaking is the heavenly messenger who explains to Daniel what is to come. Many scholars see here the wars between the kings of Egypt (south) and of Syria (north) after Alexander the Great, but not all agree on the exact names. The purpose is to show that God knows the future and sustains his people.

For today: human powers rise and fall, and none lasts forever. You can rest in the knowledge that God still rules, even when the news of the world troubles you.
exp.2:23:
Daniel 3:24 says that King Nebuchadnezzar suddenly jumped up in amazement. He asked his advisers, "Did we not throw three men, firmly bound, into the fire?" They replied, "Certainly, O king."

The king speaks with his advisers. He himself had ordered Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego thrown into the furnace for refusing to worship his statue. But when he looked into the furnace he saw something he did not expect: the men were walking free and unharmed. He wants to confirm what had happened. The verses that follow speak of a fourth figure; the Bible does not say clearly who he was, and it has been interpreted in several ways.

For today: when you are called to remain faithful to God in the middle of a trial, remember that He can be with you in the fire, and that your faithfulness can show others His power.
exp.1:42:
This verse says that the kingdom represented by the feet of the statue will have iron mixed with clay. A "potsherd" is a broken piece of baked clay. The verse speaks of the peoples mixing with one another, yet they will not hold together, just as iron does not mix with clay. Their mixing does not truly join them, so there will be no real unity in that kingdom.

Daniel speaks to King Nebuchadnezzar and explains to him the dream of the great statue. God gave Daniel the interpretation. Christians often see here a final, divided kingdom, although there are different views about exactly which empire is meant. What is clear is that the text announces that every human kingdom is fragile, and that God will raise up an eternal kingdom.

For today: do not put your trust in human powers that seem firm but do not last. Rest in the kingdom of God, which does not end, and seek to live in unity and truth with others.

sum.2: King Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden statue and commanded that everyone bow down to it whenever they heard the music, or else they would be thrown into a blazing furnace. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused, trusting that God could rescue them, and even if He did not, they would not worship any other god. They were thrown into the furnace, but God protected them, and the king acknowledged His power.
sum.9: Daniel spends three weeks in mourning and fasting, and beside the Hidekel River he sees a glorious being who leaves him without strength. The messenger lifts him up, tells him not to be afraid because God heard his prayer from the very first day, and explains that he was delayed by a spiritual struggle in which Michael helped him. Then he strengthens Daniel to receive what is to come for his people.
sum.11: In Daniel 12, a time of great distress is announced, during which God's people will be delivered. Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will wake up, some to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting disgrace. Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the sky, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever. Daniel is told to seal up the book until the time of the end, since he does not fully understand everything, and he is promised rest and that he will receive his allotted place at the end of the days.
sum.6: Daniel dreams of four beasts coming up out of the sea. The last one is very terrifying and has a horn that speaks with arrogance and persecutes the holy ones. Then he sees God, the Ancient of Days, take his seat to judge, and one like a son of man receives an eternal kingdom. An angel explains that in the end the kingdom will be given to the holy people of the Most High.
sum.7: Daniel sees a ram with two horns (representing Media and Persia) that is defeated by a goat with one large horn (the king of Javan, or Greece). That large horn is broken, and four horns come up in its place. From one of them comes a small horn that attacks the holy people and the sanctuary, but in the end it will be broken, without human hands. Gabriel explains the vision, and Daniel is left sick and astonished.
sum.1: Nebuchadnezzar has a dream that troubles him, and he demands that his wise men tell him both the dream and its meaning. They cannot do it. Daniel prays together with his friends, God reveals the mystery to him, and he explains the statue and the stone that will become an everlasting kingdom. The king acknowledges God and honors Daniel.
sum.4: King Belshazzar held a great feast and, in his pride, ordered the sacred vessels from the temple to be brought out, and he and his guests drank from them while praising false gods. A mysterious hand appeared and wrote on the wall, and Daniel explained that God had measured the kingdom of Belshazzar and given it to the Medes and Persians. That very night the king was killed, and the lesson taught is that God humbles the proud.
sum.8: Daniel read in the book of Jeremiah that the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolation were nearly complete. He turned to the Lord in prayer and fasting, confessing the sins of his people and asking for forgiveness, not because of anything they had earned, but because of God's mercy. While he was still praying, the angel Gabriel came to him and announced seventy weeks decreed for his people, which would bring the coming of the Messiah, his death, and the destruction of the city. Interpreters disagree about the details of these weeks.
sum.5: Daniel is a faithful official, and his enemies, out of envy, trick King Darius into signing a law that forbids prayer to anyone other than the king. Daniel keeps on praying to God and is thrown into the lions' den, but God sends his angel and protects him. Then the king declares that Daniel's God is the living God.
sum.0: Nebuchadnezzar conquers Jerusalem and takes young men from Judah to Babylon, including Daniel and his three friends, to be trained for service to the king. Daniel decides not to defile himself with the king's food, and God honors his faithfulness by giving him and his friends good health, wisdom, and favor before the king.
sum.3: King Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree that is cut down, and Daniel explains that the tree represents the king himself, who will live like an animal for seven periods of time because of his pride. A year later, while boasting about Babylon, the punishment comes to pass. When he acknowledges the Most High, he regains his sanity and his kingdom, and he praises God, who can humble the proud.
sum.10: A heavenly messenger reveals to Daniel a lengthy prophecy about wars and alliances between the kings of the south and the north, with deceptions, downfalls, and a proud king who persecutes the covenant people and desecrates the sanctuary. Those who know their God remain steadfast, and everything takes place within a time limit set by God.
